bullets: The newly released BEHAVIOR-Spatial benchmark tests whether spatial answers from vision-language models—systems that interpret images and text—carry over to vision-language-action behavior in simulated robotics. Its components separate answering spatial questions from predicting and performing actions, rather than treating visual understanding as a proxy for embodied capability. Why it matters: If you are selecting a model for robotics, this design lets you test whether high question-answering scores translate into action-relevant spatial competence before committing to physical trials. Evidence: E009. High confidence.

The new Tech Graphics Benchmark publishes its prompts, generated images and manifests, and raw human ratings as separate linked datasets. Generation identities are opaque and shuffled, and annotators do not see the model identity until after saving a rating, providing a concrete blind-review design for judging text, arrows, and layout in generated technical graphics. Why it matters: If you compare image generators for documentation or diagrams, the separated artifacts support rerunning the analysis and reduce the chance that model recognition influences human ratings. Evidence: E010, E040, E045. High confidence.

The newly released MIMIC-IV-Ext-DischargeBench provides 320 curated hospitalization cases for pre-deployment evaluation of large language model discharge educators through patient simulation. Cases cover 16 diagnostic groupings, combine structured records with discharge notes, and were manually reviewed against source notes. Why it matters: If you are evaluating patient-facing discharge assistance, this artifact supports testing across diagnoses and care-plan details before deployment instead of relying only on generic medical question answering. Evidence: E016. High confidence.

The new CLAP audio-text retrieval benchmark pins its inputs and protocol, publishes per-query results, and uses paired confidence intervals when comparing fused and unfused checkpoints. Its reported results distinguish an inconclusive difference on AudioCaps from a directional difference on Clotho, while explicitly noting that practical equivalence was not established. Why it matters: If you are choosing an audio-text retrieval model, this package supports decisions based on uncertainty and paired examples rather than a small difference between aggregate scores. Evidence: E029. High confidence.

The new benchgap reproduction package freezes an October 8 snapshot of a benchmark service that otherwise refreshes daily. It separates 6,180 measured scores from 14,314 calibrated estimates, retains provenance, and pins the processing pipeline used for 520 models and 359 benchmark versions. Why it matters: If you use inferred scores to fill gaps in model comparisons, the frozen state makes the measured-versus-estimated boundary auditable and prevents later service updates from silently changing a published analysis. Evidence: E021. High confidence.

The newly released dental implant benchmark groups its fixed five-fold splits by source radiograph rather than by cropped implant image. Its 3,276 crops come from 1,011 source radiographs, so related crops remain together instead of leaking across training and test partitions. Why it matters: If you evaluate medical-image classifiers on derived crops, this split design provides a direct check against inflated results caused by near-related images appearing on both sides of the evaluation. Evidence: E011. High confidence.

The new Model Context Protocol multi-agent file-exchange benchmark records 180 workflow runs and evaluates transport latency, scoped-link handoffs, quarantine scanning, and file-reuse ratios across several agent environments. Model Context Protocol is a standard for connecting AI applications to tools and data sources. Why it matters: If you are choosing infrastructure for agents that exchange files, this artifact broadens evaluation beyond task completion to operational handoffs and security-related checks, although the captured description does not establish independent validation. Evidence: E001, E002. Medium confidence.

The newly released AutoResearch-MLIP protocol evaluates an autonomous agent over 40 generations of scientific-model development. The agent proposes, implements, and tests machine-learned interatomic potentials—models of forces between atoms—while structured design records and prior outcomes guide later iterations. Why it matters: If you build autonomous research agents, this protocol shifts the evaluation decision from judging one final model to examining whether feedback produces a traceable sequence of scientific design changes. Evidence: E006. Medium confidence.
bullets_zh: 新发布的 BEHAVIOR-Spatial 基准测试旨在检验视觉语言模型（即能够理解图像和文本的系统）给出的空间答案，能否迁移到模拟机器人中的视觉-语言-动作行为。其组成部分将空间问题回答与动作预测及执行分开评估，而不是将视觉理解视为具身能力的替代指标。Why it matters: 如果你正在为机器人选择模型，这种设计可让你在投入实体试验之前，检验较高的问题回答得分能否转化为与动作相关的空间能力。Evidence: E009. High confidence.

新的 Tech Graphics Benchmark 将其提示词、生成图像及清单和原始人工评分分别发布为相互关联的数据集。生成系统的身份被隐藏并随机打乱，标注者在保存评分后才能看到模型身份，从而为评判生成技术图形中的文本、箭头和布局提供了具体的盲审设计。Why it matters: 如果你要比较用于文档或图表的图像生成器，这些彼此分离的材料有助于重新运行分析，并降低模型辨识影响人工评分的可能性。Evidence: E010, E040, E045. High confidence.

新发布的 MIMIC-IV-Ext-DischargeBench 提供了 320 个经过整理的住院病例，用于通过患者模拟，在部署前评估大语言模型出院教育工具。这些病例涵盖 16 个诊断类别，将结构化病历与出院记录结合起来，并已依据源记录进行人工复核。Why it matters: 如果你正在评估面向患者的出院辅助工具，该材料支持在部署前跨诊断类别和护理计划细节开展测试，而不是仅依赖通用医疗问答。Evidence: E016. High confidence.

新的 CLAP 音频-文本检索基准固定了输入和评估协议，发布逐查询结果，并在比较融合与未融合的检查点时使用配对置信区间。其报告结果区分了 AudioCaps 上无法得出结论的差异与 Clotho 上具有方向性的差异，同时明确指出尚未确立实际等效性。Why it matters: 如果你正在选择音频-文本检索模型，该评估包支持基于不确定性和配对样本做出决策，而不是依据汇总得分之间的微小差异。Evidence: E029. High confidence.

新的 benchgap 复现包冻结了一个原本每日刷新的基准服务在 October 8 的快照。它将 6,180 个实测得分与 14,314 个校准估计值分开，保留数据来源信息，并固定了用于 520 个模型和 359 个基准版本的处理流水线。Why it matters: 如果你使用推断得分来填补模型比较中的空缺，这一冻结状态可使实测值与估计值之间的界限可供审计，并防止该服务后续更新在未被察觉的情况下改变已发布的分析。Evidence: E021. High confidence.

新发布的牙科植入体基准按源 X 光片而非裁剪后的植入体图像，对固定的五折数据划分进行分组。其 3,276 个裁剪图像来自 1,011 张源 X 光片，因此相关裁剪图像会保留在同一分组中，而不会泄漏到训练分区和测试分区两侧。Why it matters: 如果你在派生的裁剪图像上评估医学图像分类器，这种划分设计可直接检查评估两侧出现近似相关图像所导致的结果虚高问题。Evidence: E011. High confidence.

新的 Model Context Protocol 多智能体文件交换基准记录了 180 次工作流运行，并在多个智能体环境中评估传输延迟、限定作用域的链接交接、隔离扫描和文件复用率。Model Context Protocol 是一种将 AI 应用连接到工具和数据源的标准。Why it matters: 如果你正在为交换文件的智能体选择基础设施，该材料将评估范围从任务完成扩展到操作交接和安全相关检查，但所记录的描述并未证实存在独立验证。Evidence: E001, E002. Medium confidence.

新发布的 AutoResearch-MLIP 协议在科学模型开发的 40 代迭代中评估自主智能体。该智能体提出、实现并测试机器学习原子间势，即描述原子间作用力的模型，同时利用结构化设计记录和先前结果指导后续迭代。Why it matters: 如果你正在构建自主研究智能体，该协议将评估重点从判断一个最终模型，转向考察反馈是否产生了可追溯的科学设计变更序列。Evidence: E006. Medium confidence.

evidence_items.summary: Background and purpose: Radiotherapy planning agents based on large language models (LLMs) decide when to submit a plan or request review but are evaluated mainly by dose. This study developed OpenGray, a benchmark of planning tasks with known correct decisions. Materials and methods: OpenGray adds tasks with known answers to the OpenKBP-Opt head-and-neck dataset, including two contradictions with dose goals proven incompatible and a feasible control with a stored plan meeting every hard goal. Four systems, from a rule-based planning script to a full LLM agent, were evaluated on 30 patients, the LLM-based ones with a commercial (Terra) and a local (Ministral 3 8B) LLM. Decisions, achieved dose, problem recognition, and technical failures were recorded and also read from logs of 39 stereotactic radiosurgery runs of SAGE, a clinical LLM agent. Results: With Terra, the script preceded by an LLM review and the full agent had decision accuracies of 95.4% and 92.1%, respectively, yet escalated only 50% (95% confidence interval, 25-75%) and 25% (10-40%) of overlap contradictions, which required arithmetic on the anatomy. All four systems submitted every feasible control, but 24% of these plans missed a hard goal that the stored plan had met. In four SAGE runs, one goal failed at every attempt; the agent identified it in every reply but had no action for stopping. Conclusions: Favorable aggregate scores concealed specific decision failures. Planning agents should be evaluated on their decisions as well as their dose and given an explicit action for stopping and requesting review.
evidence_items.title: OpenGray: a benchmark for evaluating the decisions of radiotherapy planning agents

evidence_items.summary: Claims about the cognitive capabilities of large language models are typically tested by translating behavioral paradigms into text prompts, bypassing the visual interfaces and time pressure through which human participants actually engage with experiments. At the same time, AI agents can now complete online behavioral tasks and produce human-like data, which raises concerns that online datasets in the social and behavioral sciences are increasingly open to contamination. We introduce CogArena, a benchmark of ten experimental paradigms from the social and behavioral sciences. Agents complete the experiments through a standard web browser, working with the same visual stimuli and response interfaces that online participants use. A three-level scoring procedure evaluates whether the agent completed the task, how accurately it performed, and whether its data show the behavioral signatures each paradigm reliably produces in people. Across four multimodal models, each run ten times per task, we find that finishing an experiment and reproducing its signatures are different things. Many sessions did not finish, and those that did reproduced some signatures reliably and others not at all. CogArena provides the tasks, scoring code, and a public leaderboard for new submissions.
evidence_items.title: CogArena: Benchmarking Multimodal Agents on Interactive Behavioral Experiments

evidence_items.summary: Derivative-free optimization (DFO) addresses problems where derivatives are unavailable or costly to obtain. This setting often arises in simulation-based and experimental applications, where evaluating the black-box objective can itself be costly. Thus, it remains a central challenge in DFO to effectively exploit accumulated observations to select informative evaluation points under a limited budget. In this light, we introduce the NextEval solver, an agent-based DFO solver, which integrates the capabilities of a large language model (LLM) to guide the sequential selection of evaluation points. Specifically, we establish a system that combines an LLM agent with a numerical environment. The environment provides tools for analyzing past evaluations and executing numerical methods, while maintaining a shared evaluation history and method-specific state to support continuation across method switches. Using observations and tool feedback, the LLM agent selects tools, configures their parameters, and allocates the evaluation budget, while numerical methods compute and evaluate candidate points. Building on this system, we also introduce NextEval Bench, a benchmark protocol for comparing agent configurations on shared DFO tasks using the same numerical tools under matched evaluation budgets and information constraints. Numerical results on low-dimensional DFO problems demonstrate that the NextEval solver outperforms the state-of-the-art DFO baselines in function-evaluation efficiency.
evidence_items.title: NextEval: An Agent-Based Solver and Benchmark for Derivative-Free Optimization

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Recent AI systems can autonomously execute scientific workflows and empirical software tasks. We investigate whether an autonomous agent can use evaluation feedback to iteratively develop a scientific model. To address this question, we developed AutoResearch-MLIP, a research protocol in which the agent follows predefined instructions to propose, implement, and evaluate MLIP designs, with outcomes carried forward to guide subsequent iterations. Starting from a simple pair-distance MLIP, each generation selects a parent model by balancing exploration and exploitation, while structured design records guide subsequent proposals. Across 40 generations, the agent explores MLIP designs spanning local message passing, radial representations, scalar-vector states, body-order terms, residual readouts, long-range-inspired terms, and periodic image-offset graph construction. The final G40 model is competitive with established MLIP baselines in post hoc benchmarks. These results show that, within predefined rules, an autonomous agent can use evaluation feedback to iteratively improve MLIP implementations.

evidence_items.summary: Perceiving human body motion is critical for multimodal systems that understand and assist people. Yet current evaluations of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) largely focus on objects, scenes, and coarse actions, leaving their ability to reason about the body itself poorly assessed. This is especially challenging from the egocentric perspective, in which the body is only partially visible and motion must be inferred from occluded and temporally distributed cues. We introduce SOMA, a benchmark for fine-grained body-motion understanding from egocentric video, comprising 1,632 human-verified questions across three capability axes: body configuration, motion dynamics, and temporal reasoning. We evaluate 37 leading closed-source, open-source, and specialized egocentric MLLMs, complemented by an extensive human evaluation. We find that humans also find this task difficult from video alone (68.5% accuracy), yet clearly outperform the strongest MLLM (Qwen3.6-27B), which reaches 50.0% zero-shot accuracy. Our error analysis shows that MLLMs often misread the wearer's own body, misjudge events in time, and are prone to biases such as favoring the right hand or under-counting repetitions. To narrow the gap to human performance and support further progress, we introduce a training dataset of aligned video, body motion, and language supervision, and a multimodal baseline that jointly learns from these modalities. By identifying common failure modes and missing capabilities in current MLLMs, we hope SOMA will inspire future research on body-motion understanding and multimodal reasoning. Full benchmark, training data, and code will be released at: https://cnai.epfl.ch/soma
evidence_items.title: SOMA: A Benchmark for Fine-Grained Egocentric Behavior and Body-Motion Understanding

evidence_items.summary: Synthetic medical tabular data generation has become essential for developing and validating computer-based medical systems (CBMSs) when real clinical data is restricted due to privacy, ethical, or data availability limitations. Existing probabilistic and deep generative models often lack interpretability and fail to preserve clinically meaningful dependencies, limiting their suitability for safety-critical applications. This paper proposes a novel application of Fuzzy Cognitive Maps (FCMs) in a framework for synthetic medical tabular data generation with explicit causality and privacy preservation. Clinical features are described using linguistically interpretable fuzzy sets, and inter-feature dependencies are encoded as FCM edge weights computed from fuzzy set intersections. Synthetic patient records are generated by propagating randomly initialized linguistic activation vectors through the FCM until convergence, followed by defuzzification to produce clinically coherent numerical values. The approach natively handles mixed data types, and domain constraints common in health records. Experimental evaluation on UCI medical benchmark datasets demonstrates competitive performance under a Train-on-Synthetic-Test-on-Real (TSTR) protocol. The proposed method achieves accuracy of up to 0.81 and AUROC of up to 0.90 on the Heart Disease dataset, matching or exceeding TVAE and Gaussian Copula baselines while running exclusively on CPU. Fidelity metrics including KS Complement (up to 0.91) and Correlation Similarity (up to 0.95) confirm strong statistical coherence, and DCR Baseline Protection scores consistently exceed those of TVAE, confirming adequate privacy guarantees. These results demonstrate that causally grounded, interpretable fuzzy modeling offers a computationally efficient and transparent alternative to deep generative models for trustworthy synthetic data generation in CBMSs.
evidence_items.title: Interpretable Synthetic Medical Tabular Data Generation for Clinical Decision Support Using Fuzzy Cognitive Maps

evidence_items.summary: Parametric knowledge in large language models (LLMs) is a cornerstone of their success, yet remains poorly understood. Existing knowledge benchmarks typically rely on predefined questions (e.g., "What is the birth date of M.L. King?"), evaluating only knowledge that benchmark designers explicitly choose to query, a problematic availability bias. In this paper, we introduce open knowledge evaluation, a new paradigm for benchmarking the stated knowledge of LLMs. Instead of asking narrow questions, it evaluates models on the knowledge they choose to surface in response to open-ended elicitation prompts (e.g., "Tell me everything you know about M.L. King"). This shifts the focus from predefined answer retrieval toward characterizing the knowledge models naturally express. We instantiate this paradigm with BeQu (Beyond Questions), a benchmark of 10,000 entities paired with reference corpora for statement verification. Using BeQu, we evaluate a broad range of language models and analyze the effects of reasoning effort, model scale, prompt format, and knowledge domain. Data and leaderboard are available on this work's GitHub repository and at ANONYMIZED.
evidence_items.title: Beyond Questions: Evaluating the Stated Knowledge of LLMs

evidence_items.summary: Benchmark researchers and developers of large language models (LLMs) and other AI systems need to find relevant evaluations, locate their benchmark datasets and code, and understand the settings behind reported scores. We present Benchmark Radar, a living database and search engine for retrieval and discovery of AI benchmarks, covering LLM evaluation, agentic and tool-use benchmarks, coding, reasoning, safety, and domain-specific evaluations. The system combines daily discovery of benchmark papers, repositories, datasets, and releases with a searchable benchmark catalog, mentions in model cards and technical reports, and score histories. It retains source identities and citations so readers can inspect candidate benchmarks and their evaluation evidence. Daily discovery draws on 37 sources: 13 direct connectors and 24 first-party research and engineering feeds. The catalog contains 1,283 source records drawn from 4 benchmark catalogs and 12,916 numeric observations on 790 records. We describe collection and retrieval, audit the full catalog, and examine benchmark saturation, adoption trends, and the limits of score comparisons. A worked example walks through a complete prior-art search, showing how to query the catalog and inspect benchmark evidence when designing a new evaluation. We release the web dashboard with a benchmark leaderboard, a Pareto frontier view of score against measured use, saturation and trend views, daily feeds, downloadable evidence, a command-line interface (CLI) for offline queries, and reproducible analysis.
evidence_items.title: Benchmark Radar: A Living Database and Search Engine for AI Benchmarks and Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: ZJU BESS Time-Series, Semantic Reports, and Downstream Benchmark Suite Overview This dataset suite provides large-scale, real-world operational time series from a lithium-ion battery energy storage system (BESS), together with structured, human-readable operational reports and three ready-to-use downstream benchmarks. Unlike battery datasets designed for a single prediction target, this release connects three levels of battery intelligence: 1. Raw multivariate operation data from 28 battery modules; 2. Structured semantic reports describing module- and cell-level temporal behavior; 3. Task-specific labels for SOC prediction, operational-anomaly analysis, and charge/discharge decision support. The suite is intended to support research at the intersection of battery management, multivariate time-series analysis, explainable AI, and large language models (LLMs). It enables both conventional numerical modeling and emerging time-series-to-language research without requiring users to reconstruct benchmark samples from the full operational archive. The operational records cover a six-month period from December 1, 2023 to May 31, 2024 . Measurements are sampled at one-minute intervals. All public identifiers are anonymized and independently assigned within the released datasets.
evidence_items.title: ZJU-o and Downstream Benchmark Datasets: Battery Operational Time Series and Semantic Reports for LLM-Assisted O&M

evidence_items.summary: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) derives its learning signal from binary rewards via on-policy exploration and becomes a powerful paradigm for improving the reasoning of large language models. Yet it faces a learning cliff on problems beyond model's current ability: when every rollout fails, the samples reveal nothing about a correct solution, and group-relative estimators (e.g., GRPO, RLOO) collapse the update to zero advantage. Expert trajectories offer a remedy, but they are incompatible with the current policy and often lie in the student's low-probability regions, so the surviving updates demand large parameter shifts and decay into surface-level imitation rather than transferable reasoning. We argue that a useful learning signal on hard problems must be both verifiably correct and sufficiently compatible with the current policy. We propose Policy-Compatible Reinforcement Learning (PICO), which performs distribution-constrained joint decoding: expert data guides decoding at the token level while preserving the student's relative token probabilities, and a dynamic top-k mechanism confines the sampling distribution under a finite divergence budget, yielding trajectories that are verified and policy-compatible by construction. These trajectories are optimized jointly with on-policy rollouts under a mixed-behavior objective that mitigates their distribution mismatch via importance sampling. Experiments across reasoning diverse datasets and agentic benchmarks demonstrate that PICO consistently outperforms standard RLVR and prior off-policy baselines.
evidence_items.title: When All Rollouts Fail: Policy-Compatible Joint Decoding for Hard-Problem Reasoning

evidence_items.summary: Speaking-style captioning (SSC) aims to generate natural language descriptions of how speech is delivered, capturing paralinguistic attributes such as vocal timbre, prosody, and expressivity. Many downstream applications, including conversational AI agents, controllable speech generation, and large-scale audio annotation, require dimension-specific style captions that describe targeted aspects of speech (e.g., speaker traits, emotion, or delivery style), rather than a single undifferentiated description. However, existing work lacks a unified formulation for controllable speaking-style captioning. We address this gap by formulating SSC as an instruction-following audio-language task, where explicit instructions specify the speaking-style dimensions to be described. We introduce StyleInstructCaps, the first standardized benchmark for controllable speaking-style captioning in audio-language models. StyleInstructCaps provides a dataset and evaluation framework that measures metadata groundedness, hallucination, instruction-following ability, generalization to unseen instructions and audio datasets, and speaker-style consistency. Across nine state-of-the-art audio-language models, we find that strong instruction-following ability does not necessarily imply grounded speaking-style understanding, and that SSC-specific instruction-diverse training substantially improves groundedness, controllability, and speaker consistency.
evidence_items.title: A Benchmark for Controllable Speaking-Style Captioning in Audio-Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Web-scale 3D asset collections are abundant but rarely ready to ingest without cleanup, suffering from arbitrary metric scaling, incorrect pivots, brittle geometry, and incomplete textures, defects that limit their use in embodied AI, robotics, and spatial computing. We present AmaraSpatial-10K, a dataset of 10,071 synthetic 3D assets standardised for direct ingestion. Each asset ships as a metric-scaled, deterministically anchored .glb with separated PBR maps, a convex collision hull, a paired reference image, and multi-sentence text metadata. Alongside the dataset we introduce a reusable evaluation suite for 3D asset banks, a continuous Scale Plausibility Score (SPS), a keyword-based Concept Density metric, anchor-error auditing, and a cross-modal CLIP coherence protocol, and apply it to AmaraSpatial-10K alongside matched subsets of Objaverse, HSSD, ABO, and GSO. We check the annotations independently of the LLM/VLM pipeline that produced them: measured ABO object heights fall inside our scale intervals 88.7-90.7% of the time, and three non-author raters auditing a stratified sample of 314 assets judge 95.5% plausibly scaled and 99.7% correctly anchored. AmaraSpatial-10K improves CLIP Recall@5 by 3.4x over Objaverse (0.612 vs. 0.181, median rank 267 -> 3), achieves a 99.1% settling-stability rate under Habitat-Sim in static placement and collision tests, with ~20x lower per-load wall time, and as a drop-in Holodeck asset bank improves planned-scale matching and is preferred by blinded human raters in 27 of 40 paired scenes. Controlled ablations on the same asset bank attribute the retrieval gain to description richness.
evidence_items.title: AmaraSpatial-10K: A Spatially and Semantically Aligned 3D Dataset for Spatial Computing and Embodied AI

evidence_items.summary: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) describe satellite images fluently but struggle with the quantitative spatial reasoning that remote sensing (RS) analysts perform routinely, such as counting buildings, measuring forest area in hectares and computing distances in meters. We introduce SQuID (Satellite Quantitative Intelligence Dataset), a benchmark of 2,000 questions over 587 images from four sources at 0.3 to 1.0 m ground sampling distance, covering 24 question types in three difficulty tiers. Answers are computed from curated segmentation masks or, for 50 questions, from human consensus, and numeric answers are scored against tolerance ranges informed by human annotations. SQuID also releases the reference masks behind its answers, so that modular systems can be evaluated using reference rather than predicted masks, and 75,687 training question-answer pairs on disjoint images (SQuID-Train). Among 15 evaluated systems, the best zero-shot end-to-end VLM reaches 28.1%, and RS-specialized VLMs score lower. As a baseline, we propose QASR (Quantitative Agentic Spatial Reasoning), in which an LLM writes a program that segments the image and measures the masks with geometric operators. QASR reaches 42.0%. On the 1,950 mask-derived questions, running its programs on the reference masks instead of predicted masks raises accuracy from 42.2% to 82.6%, so segmentation is its main source of error. Fine-tuning Qwen2.5-VL-7B on SQuID-Train raises its accuracy from 16.1% to 40.7%, close to QASR. Multi-condition questions (Tier 3) remain the hardest in every setting, at 62.0% for QASR with reference masks and 13.2% after fine-tuning. These results leave clear room for end-to-end models that learn metric spatial reasoning, and SQuID provides the data to train and evaluate them.
evidence_items.title: SQuID: A Benchmark for Quantitative Spatial Reasoning on Satellite Imagery

evidence_items.summary: Description VP Recovery: A Human-Evaluated Benchmark for Post-Contamination Recovery in Japanese LLM-Based Virtual Patients (v0.6–v0.9) Overview This repository provides experimental datasets, human evaluation results, and reproducibility materials supporting a study of post-contamination recovery in Japanese-language large language model (LLM)-based virtual patients. The research investigates whether an LLM-based virtual patient can recover from prompt-induced role deviation and whether restoration of the patient role is accompanied by recovery of fidelity to predefined clinical case information. A central contribution is the distinction between patient-role restoration and scripted-case fidelity recovery. A virtual patient may resume its intended conversational role while continuing to provide incomplete, inconsistent, or unsupported clinical information. The repository documents two related but analytically distinct research phases: an initial exploratory experiment (v0.6) and a subsequent new-case validation experiment (v0.9). Experimental Design The study compared four recovery conditions: A — Natural recovery: Retaining contaminated conversation history without additional instructions. B — Role re-instruction: Retaining contaminated history while providing a system-level instruction to restore the patient role. C — History removal: Removing contaminated conversation history without additional re-instruction. D — History removal with re-instruction: Combining contaminated-history removal with patient-role re-instruction. Recovery was evaluated over five subsequent clinical interview turns. The primary endpoint assessed patient-role restoration during the final two turns, while secondary analyses examined stricter recovery criteria and alternative evaluation windows. Additional Validation (v0.9) The v0.9 experiment introduced five new fully synthetic Japanese clinical cases, covering knee pain, sore throat, heartburn, shoulder pain, and nasal congestion.
evidence_items.title: VP Recovery: Japanese LLM Virtual-Patient Recovery Benchmark and Human Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: MIMIC-IV-Ext-DischargeBench is a derived dataset of 320 curated hospitalization cases (v1.0.0) built from MIMIC-IV (v3.1) and MIMIC-IV-Note (v2.2). Each case is a structured patient profile drawn from the discharge documentation of a single hospitalization, covering diagnoses, medications, follow-up instructions, and post-discharge care plans. Cases were sampled from adult patients evenly across 16 diagnostic chapters, which combine matching ICD-9 and ICD-10 chapters into a single version-neutral grouping. Profiles were extracted from the structured tables and discharge notes with a large language model and manually reviewed against the source notes. Each case is paired with simulated-patient traits (personality, education level, health literacy, and medical-history recall). The dataset was developed for DischargeBench, a framework that simulates conversations in which an LLM educator explains discharge instructions to a simulated patient. The release also includes the complete simulation records of eight closed- and open-source models (GPT-5.5, GPT-5.4-mini, GPT-5.4-nano, Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct, Qwen3-32B, Qwen3-4B, MedGemma-27b-text-it, and MedGemma-4b-it), each run five times on every case. The simulation code and prompts are publicly available on the DischargeBench GitHub repository.

evidence_items.summary: Reproduction package for the paper Mind the Gap: Explicit Cross-Benchmark Calibrations for Estimating Missing LLM Evaluation Scores (Süli, Eigner, Hollós). benchgap estimates missing large language model benchmark scores from explicit per-pair calibrations between benchmarks of the same capability. The live system (benchgap.net) refreshes daily and cannot regenerate a past state; this record freezes the state the paper analyses: the measured data retrieved on 8 October 2026, refitted end to end with the pipeline at commit 920b1c4. Contents: the SQLite snapshot (520 models, 359 benchmark versions, 6,180 measured scores with source and retrieval date, 14,314 estimates with provenance, 1,147 univariate calibrations, 21 multivariate mappings); the harness-tax analysis and its exports; the masked-holdout results (three random seeds and two sparse settings); the scripts that produce the paper's statistics, holdout evaluation and figures; and the pipeline source at commit 920b1c4. evidence_items.summary: Text-to-image models learn associations between concepts - in the case of this paper, people's professions, which we refer to as roles - and visual attributes. These associations can underpin many observed forms of stereotypical bias. A key open question in this area is whether these associations are stable or change when visual representations of people in professional roles are placed in different prompted contexts. We introduce ContextBias, a controlled evaluation framework, and ContextBench, a benchmark spanning 92 roles and 1,656 semantically controlled prompts, designed to isolate the effect of contextual variation on role-linked visual representations. Evaluating four state-of-the-art models on 66,240 generated images, we find that placing a role in a semantically unrelated context does not suppress role-linked attributes; instead, cross-role attribute concentration increases (pooled BI + 0.047 ). Demographic cues, characteristic garments, and role-specific tools remain highly prevalent across context-free, related, and unrelated conditions, and are robust to semantic prompt reformulation. Scene composition and camera framing show the greatest context-sensitivity. These findings reveal a form of stereotypical persistence that remains largely invisible to context-free evaluations, highlighting the need for controlled contextual variation in bias benchmarking. Code and dataset: this https URL , this https URL
evidence_items.title: ContextBias: Controlled Evaluation of Bias Persistence Under Context Shift in Text-to-Image Models

evidence_items.summary: Lunar orbital missions, such as Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, Kaguya/SELENE, Gravity Recovery and Interior Laboratory, and Lunar Prospector, among others, provide rich multi-instrument observations, but their heterogeneity in sampling, projection, and conventions limits reproducible machine learning (ML). We introduce SomBench, a unified, spatially-aligned, ML-ready lunar dataset aggregating 30+ co-registered layers from ten instruments across four missions, spanning 1 meter to 20 kilometer/pixel and covering 82 degree latitude in 90 Lunar Transverse Mercator zones with two polar stereographic caps. An image-anchored tiling pipeline yields pretraining-ready multimodal tile views with leakage-safe splits, distributed as netCDF with Parquet catalogs. An application benchmark suite spans impact processes, volcanic history, and polar volatiles. Baseline experiments with ResNet-50 and SwinV2-B models confirm that each benchmark task is learnable from the released inputs, establishing reference points for future model development.
evidence_items.title: SomBench: Benchmark Dataset for Advancing Machine Learning in Lunar Science

evidence_items.summary: Large language models often deviate from the target word count when following length constraints such as “generate X words.” Existing studies mostly focus on content quality, while paying relatively less attention to format control, especially the accuracy of length control. To address this issue, this study builds a Chinese text generation benchmark covering 5 topics and 4 word-count levels, and evaluates three representative models: DeepSeek-V3, Tongyi Qianwen (Qwen2.5), and Kimi. Based on this, a lightweight post-processing framework, LAPP (Length-Aware Post-Processing), is proposed. When the output is too long, LAPP uses sentence-level intelligent truncation; when the output is too short, it calls Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct for semantics-preserving expansion, and controls the length error within ±10% through iterative correction. The experimental results show that the original average deviation rates of the three models are 11.93%–38.70%, which are reduced to about 5% after LAPP correction, and the pass rate increases from 20%–70% to 85%–100%. The semantic preservation results show an average BERTScore of 0.97 between the corrected and original texts, suggesting that the framework improves length control while largely keeping the original meaning. This study shows that the “rough generation + precise correction” approach is effective for word-count control, and offers a low-cost, transferable way to improve the instruction-following ability of large language models.
evidence_items.title: Research on the Length Controllability of Chinese Large Language Model Outputs Based on Post-Processing Correction

organizations: Symbiosis International (Deemed University) Symbiosis Centre for Information Technology, , Pune,
evidence_items.summary: Purpose This study aims to examine how prompt design influences the quality of large language model (LLM)-generated business-to-business (B2B) market research outputs. It also proposes a switch-point governance mechanism for converting LLM-generated drafts into decision-ready market intelligence artefacts. Design/methodology/approach The study uses an exploratory pilot evaluation of three market-facing LLM-based tools: ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity AI. The tools are compared across three benchmark B2B market research tasks and three prompt types: basic, context-augmented and role-specific. In total, 81 outputs were generated. A role-specific benchmark subset of 27 outputs was then assessed using automated metrics and blinded human ratings. The automated metrics included relevance through cosine similarity, reference overlap through ROUGE-F1, cross-run semantic stability, latency, token length and readability through Flesch Reading Ease. Human evaluators rated the outputs on relevance, completeness, factuality, instruction-following and insightfulness. One-way ANOVA and non-parametric checks are reported as exploratory task-level tests, not as confirmatory evidence of model superiority. Findings Role-specific prompts produced the strongest descriptive scores in this pilot setting. Within the benchmark subset, Gemini showed the strongest observed profile, with higher average relevance, reference overlap and semantic stability, along with lower latency. ChatGPT produced relevant outputs but tended to generate longer and less readable drafts. Perplexity generated concise and readable summaries, but its outputs were less aligned with the reference brief and decision-facing requirements. Human ratings followed a similar descriptive pattern. Cross-run semantic stability showed directional alignment with higher decision-readiness ratings, offering preliminary support for P1.
evidence_items.title: Advancing value creation in B2B market research – a human–AI collaboration framework for large language model

organizations: Jan Evangelista Purkyně University in Ústí nad Labem
evidence_items.summary: Abstract User reviews of mobile applications provide a source of citizen feedback on digital public services, yet their automated analysis in non-English settings is constrained by the limited availability of domain-adapted classifiers. This study develops and evaluates a documented procedure for three-class sentiment classification of Czech reviews of government mobile applications using a large language model without task-specific fine-tuning. The corpus comprised 10,198 reviews of six applications. An adjudicated human reference was created for a stratified random sample of 500 reviews, and LLM performance was compared with a majority-class baseline, two lexicon-based methods, and two readily deployable encoder-based transfer models. The validation included five repeated runs under identical settings and an analysis of classification errors. Across five GPT-5.6 Sol validation runs, mean accuracy was 93.0%, mean macro-F1 was 0.827, and mean Cohen's kappa was 0.857. Macro-F1 ranged from 0.814 to 0.845, while agreement among the five runs was high (Fleiss' kappa = 0.918). The neutral class was the most challenging, with most disagreements occurring at its boundaries with negative and positive sentiment. In the full corpus, 65.9% of reviews were classified as negative, 7.9% as neutral, and 26.2% as positive. Textual sentiment was strongly associated with star ratings but was not identical to them. These findings provide corpus-specific evidence that a standardized LLM procedure can help analyze short-form non-english citizen feedback. They also underscore the need for human reference labels, stability checks, and precise documentation of the model, prompt, settings, and execution workflow.
evidence_items.title: Sentiment Analysis of Government Mobile App Reviews: Validating Zero-Shot Classification with a Large Language Model

Department of Physics and Astronomy, Uppsala University
Villanova University, Dept. of Astrophysics and Planetary Sciences
evidence_items.summary: Context. Detached eclipsing binaries (DEBs) provide model-independent measurements of stellar masses and radii, which are essential for testing stellar-evolution models and calibrating space-based photometric missions. Aims. We aim to deliver ultra-precise fundamental parameters for the DEB UX Men and to assess its suitability as a benchmark for upcoming missions such as PLATO . We evaluate the temporal stability of the photometric solutions and the way intrinsic stellar variability and instrumental systematics affect the derived parameters. Methods. We analysed 31 TESS sectors (∼882 d) with the LIGHTKURVE package, and detrended spot-induced variability. Light-curve modelling was performed independently with JKTEBOP and ALLESFITTER . Radial velocities from HARPS (HAM/EGGS), FEROS, CORALIE, and UCLES were extracted via TODCOR and fitted with a Keplerian orbit. Spectral disentangling (5350–5800 Å) yielded individual component spectra, which were processed with ISPEC to determine T eff , [M/H], and micro- and macroturbulence. Eclipse-timing variations were examined through O-C diagrams. We also used multi-band photometry to determine the fluxes, flux ratios, and ultimately, to measure the photometric T eff . Results. We obtained masses of M A = 1.2300 ± 0.0012 M ⊙ , M B = 1.1946 ± 0.0012 M ⊙ and radii of R A = 1.3605 ± 0.0031 R ⊙ , R B = 1.2801 ± 0.0069 R ⊙ , with a sub-percent precision. Uncertainties were found to be dominated by systematic effects coming from (weak) stellar activity. The metallicity estimates are [ M / H ] A = 0.02 ± 0.13 dex and [ M / H ] B = 0.07 ± 0.10 dex. An isochrone fitting yielded a consistent age of τ = 2.75 ± 0.13 Gyr. The system exhibits a ∼673-day periodicity in eclipse-timing variations, likely due to stellar activity, with no evidence of a third body. Conclusions.
evidence_items.title: UX Men: Detached eclipsing binary as a benchmark candidate

Department of Structural Engineering, University of California, San Diego, La Jolla, CA, USA
evidence_items.summary: Vibration measurements from civil structures inherently contain fundamental dynamic characteristics and are widely used to monitor structural behavior to inform condition assessment. Machine learning, particularly unsupervised deep learning models, has demonstrated strong potential in automatically learning patterns from baseline vibration data and detecting anomalous structural behaviors. Complex multiscale temporal patterns may arise in structural responses, particularly under rapidly varying external loads, potentially leading to obscured anomalies and reduced anomaly detection accuracy. The primary contribution of the study is the establishment of a benchmark dataset from vibration tests of a laboratory-scale truss bridge. The benchmark vibration dataset contains structural responses under stationary and moving-load excitations, including multilocation and multilevel structural anomaly scenarios. The established dataset can be further used as a benchmark for moving load identification, modal identification, structural model updating, and structural anomaly detection, among others. Additionally, a multiscale pattern learning approach for vibration-based structural anomaly detection by integrating the TimeMixer network with the one-class support vector machine (TimeMixer-OCSVM) is introduced. The methodological contribution lies in establishing a TimeMixer-OCSVM validation baseline, which demonstrates the capability of the benchmark dataset to support anomaly detection studies. The TimeMixer model is adopted to learn multiscale patterns from structural vibration data, improving the anomaly detection performance under varying external excitations. The constructed benchmark dataset is used to validate the proposed method, and the results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in identifying structural anomalies. Compared to the other typical methods, the proposed method achieves higher structural anomaly detection accuracy.
evidence_items.title: Multiscale pattern learning for vibration-based structural anomaly detection: A benchmark dataset and validation study

evidence_items.summary: Vancomycin has a narrow therapeutic window requiring individualized dosing and repeated monitoring, a process health systems delegate from physicians to pharmacists for consistency. We silently deployed PharmaAgent, LLM-based vancomycin dosing agentic systems, at Stanford Hospital for two months and compared high- and low-autonomy configurations, each with and without institutional guidelines. Across 403 dosing events in 316 patients, mean absolute percentage error against the treating pharmacist's order was 21.8% with high autonomy versus 37.8% with low autonomy, and recommendations were within 25% of the order in 73.4% versus 50.9% of events (P < 0.001); a second pharmacist was within 25% in 90.2%. Pharmacist review of 196 out-of-tolerance recommendations found a safety concern in 65.8%, more often with low autonomy (odds ratio 2.37). A higher-autonomy agent that self-debugged its intermediate steps proved more robust than stricter engineering, but neither configuration is ready to dose patients without pharmacist oversight.
evidence_items.title: PharmaAgent: a real-world evaluation of high- and low-autonomy agentic systems for inpatient vancomycin dosing

evidence_items.summary: A benchmark leaderboard reports one accuracy number, but that number is a joint product of a model and a scoring rule. We ask what changes when only the rule changes, and find that model ordering is highly sensitive to it. IndiaFinBench is a 406-item expert-annotated benchmark over SEBI and RBI regulatory text covering regulatory interpretation, numerical reasoning, contradiction detection, and temporal reasoning. We score twelve LLMs zero-shot under two primary regimes over the same predictions - strict four-stage string matching, and the verdicts of a cross-model judge sharing no model family with any evaluated system - plus one operational composite regime. The two primary regimes show no positive rank correspondence (Spearman rho = -0.273, p = 0.39, not significant), and no model holds its rank across all three regimes. Strict accuracy spans 75.12-89.66%; judge-only accuracy spans 87.19-94.83% with a different leader and trailer; the composite compresses the field to 94.1-98.0%, under which DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B ties for first despite ranking last under strict scoring, because the judge reclassifies 93.9% of its strict errors as correct. Output verbosity does not explain the reclassification once task and model composition are adjusted for, a negative result we report as such. Item-level analysis compounds the finding: 148 of 406 items (36.5%) are answered identically by all twelve models and separate no pair of systems, while a predefined higher-discrimination band captures 134 items. We also anchor the scale against one non-specialist evaluator, who scored 80.0% (48/60; 95% Wilson CI [68.2, 88.2]) on a 60-item medium/hard subset; paired bootstrap tests find no significant difference against any model after multiplicity correction. Data, harness, judge verdicts, predictions: https://github.com/Rajveer-code/IndiaFinBench
evidence_items.title: Scoring-Rule Sensitivity in LLM Evaluation: Evidence from Indian Financial Regulatory Text

evidence_items.summary: Analogical reasoning is widely considered a fundamental component of human intelligence. Few benchmarks are designed to explicitly test far analogical reasoning - reasoning between domains that are superficially dissimilar yet share deep relational or structural similarities. In this work, we introduce an analogical reasoning benchmark called Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus of ANAlogy (ARCANA). The tasks of ARCANA require performing far analogical mappings from real-world objects or physical phenomena to abstract grid-based transformations, different from the well-known ARC-AGI benchmark which primarily emphasized innate human priors. We validate ARCANA through a human study, demonstrating that humans solve these tasks reliably. In contrast, evaluations across a range of large language models show a distinct performance gap compared to humans, revealing systematic failure modes that remain challenging for current models. To address this gap, we propose ConceptSIR, a reasoning framework based on concept slippage, introspection, and reflection. Experiments demonstrate that ConceptSIR enables standard LLMs to solve several challenging ARCANA tasks that were unsolved by direct prompting in our evaluation. Overall, our results suggest that far analogical reasoning remains an open problem for contemporary LLMs. All the materials are available at sites.google.com/view/arcanacogtest. The complete codebase, including benchmark, and ConceptSIR, is publicly available at https://github.com/density-11/arcana-test. All ARCANA data and task instances can be accessed and explored at https://arcanacogtest.org/.
evidence_items.title: ARCANA: A Benchmark for Abstraction and Analogical Reasoning

evidence_items.summary: Long-horizon agentic systems become long-context systems by accumulation rather than through a single long document, since every step reassembles a prompt from role instructions, tool and sub-agent descriptions, recalled memories, dialogue history, and previous tool outputs, separately for every agent. This paper studies how such accumulated context can be trained, evaluated, and managed in hierarchical multi-agent assistants. We present HiMA-Ecom, a hierarchical multi-agent benchmark for e-commerce assistants with 22.8K instances, of which 17.7K carry memory entries in context, pairing agent-specific supervised fine-tuning data with system-level supervision for end-to-end multi-agent reinforcement learning. Building upon it, HiMA-R1 keeps the context budget of a trajectory under control through Variance-Reduction Group Relative Policy Optimization (VR-GRPO), which samples along an initial trajectory so that sampling cost grows additively with trajectory length and updates the agents with the largest reward variance, together with an efficiency reward on trajectory length and a memory evolution mechanism that repurposes GRPO rewards as cost-free signals for what stays in context. Agents built upon 3B and 7B open-source models match DeepSeek-R1 and surpass DeepSeek-V3 by 6.0 points on average, while reward-driven memory reduces the update steps needed for convergence by roughly 55%.
evidence_items.title: HiMA-Ecom: A Long-Horizon Memory Benchmark for Hierarchical Multi-Agent E-commerce Assistants

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background Radiology reports serve as the definitive clinical record of imaging diagnoses, with their accuracy being directly critical to patient safety. However, amid escalating workloads, manual review remains inadequate for capturing subtle errors in reports on a large scale. Although large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated considerable promise in medical text processing, previous studies have predominantly been confined to radiology report text from a single imaging modality or datasets with synthetic errors. Objective This study aimed to evaluate the feasibility, accuracy, and generalizability of general-purpose LLMs for quality assurance of radiology report text from multiple imaging modalities (x-ray, computed tomography [CT], and magnetic resonance imaging [MRI]), multi-anatomical regions, and multicenter clinical settings, with head-to-head comparisons conducted against radiologists of varying seniority. Methods Radiology report texts from 3 aforementioned imaging modalities and 5 anatomical regions (head, chest, abdomen, spine, and knee) were retrospectively collected from center 1 (March 2025-May 2025) and reviewed using a clinician-annotated 5-category error taxonomy (type 1: interpretive; type 2: factual). Five LLMs (Qwen3, GPT-5.4 Pro, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Llama 4, and DeepSeek-V3.1) were benchmarked on 10,000 randomly selected reports, and the best-performing model was evaluated on the full cohort. A blinded head-to-head comparison with 3 radiologists (3-10 years of experience) used a modality-stratified, error-enriched challenge set. The radiologists subsequently rated the model-generated explanations using a 5-point Likert scale. Cross-center performance was evaluated in an independent external cohort. The same 2 senior radiologists labeled reports from both centers using the same protocol, resolving disagreements by consensus.
evidence_items.title: Large Language Model–Assisted Radiology Report Quality Assurance: Real-World Multicenter Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Scientific evidence is predominantly communicated through unstructured articles, while many downstream workflows require structured representations of study populations, variables, methods, and quantitative findings. Large language models (LLMs) offer a promising route toward automating this transformation, yet their reliability in constructing schema-constrained evidence records from parsed scientific full texts remains insufficiently understood. Evidence synthesis is a representative use case in which systematic reviews and meta-analyses require accurate, structured study information before quantitative integration can begin. We present a schema-grounded, tiered evaluation framework for structured scientific evidence extraction that increases task difficulty from single-entity identification to relational tuples and corpus-level statistical tasks. We evaluate frontier commercial and open-weight models across five scientific domains under a stricter multi-level assessment protocol, complemented by human validation of model-based judging and process-level inspection of intermediate reasoning for statistical tasks. Results reveal a clear pattern: models perform substantially better on low-complexity extraction tasks than on tasks requiring correct bindings among entities, numerical values, and methodological attributes. Intermediate-step analysis further indicates error amplification under exact downstream aggregation, where small upstream errors often prevent correct final outputs. Scaling model size yields uneven gains and does not remove these weaknesses. These findings show that recent advances have not resolved the fundamental challenges of structured scientific evidence extraction. We provide a reusable query suite and diagnostic evaluation framework to support future fine-grained benchmarks and more rigorous assessment of models for evidence-intensive scientific workflows.
evidence_items.title: Diagnosing the limits of large language models for structured scientific evidence extraction

evidence_items.summary: The expertly rectified extraction of cropland parcel boundaries is a critical basis for precision agriculture deployment and land resource management. However, the scarcity of large-scale, high-quality, cross-regional reference datasets limits the generalizability of deep learning models. To address this data bottleneck, we created a standardized, multi-source cropland parcel boundary benchmark dataset. The collection, which covers Europe (Denmark, the Netherlands, Spain) and Asia (Central China), encompasses over 180,000 expert-rectified parcels, with average parcel sizes ranging from 0.05 to 10 hectares and spatial resolutions spanning 0.2 to 10 m. Based on this dataset, we evaluated nine representative deep learning models belonging to three architectural paradigms (edge detection, multi-task semantic segmentation, and instance segmentation) and analyzed the effects of spatial resolution, parcel scale, and topographic relief on extraction accuracy. The experimental results indicate the following: (1) Spatial resolution exerts a non-linear influence on boundary extraction fidelity, where some medium-resolution data conditions (such as 4.8 m imagery in large-scale fields) retained competitive boundary extraction performance for certain models. (2) Even small but regular parcels of merely 0.22 hectares can be extracted with high accuracy, achieving a maximum F1 score of 86.58%. (3) Topographic variations lead to contrasting model performance. In plain and hilly terrain, multi-task semantic segmentation models exhibit obvious advantages. BsiNet yields the highest F1 score of 86.58%, but this value drops to 36.56% in complex mountainous regions. By comparison, edge detection models perform better in mountainous areas, where RCF attains the maximum F1 of 70.85%.
evidence_items.title: A Multi-Source Benchmark Dataset for Deep Learning-Based Cropland Parcel Boundary Extraction

evidence_items.summary: Abstract While deep learning has significantly advanced image reconstruction of electrical capacitance tomography (ECT), most public datasets retain only capacitance vectors and permittivity distributions and do not expose the excitation-wise electric potential field, a physical intermediate in the forward mapping. To address this, we present an electric-potential-augmented ECT benchmark dataset generated via a COMSOL–MATLAB pipeline for a fixed eight-electrode sensor. The dataset comprises 20 000 randomized samples across four typical flow-pattern families. Alongside conventional capacitance vectors and permittivity images, each sample preserves eight spatially registered full-field potential maps. Governing equations and field-perturbation visualizations characterize the relation between potential and dielectric structure. As an initial use of this physical information, we introduce potential-field intermediate supervision to guide representation learning in simple forward and inverse models. Under sample-disjoint independent and identically distributed (IID) and fully held-out two-bar out-of-distribution (OOD) evaluation, potential supervision reduces forward capacitance-prediction mean squared error (MSE) by 56.8% and 74.6%, respectively, relative to a structure- and capacity-aligned control. In an exploratory forward experiment, a low-weight partial differential equation residual yields 5.3%–8.3% lower mean potential-prediction MSE. For inverse reconstruction, the simple model reduces mean MSE by 14.3% and 3.0% on IID and OOD data, respectively, relative to the same control. The more modest inverse gains are consistent with the difficulty of recovering dense potential maps from limited capacitance measurements. These results provide initial controlled evidence for the value of potential-field supervision.
evidence_items.title: An electric-potential-augmented benchmark dataset for electrical capacitance tomography: electric-potential supervision for future physics-guided learning

evidence_items.summary: Developing on-device image models requires considering practical user needs, task types and device resource constraints. However, existing benchmarks provide limited guidance on identifying capability gaps between on-device models and server-side models. We introduce MoI-Bench, a benchmark grounded in mobile user needs, comprising 64 subtasks and 1150 samples. It defines 16 operations, such as removal and replacement, and eight visual target categories covering content such as portraits and text. These form two orthogonal axes whose applicable combinations define specific tasks, such as removing facial makeup. To better guide model improvement, we further propose MoI-Eval, which introduces task-specific criteria covering instruction following, visual quality and detail preservation. We further construct sample-level evaluation questions and aggregate their scores into overall quality and capability profiles along the operation, target and criteria axes. We evaluate representative on-device and server-side models and measure mobile deployment costs. Results show that this decoupled Operation x Target design provides finer-grained guidance for improving compact models. For example, it highlights the need to prioritize specific capability gaps (e.g., text-replacement) over broad application-level goals (e.g., improving text editing). Unlike conventional benchmarks that rank models using a single score, we introduce a two-dimensional Quality-Deployability capability map to assess models for practical mobile use. The map shows that current on-device models can achieve efficient generation or editing but expanding their task coverage deserves greater attention than further improving deployment efficiency. Further progress requires improving editing quality, particularly identity preservation and text rendering, while broadening task coverage.
evidence_items.title: MoI-Bench: A Benchmark for Image Generation and Editing on Mobile Devices

evidence_items.summary: Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) syndrome differentiation is usually evaluated as static final-label selection over complete clinical records. This setting hides three diagnostic behaviors: whether a model distinguishes semantic-neighbor syndrome labels from easy random distractors, whether it updates predictions as evidence fields are revealed, and whether it should commit under uncertainty. We introduce TCM-DiagCommit, a benchmark derived from the public TCM-SD/ZY-BERT resource while retaining its source syndrome labels; it converts 1,834 source cases into 23,842 task rows over 148 syndrome labels. The benchmark combines random, profile-neighbor, and full-vocabulary candidate ladders with staged t1/t2/t3 evidence. It also includes fixed-label tongue/pulse perturbations and insufficient-evidence variants. A benchmark-defined action contract scores commit, acquire, defer, and abstain. Across five zero-shot DirectLLM calibrations, random10 top-1 accuracy is 63.2% to 66.4%, but hard20 falls to 24.7% to 30.3% and full148 to 14.8% to 22.3%; on hard20, WT(all) wrong-terminal commits remain 62.2% to 74.3%. These results show that final-answer accuracy alone is insufficient for diagnostic benchmark evaluation: answer selection, evidence use, and benchmark commitment scoring should be measured separately.
evidence_items.title: TCM-DiagCommit: A TCM-SD-Derived Benchmark for Evidence-Conditioned Syndrome Selection and Commitment

evidence_items.summary: Skill optimizers adapt an agent to long-horizon tasks, such as repairing a terminal environment, by rewriting its skill, a natural-language procedure in its context, and keeping the edits that raise success on a small dev set. On such tasks success is noisy, so a gain on a small dev set does not show that an edit helps, and a success score does not show what the edit costs. We introduce BiPA, which replays an optimizer's acceptance rule on candidates identical to its seed to measure what selection alone reports, and records each episode as a bipartite graph of turns and the text they read to trace extra input tokens to the behavior behind them. Across three optimizers, three agentic benchmarks and two models, the learned skills succeed about as often as their hand-written seed, 0.1 points higher on average. Their dev gains vanish on test: keeping the best of several candidates on at most 30 tasks reports gains this large even when none changed. They read about 16% more input tokens: the optimizers almost always add rules, half to re-check work and some to act one call at a time, and the agent follows them as extra turns, each re-sending the whole conversation. Four principles follow: accept an edit only if its gain exceeds what selection alone reports; charge it for the turns it adds, not for its length; let the editor delete and merge rules; show it what earlier rules cost. Code is available at https://github.com/valleysprings/BiPA.git.
evidence_items.title: Does Your Generalist Skill Optimizer Really Incentivize Agentic Tasks? Rethinking Skill Optimization via Bipartite Attribution

evidence_items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have made remarkable progress on solving competition-level mathematics, yet their ability to verify natural-language mathematical proofs remains relatively underexplored. This gap is especially pronounced for Olympiad-level proofs, which require meticulous assessment of each claim in a long reasoning chain. Current proof verification thus primarily relies on expert inspection, which is costly to scale. In this paper, we present a systematic study of LLM-based verification in this setting. Specifically, we introduce a human-curated dataset of USAMO 2025 candidate solutions with expert grading, and conduct a broad evaluation of existing LLM verifiers across frontier models. We also propose TROJAN, an iterative self-critique pipeline for generating high-fidelity adversarial proofs at scale. Our comprehensive evaluation covers 20 models spanning seven metrics, two prompt styles, three inference methods, and three prompt templates, showing that state-of-the-art models still leave considerable room for improvement. To narrow this gap, we propose MABGrader, a Multi-Armed Bandit framework that reframes grading as arm selection over the discrete score space. MABGrader outperforms the SOTA ProofGrader by 26.4% in Quadratic Weighted Kappa and reduces grading error by 14%. Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/aziksh-ospanov/TROJAN.
evidence_items.title: Can LLMs Reliably Grade Olympiad Proofs? A Study of Mathematical Verification with LLMs

evidence_items.summary: Robotic agents operating in real-world environments must adapt continuously from a stream of multimodal demonstrations, often under constraints that preclude storing or revisiting past data. In this replay-free, single-pass lifelong imitation learning setting, sequential updates can progressively distort the representation space, making expert-based approaches particularly sensitive to routing interference, causing expert selection to degrade over time. We propose HIDRA, a structured routing framework that mitigates this issue through a hierarchical dual-attention mechanism, which decouples instruction-level expert retrieval from context-dependent refinement. To further stabilize routing under representation drift, HIDRA introduces a key-level geometric regularization that enforces both alignment within tasks and separation across tasks. The resulting approach enables reliable expert selection while supporting an expandable set of experts for continual adaptation. We evaluate HIDRA on several LIBERO benchmark suites, including more challenging variants with heterogeneous task sequences and paraphrased language instructions. Our approach consistently outperforms both replay-free and replay-based baselines, improving AUC and forward transfer while maintaining low forgetting, with stronger gains under high interference and language variation. The code is available at: https://github.com/yfqi/HIDRA.
evidence_items.title: HIDRA: Hierarchical Dual-Routing Attention for Replay-Free Lifelong Imitation Learning

evidence_items.summary: Memory-agent benchmarks often collapse retrieval and answer generation into one score, making it hard to tell whether a failure comes from missing an update or from not using an update that was already retrieved. We examine this distinction on the single-hop FactConsolidation task of MemoryAgentBench. With Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on 6K-history BM25 accuracy drops from 45% to 32% when the retrieved evidence budget grows from 64 to 512 tokens, even though a gold-assisted post-hoc audit finds the newest statement in every retrieved set. Most of the errors occur on questions that also contain an obsolete statement version. Under a frozen prompt and equal four-statement evidence size, replacing one unrelated statement with the obsolete competing statement reduces accuracy from 100% to 44.6% for Qwen2.5 and from 100% to 87.8% for Qwen3-14B, with all 50 harmful paired flips classified as stale. A 32K-history replication likewise favors BM25-64 over BM25-512 (69% versus 58%). These results suggest that retrieving the correct fact is not enough. An obsolete competing statement can be more harmful than an unrelated piece of evidence of the same size.
evidence_items.title: When Retrieval Is Not Enough: Obsolete Facts in Agent Memory

evidence_items.summary: Reliable probability estimates are critical in many machine learning applications, yet modern classifiers are often poorly calibrated. Post-hoc calibration provides a simple and widely used solution, but the large number of proposed methods, combined with small-scale and inconsistent evaluations, makes it difficult to determine which approaches are truly effective in practice. We introduce a large-scale, standardized benchmark for post-hoc calibration, covering nearly 2000 experiments across tabular and computer vision tasks, including binary, multiclass, and large-scale classification settings. Our benchmark aggregates predictions from a diverse set of classical models, modern deep learning architectures, and foundation models, and provides unified, reproducible implementations of dozens of calibration methods within a common evaluation framework. We argue that Post-Hoc Improvement (PHI) in proper scoring rules offers a principled alternative to traditional calibration error estimators for comparing post-hoc methods, capturing both calibration quality and potential degradation to the model's predictive performance. Using this framework, we conduct the most comprehensive empirical study of post-hoc calibration to date. Our results reveal consistent patterns across domains: smooth calibration functions outperform binning-based approaches, dedicated multiclass methods are essential in high-dimensional settings, and generic machine learning models are not competitive without calibration-specific design. To facilitate future research, we release all data, code, and evaluation tools, providing a plug-and-play benchmark for developing and comparing calibration methods.
evidence_items.title: CalArena: A Large-Scale Post-Hoc Calibration Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: We introduce ControlAugment (Ctrl-A), an automated data augmentation algorithm for image-vision tasks, which incorporates principles from control theory for online adjustment of augmentation strength distributions during model training. Ctrl-A eliminates the need for initialization of individual augmentation strengths. Instead, augmentation strength distributions are dynamically, and individually, adapted during training based on a control-loop architecture and what we define as relative operation response curves. Using an operation-dependent update procedure provides Ctrl-A with the potential to reduce the use of augmentation operations that negatively impact model performance, alleviating the need to manually engineer augmentation policies for new image classification tasks. Experiments on the CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SVHN-core, and Tiny ImageNet benchmark datasets using WideResNet-28-10 and ResNet architectures demonstrate that Ctrl-A provides competitive performance across a range of image classification benchmarks.
evidence_items.title: Ctrl-A: Control-Driven Machine Learning using Adaptive Online Data Augmentation

evidence_items.summary: Image editing models can modify visual content through natural language, but editing dense documents requires precise local changes amid tightly coupled text, tables, and layout. We introduce VDE Bench, an evaluation resource for studying instruction-guided editing of Chinese and English document images. VDE Bench contains 3,506 instruction-guided image editing samples, including 1,578 text-region edits and 1,928 table-region edits. The benchmark pairs editing instructions and reference images with annotated editing regions and structured OCR outputs. Its evaluation protocol combines region-level and full-page measurements to assess textual correctness, structural fidelity, and visual content preservation. By focusing on the interaction between local edits and their surrounding document context, VDE Bench complements existing visual text editing benchmarks and provides a resource for diagnosing document-specific editing failures.
evidence_items.title: VDE Bench: Evaluating The Capability of Image Editing Models to Modify Visual Documents

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Causality extraction—the identification of cause–effect relations in natural language text—has been approached through three successive methodological paradigms: rule-based systems relying on lexical and syntactic cues, deep learning models exploiting neural architectures and pre-trained encoders, and, most recently, large language models (LLMs) applied through prompting or fine-tuning. Each paradigm has been evaluated on different datasets, under different annotation schemes, and with different metrics, making it difficult to determine how far apparent performance differences reflect genuine methodological advantages rather than benchmark artifacts. This study addresses that problem by constructing a unified benchmark for comparative evaluation of rule-based, deep learning, and LLM approaches to causality extraction. We consolidate multiple existing corpora—covering news, biomedical, and safety-incident text—into a harmonized annotation format, re-annotate a stratified subset to ensure consistent treatment of implicit and explicit causal relations, and evaluate representative methods from each paradigm under identical preprocessing, train–test splits, and evaluation protocols. We report span-level precision, recall, and F1, document-level F1, calibration error, inference cost, and annotation efficiency, and we conduct cross-domain transfer experiments to assess generalization. Results are analyzed to disentangle the contributions of architecture, training data, and task formulation, with particular attention to the conditions under which each paradigm retains a comparative advantage. We further examine error profiles across paradigms, identifying whether failures are concentrated in explicit versus implicit relations, local versus distributed constructions, and domain-specific versus general-language contexts.
evidence_items.title: Comparative Analysis of Rule-Based, Deep Learning, and LLM Approaches for Causality Extraction: A Unified Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Reproducible offline benchmarks for electric vehicle charging require explicit transition definitions and auditable data processing. We introduce IoEV-MARL, comprising 157,071 decision-level transitions from SUMO simulations of the road network of Tangier, Morocco, organized in a 62-column table. The corpus covers 700 collection episodes, seven seeds, four traffic regimes, and five behavioral arms: NEAREST, WEIGHTED, tabular Independent Q-Learning, and two QMIX checkpoint/exploration configurations. Learned collection policies originate from 120-episode training campaigns. A three-layer contract distinguishes decision-time observations, inter-decision elapsed time, and outcome/evaluation fields. Elapsed time is missing when no subsequent decision is recorded. The ETL protocol documents horizon censoring, missing successors, dimensional grain, and file-level provenance. Seven-fold leave-one-seed-out evaluations benchmark Behavior Cloning and offline Implicit Q-Learning on accept/reject decisions conditional on the selected station. Mean Behavior Cloning balanced accuracy ranges from 0.758 to 0.928 across tiers and feature sets, measuring imitation rather than operational performance. In matched greedy evaluation, QMIX has lower station-load dispersion in 7/7 seeds under Normal traffic, versus 2/7, 4/7, and 4/7 under Light, Peak, and Surge. Discrete-state audits characterize coverage gaps and structural reachability constraints. IoEV-MARL supports offline decision-learning research without establishing closed-loop performance gains.
evidence_items.title: IoEV-MARL: A Reproducible Offline Dataset and Benchmark for Electric Vehicle Charging Coordination Under Centralized and Decentralized Training

evidence_items.summary: As frontier language models grow increasingly capable and autonomous, independent third-party evaluations are critical for characterizing their systemic safety risks. While closed-source releases are routinely accompanied by comprehensive system cards, open-weight models receive less scrutiny regarding frontier risks. To address this gap, we present an independent safety evaluation of DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017, the latest version of V4.1 Flash that departs from V4 with a new architecture, scaled-up training, and strong agentic capabilities. Drawing on the EU General-Purpose AI Code of Practice, we evaluate the model across 34 benchmarks, including 5 in-house suites, spanning evaluation integrity, loss of control, and harmful manipulation. Conforming to the AEF-1 standard, we compare V4.1 Flash-1017 against V4.1 Flash, earlier DeepSeek V4 models, and leading closed-source systems (GPT-6 Astra, GPT-5.6 Sol, and Gemini 3.8 Flash). Overall, V4.1 Flash-1017 shows substantial safety improvements over the V4 generation and approaches or matches leading closed-source baselines on several dimensions, while still exhibiting notable behaviors that warrant continued attention. Building on our findings, we highlight three key observations and recommendations. First, because safety can shift and even regress across minor updates, developers should integrate safety evaluation into incremental releases. Second, as final-turn outputs and end-state checks alone cannot reliably detect loss-of-control behaviors, deployments require process-level observability across both reasoning traces and action logs. Third, because public benchmarks elicit strong evaluation awareness and face data contamination risks, developing private benchmarks is essential for trustworthy frontier evaluation.
