evidence_items.summary: CARDIO-REVIEW: Research Data and Reproducibility Package This dataset accompanies CARDIO-REVIEW, a clinical artificial intelligence safety benchmark evaluating large language model (LLM) generation and automated review of clinician-authored synthetic cardiovascular scenarios. The study comprises 60 synthetic clinical scenarios organised into 30 matched A/B case pairs, with an independent repeatability assessment involving 12 scenarios from six matched pairs. Dataset contents The repository includes: 1,008 recorded model outputs, comprising 720 primary and 288 repeatability outputs. Clinical safety classifications independently assessed by cardiologist investigators and final adjudicated severity ratings. Reviewer ACCEPT/REVISE decisions, source-to-review linkages, and clinical safety transitions. Frozen model configurations, prompt templates, and methodological documentation. Six R analysis scripts and reference outputs supporting reproduction of the reported descriptive statistics, reviewer analyses, 20,000-draw matched-pair cluster bootstrap confidence intervals, and repeatability assessments. A data dictionary, reproducibility instructions, and SHA-256 integrity verification tools. Reproducibility The supplied R scripts reproduce the reported analyses from the released linked and adjudicated data tables. The repository also preserves model response texts and synthetic case descriptions. Automated reconstruction of every intermediate analysis table from the original provider-level acquisition files and internal historical adjudication workbooks is outside the scope of this public release. Data protection and intended use All clinical scenarios are fictional. No real patient records are included. Direct clinician identifiers, confidential operational metadata, API credentials, and internal blinding records have been excluded. Some preserved model responses contain clinically unsafe recommendations.

evidence_items.summary: This study presents a comprehensive benchmarking evaluation of large language models(LLMs) and agentic coding systems for automated analysis and visualization workflows for transcriptomic data, in particular human responses to COVID-19 infection. Multiple models, including ChatGPT 5.5, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 3.1, and Llama4-Scout, were assessed across a series of scientific prompts designed to test their ability to reproduce workflow components such as dimensionality reduction, clustering, outlier detection, reproducibility, and code generation. The benchmark protocol involved varying prompt specificity and examined both quantitative metrics such as clustering scores and outlier counts as well as qualitative aspects such as code quality and reproducibility. Results indicate that prompt specificity improves code structure and methodological correctness, but quantitative performance depends heavily on preprocessing choices and execution environment. While some models produced strong code and reproducible outputs, alignment with scientific targets like label-based clustering was inconsistent. The findings highlight the promise and limitations of current LLMs for automating scientific data analysis and visualization and suggest directions for future benchmarking and workflow standardization.
evidence_items.title: Benchmarking Large Language Models for Transcriptomic Data Analysis and Visualization: Multi-Model Workflow Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Plant metabolism produces a vast diversity of molecules, yet identifying the enzymes that catalyse biosynthetic reactions remains a major open problem. Existing benchmarks typically reduce this problem to isolated enzyme–reaction pairs, overlooking pathway and metabolite context that determines biological plausibility, leaving no standardised way to evaluate approaches that exploit this richer multimodal and relational structure. We present PlantMetBench, a multimodal graph benchmark built on PlantMetWiki, a curated knowledge graph of plant metabolism spanning 424 organisms. The resulting benchmark graph comprises 13,682 proteins, 2,741 genes, 4,577 metabolites, and 11,980 experimentally curated enzyme–reaction pairs. PlantMetBench frames enzyme–reaction prediction as an organism-disjoint link-prediction task and provides graph-native dataset splits, precomputed multi-modal node features, and evaluation protocols. Using PlantMetBench, we evaluate heterogeneous graph neural networks, standard architectures (HeteroSAGE, GAT, HGT, and R-GCN), alongside residual and jumping-knowledge variants, against non-graph models. Most heterogeneous graph architectures consistently outperform non-graph baselines on our rank-based evaluation, suggesting the value of relational context for enzyme–reaction prediction. Yet, performance remains far from saturated, indicating substantial room for improved representations and modelling strategies. Also, we show that benchmark design choices (shortcuts, splits, and metrics) are key to aligning evaluation with biologically meaningful tasks. PlantMetBench provides a standardised, reproducible framework to evaluate multimodal biosynthetic data, establishing a foundation for future work on graph-based architectures for enzyme–reaction prediction. Code and data are publicly available.
evidence_items.title: PLANTMETBENCH: A MULTIMODAL KNOWLEDGE GRAPH BENCHMARK FOR BIOSYNTHESIS PREDICTION

evidence_items.summary: Reliable heat transfer correlations are needed in the thermal-hydraulic design and safety analysis of advanced nuclear energy systems, especially liquid-metal fast reactors. Liquid-metal coolants, such as sodium, have high thermal conductivity and strong heat removal capability, which makes the prediction of heat transfer behavior an important issue in reactor analysis. In practical calculations, empirical heat transfer correlations are still commonly used because they are simple and computationally inexpensive. However, these correlations were obtained from different experiments and were reported with different applicability ranges, so a direct comparison without considering these ranges may be misleading. This study presents a validity-range-based benchmark for 11 classical empirical heat transfer correlations for axial liquid-metal flow in triangular rod bundles, as summarized in the Sodium Coolant Handbook. A reconstructed benchmark dataset with 597 data points is used, including pitch-to-diameter ratio <i>P/D</i>, Peclet number <i>Pe</i>, and experimentally measured Nusselt number Nu. In the strict in-domain assessment, only correlations expressed as functions of <i>P/D</i> and <i>Pe</i> and having applicability ranges defined by the same variables are considered. Prediction performance is evaluated using multiple statistical indicators. The <i>P/D–Pe</i> parameter space is also divided into grid cells according to the reported validity limits, so that the locally best-performing correlation can be identified in each region. The resulting benchmark gives a reproducible basis for comparing empirical heat transfer correlations and may also serve as a reference for assessing empirical models in other advanced energy systems.
evidence_items.title: A validity-range-based benchmark of liquid-metal heat transfer correlations for nuclear energy systems

evidence_items.summary: Language-model agents act through tools and credentials. A score from one tested configuration should not keep authorizing actions after the system, permissions, or threat model change. We argue that agentic AI is the first high-stakes domain in which assurance-invalidating change routinely outpaces evidence renewal. Continuous assurance is therefore not an improvement on benchmark evaluation, but a precondition for an authorization claim being true when it is relied upon. The machinery exists in nuclear, aviation, and medical-device regulation. Three requirements do not: a configuration baseline that makes change detectable, a change taxonomy calibrated to hazard relevance, and qualification criteria for evaluation environments. We propose the Agentic Assurance Stack (Stack), a versioned assurance profile linking each action path to a bounded claim, five evidence obligations, and a renewal rule.
evidence_items.title: Agentic AI Risk Evaluation Should Become a Continuous Assurance Discipline

evidence_items.summary: Permission-based static analysis is still one of the lightest methods for catching ransomware prior to installation, and ransomware is continuing to become more sophisticated on the Android platform. In a previous work, a well-balanced set of 1,990 Android applications (995 for ransomware and 995 for benign) and 365 permission attributes was collected, and Logistic Regression to achieve an accuracy of 97.69% under 10-fold cross validation had been obtained. This paper is along two lines of extension, scale and algorithmic breadth, of this study. The 20,012 applications in the permission dataset are a public-permission version that has been substantially-expanded from the known ransomware/benign dataset included with the publication, and are defined by 2,317 cleaned binary permission/Api Usage features used on each sample; we test the performance of six popular supervised learning algorithms (Random Forest, XGBoost, linear-kernel SVC, MLP, a single decision tree, and linear regression). A common preprocessing pipeline was performed across all models and training was performed on a synthesis of a 70/30 split and 10-fold stratified cross-validation. We present accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score, ROC area, false positive rate, confusion matrix, training time and a gini impurity feature ranking. The MLP, Linear SVM, and Random Forest achieved comparable results as Random Forest is the second best (91.72% ± 0.72% accuracy under cross-validation and 91.72% when performing a held-out test on the train/test split, with an F1-score of 0.922 and an ROC-AUC score of 0.942). The single Decision Tree model was once again the most poor with thresholded Linear Regression being not far behind the dedicated classifiers, meaning that many of the signals in permission space are approximately linear — as seen in our previous study where Logistic Regression performed well.
evidence_items.title: A Baseline Machine Learning Benchmark for Permission-Based Android Ransomware Detection: Comparative Evaluation of Random Forest, XGBoost, Support Vector Machines, Neural Networks, Decision Trees, and Linear Regression

evidence_items.summary: Customer churn is one of the most critical and cost-intensive challenges facing the telecommunications industry today. With the rapid expansion of mobile networks and the saturation of the digital market, retaining existing customers has proven to be significantly more cost-effective than acquiring new ones. The present study proposes a comprehensive, data-driven framework utilizing Machine Learning (ML) techniques to predict customer churn proactively within the Cameroon National Operator (CNO) mobile network. By extracting and preprocessing real-world data from the Evolved Packet Core (EPC), specifically the Home Subscriber Server (HSS), a dataset of 13,937 valid customer records was established from an initial pool of 797,508. To address the inherent class imbalance between active and churned users, the Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (SMOTE) was applied. Four supervised machine learning algorithms were trained and evaluated namely: Logistic Regression, Random Forest, LightGBM, and a heterogeneous Stacking Ensemble classifier. Evaluation metrics demonstrate that the Stacking Ensemble model achieved the highest predictive performance. The model yielded an accuracy of 97.51%, a precision of 97.46%, a recall of 97.54%, and an F1-score of 97.50%. Furthermore, Kaplan-Meier survival analysis and feature importance evaluations revealed that early subscription phases (the first 50 days) and specific financial dynamics (monthly charges and recharge frequencies) are the most critical determinants of customer loyalty. The developed system empowers telecommunication decision-makers to identify at-risk subscribers in real-time, facilitating the deployment of personalized, proactive retention strategies.
evidence_items.title: Machine Learning Methods for Proactive Customers Churn Prediction in Mobile Networks: A Case Study

evidence_items.summary: This record holds the complete evaluation results for the paper Improving Repair Agents with Cause-Chain Diagnoses . FORECAST is a debugging approach that gives repair agents a diagnosis of the failure before they start. From the executions of passing and failing tests, it infers a cause chain . This is a short sequence of execution features, such as conditions, data flow, values, and calls, that separate the failing from the passing runs. FORECAST appends this chain to the issue an agent receives, so it works with any agent without modifying it. The evaluation covers all 300 instances of SWE-bench Lite (test split). Five repair agents (mini-swe-agent, SWE-agent, AutoCodeRover, RepairAgent, and Agentless) ran with two models, Claude Haiku 4.5 ( claude-haiku-4-5-20251001 ) and Qwen3.5 27B ( qwen3.5:27b ). Each agent ran in two modes. In the baseline mode it received the issue, and in the forecast mode it received the issue plus FORECAST's diagnosis. This gives 20 runs of 300 instances each. Over all agents, the share of resolved issues rises from 48.5% to 70.9% with Claude Haiku 4.5 and from 31.2% to 56.1% with Qwen3.5. Contents forecast-results.tar.zst (320 MB, about 54 GiB and 908,277 files extracted) contains: README.md , which documents the layout of the archive and how to reproduce the analysis results.json , the per-instance results that all numbers in the paper are computed from diagnoses/ , FORECAST's diagnosis for each instance (cause chain with discriminability, the text appended to the issue, spectrum-based fault localization, and FORECAST's step report with times) <model>/<mode>/ , every repair run: the submitted patch, the agent's log, every LLM call with messages, responses, tokens and cost, the upstream agent's own trajectory, and the SWE-bench harness verdict with per-test status The files are archived byte for byte as the evaluation wrote them. The archive contains no API keys and no timestamps from the runs.
evidence_items.title: Improving Repair Agents with Cause-Chain Diagnoses

evidence_items.summary: This archive contains the Delphi 6 source code and a precompiled Win32 application used for benchmark calculations accompanying a study of quantile oriented sensitivity analysis based on a four-moment Hermite approximation. The software includes the local completion of the admissibility gap in the Hermite model. The application computes first-order and total QOSA indices for the four-input response Y1 and the five-input compressed steel member response Y3. The Y1 implementation includes shifted-sinh and exponential benchmark definitions. The application also evaluates unconditional moment diagnostics and the tail-hardness indicator and can generate Monte Carlo samples for Y1 and Y3. The QOSA calculations use a shared MRG32k3a pseudorandom number generator and the completed Hermite density and quantile functions. The archive contains the complete Delphi 6 source code and a precompiled Win32 executable. The code and parameter values are provided for transparency and reproducibility. Monte Carlo results may differ slightly between program runs because the generator is initialised from the system time.

evidence_items.summary: Cognitive screening is typically episodic and confined to clinical settings; however, early functional changes may first emerge during everyday activities and remain undetected in formal assessment. To examine such changes under realistic conditions, this study adopts a Living Lab approach, collecting Meta Aria first-person (egocentric) recordings during controlled daily-living tasks. Participant feedback and recording review informed successive protocol refinements and data- quality safeguards. The approach was evaluated in 30 clinician-labelled older adults (20 controls; 10 with mild or subjective cognitive impairment [MCI/SCI]) through two exploratory modelling paths governed by a shared evaluation contract. Path A uses learned multimodal representations to predict a 7-test cognitive composite (R² = 0.417) and distinguishes the MCI/SCI group from controls at balanced accuracy 0.80 [0.63–0.95], above an age + education + sex baseline (0.68) and below a neuropsychological-test comparator (0.85). Path B derives interpretable behavioural markers from head-motion, trajectory and gaze features, producing an auditable inventory of candidate cognitive markers. Together, the paths suggest that egocentric daily-living data contain cognition-relevant signal, that Living Labs can de-risk emerging egocentric AI for cognitive health, and that interpretable markers may support downstream Ambient Assisted Living applications.
evidence_items.title: From egocentric data to candidate cognitive markers: AI modelling with Meta Aria glasses in daily-living Scenarios

evidence_items.summary: Conformance vectors for agent execution evidence, and the reference verifier that judges them. This release carries 49 corpus manifests across 48 suites and 2,476 vectors in all, among them the in-toto adversarial-execution-evidence predicate, the in-toto ai-agent-action predicate, an AI generation predicate, the observed-effect predicate, SCITT COSE carriage, signed decision receipts and receipt chains, an anchor-stream verifier, ACS core, artifact binding, MCP response-phase interception, the OWASP MCP verification draft, the W3C per-check reporting format and intake, A2A agent-card canonicalization, delegation lifecycle, authority at dispatch, done contracts and receipts, grader isolation, spoofed tool output, test tampering, ACI deployments, and uncertain-effect cases. One binary judges every one of them, selected by the suite each corpus manifest declares. Each corpus digest is listed, recomputed from the vector files, in CORPUS-DIGESTS.txt, which the GitHub release signs and timestamps. The predicate's model is execute-and-attest rather than match-and-assert: a consumer recomputes the outcome from the bytes the statement carries, instead of trusting a verdict the producer asserted about itself. This repository is a second, independently usable implementation of that contract, so that any producer of the predicate type can self-certify and any consumer can reject a lying emitter. For the adversarial-execution-evidence corpus this deposit covers suite revision 32: 288 vectors, of which 63 accept, 223 reject and 2 are indeterminate. Its bytes are fixed by the corpus digest bf3e5befd71640757ff1b3f0af63507364b823b5e3f9059678f72f64a46e11c1 recorded in vectors/MANIFEST.json. A published revision is never mutated in place; a normative change to the predicate, or an addition to the corpus, bumps the revision and regenerates every vector byte-identically from its generators, because the vendored specification's digest is itself a corpus input.

evidence_items.summary: Industrial multimodal large language model (MLLM) benchmarks summarize performance with one accuracy, although that value also depends on test-set composition. We define a correct-option surface profile from relative word-like segment count, character length, question-option lexical overlap, and special expressions. Using 216,000 frozen responses to 2,400 MMAD-derived items, we audit specification robustness, adjusted associations, and profile-indexed consequences. Adjusted High-Low risk differences are 5.20-5.90 percentage points, but only 19 of 90 model-condition-context cells follow a strict Low-Medium-High order. Empirical composition profiles change standardized accuracy by -0.46 to +0.48 points relative to exact Balanced and produce four local point-order swaps in ten leaderboards, while Top-3 membership remains stable. The surface profile is therefore most informative for composition-aware interpretation of near-tied models, rather than as a stable shortcut-strength scale.
evidence_items.title: Correct-option surface profiles and composition sensitivity in industrial multimodal large language model evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Customer journey mapping (CJM) has fragmented into heterogeneous modelling practices, yet the epistemic consequences of that fragmentation remain poorly understood: it is unclear what each modelling logic makes visible and what it leaves out. This paper addresses that gap through a Design Science Research (DSR)–based Living Lab case study in a B2B membership organization, comparing two customer journey artefacts built on the same journey structure: a human-led, co-created journey and an AI-led journey derived from 2,379 customer comments. The two artefacts do not offer alternative pictures of the same experience; they produce different forms of emotional knowledge. The human-led artefact makes felt emotion visible: lived, situated experience articulated through narrative, meaning and identity. The AI-led artefact surfaces evaluative emotion: cumulative, judgement-based assessments of trust, fairness, tolerance and value for money that govern continuation or exit. The article therefore repositions customer journey mapping as comparative emotional knowledge production rather than the pursuit of a single accurate customer journey. For Living Lab research, it shows that human-led co-creation and AI-led synthesis are complementary participation logics, and that reading the two artefacts against each other is what renders an organization’s own assumptions about its customers visible and contestable.
evidence_items.title: Human-Led and AI-Led Customer Journey Mapping as Complementary Knowledge Production in a Living Lab

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can generate fluent responses but may overlook relevant evidence or violate task and safety constraints. This survey examines MLLM alignment through two complementary gaps: the Modality Gap, concerning cross-modal correspondence and the use of task-relevant evidence, and the Intent Gap, concerning behavior relative to specified goals, constraints, and human expectations. We organize the literature along six dimensions: architecture, objective functions, data construction, training, evaluation, and applications. Across these dimensions, we link alignment mechanisms and supervision assumptions to the failures they target and the evidence supporting their effectiveness. Our analysis clarifies what interface compatibility, target imitation, preference learning, and verifiable rewards can each demonstrate about alignment, together with the limitations of their underlying supervision. We further summarize evaluation at the representation, task, and behavior levels, emphasizing evidence dependence, constraint compliance, and the distinction between observed improvements and explanations of their underlying mechanisms. Applications in robotics, safety, healthcare, recommendation, and climate decision support reveal three recurring requirements: traceable evidence, valid supervision, and decisions that respect domain constraints. Building on this synthesis, we identify four research directions: evidence-consistent alignment across modalities, verified self-correction and test-time alignment, diagnosis-guided repair, and reliable transfer to underrepresented settings.
evidence_items.title: Alignment in Multimodal Large Language Models: A Survey

evidence_items.summary: Educational institutions face increasing pressure to adapt their curricula to the rapidly evolving demands of the job market, and recommender systems can be important tools to guide students in selecting courses that align with their career goals. We present EdFitter, a hybrid course recommendation system that combines pretrained text embeddings for retrieval with large language models (LLMs) used offline for semantic skill extraction. The system is designed for a cold-start setting in which free-text job queries must be matched to a university’s institutional course catalog. Instead of relying on direct generative recommendations, EdFitter ranks stored course descriptions by cosine similarity and augments the output with extracted skills and matching vacancy examples. We evaluate the system in a pilot institutional deployment at Higher School of Economics (HSE) using a multi-level study with student respondents, controlled assessors, and interviews with program directors. The results indicate that users perceive the recommendations as sufficiently relevant and potentially useful to justify further development. Overall, the study suggests that EdFitter is a valuable tool for supporting course exploration and curriculum-to-labor-market alignment; we also highlight important limitations and directions for future work.
evidence_items.title: EdFitter: a hybrid course recommendation system using large language models

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being explored for patient education and medical information delivery. However, their outputs may involve trade-offs among medical accuracy, comprehensiveness, empathy, and readability. Type 2 diabetes remission is a clinically nuanced concept that is readily misunderstood by patients, making it a suitable context in which to evaluate both the medical quality and patient accessibility of artificial intelligence–generated health information. To systematically compare the medical quality and readability of responses concerning type 2 diabetes remission generated by different LLMs and prompting strategies, and to characterize their joint quality–readability profiles. We conducted a cross-sectional study using a balanced factorial design. Responses were generated for 16 core questions concerning type 2 diabetes remission using 4 LLMs—DeepSeek-V3.2,GPT-5.5,Gemini 3.1 Pro and Claude Sonnet 4.6—and 6 prompting strategies: Keyword, Question, 6th-grade, Guideline, Patient, and Doctor. This yielded 384 AI-generated responses. Two endocrinologists, each with more than 5 years of clinical experience, independently evaluated medical quality using a prespecified rubric. Five domains—Accuracy, Relevance, Comprehensiveness, Empathy, and Falsehood avoidance—were rated on 5-point ordinal scales. A descriptive Composite quality score was also calculated. Readability was assessed using the Flesch Reading Ease Score (FRES), Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level (FKGL), Gunning Fog Index (GFOG), and Simple Measure of Gobbledygook (SMOG). Quality ratings were analyzed using cumulative link mixed models, whereas readability outcomes were analyzed using linear mixed-effects models; Question ID was included as a random intercept in all models. Exploratory analyses examined Spearman correlations between readability and quality and identified Pareto-efficient model–prompt combinations.
evidence_items.title: Quality and readability of large language model–generated responses on type 2 diabetes remission: a cross-sectional balanced factorial study
Exploring the adoption and evaluation of artificial intelligence research tools in licensed electronic resources

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become an exceptionally powerful tool for analyzing scientific data. In particular, attention-based architectures have demonstrated a remarkable capability to capture complex correlations and to furnish interpretable insights into latent, otherwise inconspicuous patterns. This progress motivates the application of AI techniques to the analysis of strongly correlated electrons, which remain notoriously challenging to study using conventional theoretical approaches. Here, we propose AI workflows for analyzing snapshot datasets from tensor-network simulations of the two-dimensional (2D) Hubbard model over a broad range of temperature and doping. The 2D Hubbard model is an archetypal strongly correlated system, hosting diverse intriguing phenomena including Mott insulators, anomalous metals, and high- T c superconductivity. Our AI techniques yield fresh perspectives on the intricate quantum correlations underpinning these phenomena and facilitate universal omnimetry for ultracold-atom simulations of the corresponding strongly correlated systems.
evidence_items.title: Interpretable Artificial Intelligence Analysis of Strongly Correlated Electrons

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Marine structures such as ships and offshore platforms often suffer structural deformation during service due to factors including collision and corrosion. After deformation occurs, the rapid evaluation of the hydrodynamic performance of structures is a prerequisite for ensuring safety and formulating maintenance strategies. To this end, this paper establishes a rapid evaluation framework for the hydrodynamic performance of deformed marine structures, which integrates image acquisition, Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based Three-Dimensional (3D) reconstruction, numerical simulation, and emergency decision-making. The specific procedure of the framework consists of four steps: First, a multi-view image acquisition scheme for structures considering deformed regions is designed to collect two-dimensional images and complete preprocessing. Second, the 3D model of the structure is reconstructed based on the HunYuan3D model, followed by preprocessing operations such as hole filling and topological repair. Third, the processed model is imported into hydrodynamic software to complete the numerical simulation and performance evaluation of the structure. Finally, a follow-up disposal plan is formulated and decision-making suggestions are provided based on the evaluation results.The framework is validated on a deformed ship: the errors of the governing geometric parameters of the reconstructed model are within 3%, and the simulated deterioration of the stability reserve and motion responses is consistent with the mechanisms reported for damaged hulls. Positioning the framework as a rapid preliminary screening and decision-support tool for emergency scenarios, the results demonstrate an efficient evaluation of the hydrodynamic performance of deformed structures with a balance among low cost, high efficiency, and verifiable reliability, providing data support for the emergency decision-making of deformed ships and offshore platforms.
evidence_items.title: A fast evaluation framework for the hydrodynamic performance of deformed marine structures using artificial intelligence-based three-dimensional reconstruction

evidence_items.summary: Molybdenum (Mo) is a promising replacement for Tungsten (W) in advanced semiconductor nodes due to its low resistivity and the elimination of the need for a barrier layer. Silica particle-based acidic slurries are commonly used in the chemical mechanical polishing (CMP) process, but complete removal of these particles is critical for subsequent processes. This study investigated particle contamination and cleaning mechanisms to develop effective cleaning solutions. Mo films were polished using H 2 O 2 as an oxidizer and colloidal silica as an abrasive under varying down pressures and rotation speeds to induce contamination. Dipping cleaning for 60 seconds in de-ionized water, 2 wt% ammonia, and potassium hydroxide (KOH) solutions were performed to evaluate particle removal efficiency. High oxidizer concentration and high slurry temperature were found to result in low cleaning efficiency. Mechanical friction effects, including the rotation speeds of the carrier head and platen and the down pressure of the carrier head, were also studied. Optimal conditions of 93 rpm platen speed, 87 rpm carrier head speed, and 1 psi down pressure yielded the fewest remaining particles after cleaning.
evidence_items.title: Silica Particle Contamination and Cleaning in Molybdenum CMP

evidence_items.summary: Rigorous management of metallic contamination is crucial in microelectronics to ensure device performance. For advanced laboratories seeking to work on a wide variety of diverse projects, one challenge is, for example, to make 3D integration technology using noble metals coexist with more sensitive technologies, such as photonics. To prevent metallic cross contamination between tools, recurrent backside and bevel cleaning is mandatory throughout the process flow. The aim of the paper is to find an alternative to traditional aqua regia mixture, which is known to dissolve noble metals. For this purpose, two promising solutions for metallic contamination removal are TechniClean IK73-based and TechniClean NPS78-based solutions. The TechniClean NPS78-based solution was almost as effective as aqua regia on noble metals but introduced bromide contamination. The TechniClean IK73-based solution showed varying effectiveness depending on the metal and substrate. Silicon consumption was a key parameter for contamination removal on silicon substrates. On oxide substrates, the addition of hydrogen peroxide enhanced metal removal efficiency. Stability tests over one week and metallic loading tests showed good performance, but issues with evaporation needed to be addressed. Transferring the process to a single wafer tool is expected to optimize performance and address eco-design requirements. Further evaluation will assess the lifespan of equipment and the potential for reclaimable chemistry.
evidence_items.title: Investigate an Alternative to Aqua Regia for Backside Metal Contamination Removal

organizations: Intelligent Comprehensive Transportation Key Laboratory of Sichuan Province
evidence_items.summary: Abstract LiDAR configuration selection in roadside sensing remains constrained by limited controlled evidence across sensors. To address this gap, we present MR-LiDAR, a controlled cross-configuration benchmark comparing four LiDAR configurations from 16 to 128 beams on dynamic vehicle and vulnerable road user (VRU) targets. Its cross-configuration main set covers matched daytime, nighttime, and vehicle-occlusion conditions, while three deployment and operating condition subsets examine mounting height, target speed, and curved-road geometry. By reducing confounding from scene and trajectory variation, MR-LiDAR links sensor configuration to target point acquisition and algorithmic detection outcomes. We characterize distance-dependent point loss, define effective beam count as the number of vertical beams intersecting the target’s angular extent, and introduce a point-based Occlusion Ratio. The results show that 16- and 32-beam configurations degrade earlier with distance, while VRUs exhibit greater point sparsity than motor vehicles. Nominal beam count alone is insufficient to explain roadside scanning capability. In the cross-configuration main set, the 80- and 128-beam configurations achieve comparable results, consistent with their nearly identical downward beam layouts. A uniform 80-beam counterfactual yields only about one third of the effective beam count of the actual non-uniform configuration. Illumination and the tested speed range have little influence on target-point-count patterns, whereas mounting height and near-field road geometry can substantially alter configuration ordering. Finally, an empirical minimal-sufficient configuration matrix combines frame-level geometric sufficiency with matched-box quality and includes threshold sensitivity analysis, providing bounded configuration guidance for the tested conditions. MR-LiDAR Benchmark is publicly available at https://github.com/ShunlaiC/MR-LiDAR-Benchmark .
evidence_items.title: Mr-LiDAR: a multi-resolution roadside LiDAR benchmark for perception diagnostics and deployment guidance

evidence_items.summary: Abstract In this study, we present the full (97.3% complete) 0.8–12.5 μ m spectral energy distribution (SED) of an L/T transition object, CWISE J210640.16+250729.0 (CW 2106), using the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). We provide a full characterization of the host star’s elemental abundances and age. We empirically derive the bolometric luminosity (≈ −4.825 dex) of CW 2106, and obtain estimates of its mass ( M ≈ 50–62 M Jup ), radius ( R ≈ 0.83–0.87 R Jup ), effective temperature ( T eff ≈ 1213 K), and surface gravity ( log g ≈ 5.28 dex). We find the near-infrared (near-IR) spectrum (0.8–2.5 μ m) is best reproduced with cloudy atmospheric models while the mid-infrared (mid-IR) spectrum (5–12.5 μ m) is best reproduced with cloudless models. This suggests a cloud layer restricted to only the deepest observable parts of the atmosphere and is qualified by the lack of a 9 μ m silicate feature. Making use of the Mg/Si ratio of the primary, alongside thermochemical models, we predict the clouds in CW 2106 to be composed primarily of enstatite (MgSiO 3 ), removing ∼23% of the bulk oxygen out of the atmosphere. Future retrieval studies will be able to help investigate the existence and full impact of these cloud species.
evidence_items.title: Sinking Silicates. I. Characterizing the Benchmark System Containing the T0 Brown Dwarf CWISEJ210640.16+250729.0 using JWST

organizations: University of National and World Economy Sofia Bulgaria
evidence_items.summary: ABSTRACT Oxygen transfer control in industrial bioreactors becomes more complex when cell metabolic changes, nonlinear process dynamics, energy constraints, and biological and operational uncertainties simultaneously affect control decisions. This study presents an innovative framework for intelligent oxygenation management that integrates a synchronized digital twin, agent‐based artificial intelligence, fuzzy‐notrosophic modeling, and multi‐objective decision‐making in a closed, uncertainty‐aware loop. The proposed framework enables predictive and safe decision‐making under variable conditions by continuously monitoring and reconstructing the process state, predicting short‐term behavior, generating and screening control options, and virtually evaluating them before implementation. Evaluation under normal operating conditions and biological and process disturbances showed that the complete framework achieved 98.04% dissolved oxygen stability and reduced the recovery time after oxygen demand shock to 7.26 min. The findings show that the main value of this architecture lies not in the single maximization of oxygen transfer, but in creating an adaptive balance between oxygen delivery, energy consumption, shear stress, biological stability, and operational risk. This framework provides an extensible platform for moving toward autonomous, resilient, and sustainable bioreactors.
evidence_items.title: Agentic Artificial Intelligence‐Driven Neutrosophic Multi‐Objective Optimization of Oxygen Transfer Systems in Smart Bioreactors

organizations: Management Department, School of Business Administration, Penn State Harrisburg, Harrisburg, PA 17057, USA
evidence_items.summary: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) changes digital retail from consumer-led search to delegated decision making, increasing both the potential value and the agency risks of recommendation. This conceptual article asks the following: Under what architectural and governance conditions can an autonomous shopping agent earn calibrated consumer trust while supporting economically and environmentally appropriate consumption decisions? Using a purposive, multidisciplinary synthesis of signaling theory, principal–agent theory, the ability–benevolence–integrity model of trust, trustworthy AI, recommender system governance, and sustainable consumption research, we develop a process model linking four architectural features to consumer perceptions, delegation, reliance, and decision outcomes. The features are scoped provenance verification, disclosed and audited commercial incentives, faithful contrastive explanations, and active evaluation of retention, repair, refurbishment, and purchase. We argue that justified non-purchase advice can function as a credible signal of consumer alignment only when the operator is the signal sender, the advice creates observable opportunity or accountability costs, and compensation and audit arrangements make imitation more costly for a misaligned operator. The framework distinguishes perceived trustworthiness from overall trust, willingness to delegate, actual reliance, recommendation appropriateness, and lifecycle sustainability. A five-layer architecture, a worked decision example, and four testable propositions specify how missing data, conflicting preferences, uncertainty, authorization, privacy, and accountability should be handled. This article treats the applications as illustrations rather than empirical cases and concludes with limitations and an empirical research agenda focused on calibrated—not merely increased—trust.
evidence_items.title: Developing Consumer Trust in Sustainable Agentic Commerce: Conditional Signals, Auditable Governance, and Justified Non-Purchase Advice

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Immune-related adverse events (irAEs) affect up to 40% of patients receiving immune checkpoint inhibitors, yet identification requires laborious, inconsistent manual chart review. Here we show that agentic artificial intelligence coupled with human verification could enhance efficiency, performance and consistency for irAE assessment. We developed and evaluated an agentic large language model system to extract the presence, temporality, severity grade, attribution and certainty of six irAE types from clinical notes. Retrospectively, the system achieved a macro-averaged F 1 of 0.92 for current-event detection and 0.66 for multi-class severity grading; self-consistency improved F 1 by 0.14. The best-performing configuration cost approximately US$0.02 per note. In prospective silent deployment over 3 months, the binary F 1 was 0.72–0.79. In a randomized crossover study of clinical trial staff, agentic assistance reduced annotation time by 2.71 min ( P < 0.001), increased complete-match accuracy (odds ratio 1.45; 95% confidence interval 1.01–2.08; P = 0.045) and improved interannotator agreement (Krippendorff’s α from 0.22–0.51 to 0.82–0.85).
evidence_items.title: An agentic AI system enhances clinical detection of immune-related adverse events in a multi-phase validation study

evidence_items.summary: Learning Labs are increasingly used to support experiential and innovation-oriented education, yet the mechanisms through which they generate learning remain poorly understood. This paper examines the GEM BizLab, a technology-enabled Learning Lab designed for technology and innovation management education. Drawing on Cultural-Historical Activity Theory (CHAT), the study analyzes thirteen student projects involving emerging technologies such as AI, robotics, haptics, and smart retail systems. Using a qualitative multimodal approach combining video recordings, presentations, student reflections, and course evaluations, we investigate how learning occurs during experimentation. The findings suggest that the educational value of BizLab lies less in technology exposure than in requiring students to transform ideas into prototypes and confront the consequences of their assumptions. Learning was strongest when experimentation revealed discrepancies between expected and observed outcomes, prompting reflection, redesign, and revision of underlying assumptions. The study proposes a contradiction-driven model of Learning Lab learning in which frugal prototypes and Wizard-of-Oz simulations function as boundary objects that make assumptions visible and discussable. The findings also provide practical insights for educators and Learning Lab practitioners seeking to foster innovation skills through experimentation and reflective practice.
evidence_items.title: The GEM BizLab as a learning lab for technology and innovation management

evidence_items.summary: Long-horizon agents performing multi-step Web tasks must reuse earlier page observations and interactions to support subsequent actions. However, preserving relevant history does not ensure that it exposes the relations needed for the current decision. We call this gap representation mismatch. To this end, we propose MemPrism, a task-conditioned relational memory framework that separates persistent experience storage from decision-time working memory. MemPrism records interactions as the event stream and dynamically constructs relational views according to the current task context. A lightweight view policy selects the relation structure, evidence range, outcome condition, and granularity, while a deterministic composer and renderer transform historical facts into a temporary optical working-memory view for a frozen task policy. Experiments on long-horizon embodied and web-agent benchmarks show that MemPrism consistently improves the task performance, especially as trajectories become longer, while reducing memory token consumption. Furthermore, the learned view policy transfers across different VLMs without additional adaptation, demonstrating the effectiveness of task-conditioned relational views as a general memory interface for agents.
evidence_items.title: MemPrism: Task-Conditioned Relational Memory Views for Long-Horizon Agents

evidence_items.summary: Background Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as conversational agents for communication and guidance, but their ability to adapt responses to a patient’s emotional state and literacy level remains insufficiently characterized. In patient-facing scenarios, effective communication requires not only accurate medical content but also appropriate tone, clarity, and responsiveness to user vulnerability. Objective This study aimed to evaluate, within a controlled, single-scenario experimental design, the ability of contemporary LLMs to adapt medical guidance responses to different levels of emotional sensitivity and literacy, and to assess their consistency in both generating and interpreting such adaptations. Methods A controlled benchmark was designed to evaluate how 4 LLMs adapt medical guidance responses to predefined emotional and literacy levels for a realistic patient profile asking an open-ended question. To establish a robust performance baseline, one model was deployed locally (Gemma 3 27B), and 3 are cloud-based (Claude Opus 4.5, Gemini 3 Pro, and GPT 5.2). Each model was tested across all combinations of 5 emotional levels, 3 literacy levels, and 3 prompt-verbosity variants, yielding 45 responses per model. Generated responses were assessed against human-reviewed ground truth for emotional and literacy alignment. A separate self-evaluation procedure measured each model’s ability to interpret its own outputs using the same adaptation framework. The study also examined generation-interpretation consistency and quantitative text properties, with particular attention to response length and verbosity. Results Literacy adaptation was consistently accurate across models, often achieving near-zero error, indicating strong capability in adjusting explanatory complexity. In contrast, emotional adaptation showed greater variability and was more sensitive to model architecture and prompt design.
evidence_items.title: Emotional and Literacy Adaptation in Large Language Model–Based Medical Guidance: Development and Usability Study

evidence_items.summary: Product design is a complex, knowledge-based process that balances customer needs with engineering constraints and market realities. While traditional methods such as Quality Function Deployment (QFD) and machine learning (ML) have improved the design process and solutions, they still struggle with flexibility and a deep semantic understanding of design requirements. Advances in Large Language Models (LLMs), powered by Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), create new opportunities for intelligent, human-centred support for product design. Following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, this systematic review analyzes 1,263 studies published between 2023 and 2026 to answer three questions: (1) how LLMs are applied across design stages, (2) how these systems are evaluated, and (3) what gaps remain. We found that LLMs successfully support design requirements analysis, ideation, and documentation. However, current evaluation methods lack standardized benchmarks for design quality. Persistent challenges remain, including hallucinations, weak domain grounding, tool-integration hurdles, and ethical concerns. To guide future research, we introduce a technical maturity map that highlights current achievements and uninvestigated areas in design systems and suggests a roadmap for applying LLMs in product design.
evidence_items.title: Large Language Models in Product Design: A Review

organizations: Department of Pulmonology, Affiliated Hospital of Changchun University of Chinese Medicine
The Affiliated Hospital to Changchun University of Chinese Medicine
evidence_items.summary: Differentiating Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) respiratory syndromes requires weighing overlapping symptoms together with tongue and pulse findings, a task that most AI systems for TCM perform end-to-end but without an interpretable intermediate representation. In this study, we addressed this gap with LEAF (LLM extraction and multiobjective feature selection), a two-stage modular framework evaluated on 3,253 records covering 14 respiratory syndromes from the TCM-SD benchmark. Its first large language model (LLM) stage extracted a 35-item symptom ontology that was built entirely from public TCM sources; among three interchangeable LLMs, Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct was ranked as the best, followed by Phi-4 and the TCM domain model BianCang. Its second evolutionary-computation stage benchmarked four multiobjective evolutionary algorithms [non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm-II (NSGA-II), strength Pareto evolutionary algorithm 2 (SPEA2), competitive mechanism-based multiobjective particle swarm optimizer (CMOPSO), and non-dominated sorting differential evolution (NSDE)] over 10 seeds, and they were compared using Friedman’s and Nemenyi’s testing in terms of both classification outcome and search-process quality. The four algorithms showed no significant separation on held-out macro-F1, although NSDE led nominally, and none exceeded the full-feature baseline on point estimates. In contrast, hypervolume differed significantly and favored NSGA-II, the weakest of the four on held-out macro-F1. A four-classifier panel found no algorithm to be significantly different from either the full-feature baseline or a random-feature control, which was significantly outperformed only by the full-feature baseline. Applying NSDE to the remaining two LLM pipelines reproduced the original ranking, and its representative solution was fully attested against the knowledge base of TCM-SD, although not typically so across all the 10 seeds.
evidence_items.title: LEAF: benchmarking multiobjective evolutionary feature selection over large language model–extracted symptoms for interpretable Traditional Chinese Medicine respiratory syndrome differentiation

organizations: 1School of Earth Sciences, University of Bristol, Bristol, United Kingdom

evidence_items.summary: ABSTRACT Microseismic monitoring is often used at subsurface industrial sites, such as hydraulic fracturing for shale gas, stimulation of engineered geothermal systems, mature hydrocarbon reservoirs, and carbon capture and storage. Microseismic observations can be used to map growing fractures in the subsurface, to understand the geomechanical response of subsurface reservoirs to industrial operations, and to identify and characterize nascent induced seismicity. Downhole microseismic datasets are acquired using multistation geophone strings placed in deep boreholes at reservoir depths, with sampling rates at 1 kHz or higher. Artificial intelligence (AI) tools have driven a step-change in the processing of surface-based seismological data. However, similar improvements are yet to be realized for downhole microseismic processing tasks. To date, a major barrier in the development of AI tools for downhole microseismic monitoring has been the lack of publicly available data with which to train models. We seek to eliminate this barrier by curating an AI-ready downhole microseismic benchmark database (AMBER) consisting of waveforms and labels (arrival time picks) drawn from 10 downhole microseismic datasets. AMBER contains over 4,000 events with over 150,000 individual P and S wave picks. All picks have been manually verified. The database also contains over 10,000 examples of signal-free noise, which have also been manually verified. The database is provided in an AI-ready format, with Python functions for data ingestion and data augmentation. It is hoped that AMBER will stimulate and support the development of AI tools for downhole microseismic processing.
evidence_items.title: The AI-Ready Downhole Microseismic Benchmark Database (AMBER)

evidence_items.summary: Direct beamforming methods in photoacoustic computed tomography are often compared under idealized conditions, making it difficult to distinguish artifact suppression from the preservation of weak structures. We benchmark seven direct beamforming methods and four limited-view adaptive minimum-variance variants in heterogeneous two-dimensional photoacoustic computed tomography simulations that incorporate fluence variation, full-wave acoustic propagation, finite-aperture detection, measurement noise, and incomplete angular coverage. Eleven phantoms were evaluated over multiple signal-to-noise ratios using phantom-level statistics. The delay-and-sum method most consistently preserved extended low-amplitude structures, achieved the highest peak signal-to-noise ratio among the direct methods, and showed the lowest mean globally scaled amplitude error. Coherence-, variance-, and multiplication-based weighting reduced clutter and often narrowed point responses, but also increasingly attenuated weak targets. Under severe full-view noise, delay-multiply-and-sum and delay-and-sum-to-delay-standard-deviation-factor weighting improved structural similarity while reducing peak signal-to-noise ratio and the Dice coefficient. In limited-view imaging, spatially smoothed minimum-variance beamforming produced small gains in structural similarity at 0 and −5 dB but lower peak signal-to-noise ratio, Dice coefficient, and generalized contrast-to-noise ratio. Sound-speed perturbations did not alter the leading ranking of the direct methods, while spatial point-target analysis revealed strong anisotropy. Cleaner or narrower reconstructions did not necessarily provide better preservation of structure or amplitude.
evidence_items.title: Direct beamforming for heterogeneous photoacoustic computed tomography: a two-dimensional benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Virtual screening answers two different questions with one number: enrichment, separating actives from background molecules, and potency ranking, ordering actives by measured activity. We benchmarked both for the same score on the same compounds across five CNS binding sites (SERT, GABAA benzodiazepine site, 5-HT1A, σ1, and NMDA MK-801 pore), docking ChEMBL actives, inactives, and property-matched decoys with Uni-Dock and GNINA under a held-out normalisation/evaluation split, plus an experimentally characterised negative probe excluded from all fitting. Ranking, evaluated among pChEMBL ≥ 7 actives, was negligible for every target (median Spearman ρ = 0.020) and was not recovered by data-quality filtering, multivariate null models, scaffold-aware resampling, strict assay–site matching with rebuilt decoys, or stricter curation. Enrichment proved strongly benchmark-dependent: an apparent ΔAUC gain of +0.153 against molecular weight-matched decoys decreased to ≤0.05 once the decoys were matched to seven descriptors, and the residue was not robust to compound resampling. A classifier using no structural information separated the same actives from the same decoys at ROC-AUC 0.959–0.993, and cognate ligand redocking reproduced the crystallographic pose as the top-ranked solution for one of five targets. Benchmark enrichment should not be equated with protein-specific recognition; the benchmark, the poses, and the ranking require separate validation.
evidence_items.title: A Decision-Centric Benchmark of Enrichment and Potency Ranking in CNN-Rescored Molecular Docking

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Dependable comparisons of minimum weighted feedback arc set (MWFAS) heuristics require consistent inputs, computational budgets, and treatment of incomplete runs. We present an audited benchmark linking weighted graphs and source-parent relationships to validated saved orders, original outcomes, and numerical optimization references. This resource extends an earlier metrics-only release and supports comparisons across graph families, paired weight regimes, and empirical sources. Incumbent-protected strongly connected component neighborhood search (IPSNS) showed family-dependent gains over its better initializer. Across all tested graph--seed groups in two generated-graph campaigns, ten iterations produced the same saved objectives and permutations as every larger tested budget. In the replicated campaign, family median process-wall ratios relative to the selected initializer were 1.27--1.60 at ten iterations, compared with 3.19--9.82 at 200. This observed trade-off is not a convergence or stopping guarantee. Under matched wall-clock horizons, IPSNS seed~1 beat RASstar on seven of nine selected synthetic topologies but only one of four selected empirical parents. At 300~s, single-node insertion from either evaluated initializer beat IPSNS seed~1 on all four parents. In a separate empirical campaign, complete 200-iteration comparisons covered only 18 of 38 views, all from one source parent. These findings show how budget, availability, dependence, and comparator choice affect interpretation. Public saved-output replay covers all ten numerical tables, Figure~2, and 11/17 tracked claim groups; six broader groups and historical-source reconstruction remain unresolved. The evidence supports scoped comparisons of existing methods rather than a universal ranking.
evidence_items.title: An Audited Benchmark for Minimum Weighted Feedback Arc Set: Graph Identity, Algorithm Comparison, and Reproducibility

evidence_items.summary: Multi-criteria decision systems often interpret disagreement among criteria as evidence that some criteria are unreliable. This is problematic when the disagreement reflects a genuine operational trade-off. We develop a reliability-and-admissibility-calibrated q-rung orthopair neutrosophic soft ranking procedure (RAC-qRON) that distinguishes recorded evidence quality from the direction of criterion preferences. An explicitly bounded interval for each alternative–criterion observation is mapped to truth, indeterminacy and falsity memberships, with an admissibility proof for every integer rung q ≥ 1. Criterion weights are adjusted according to recorded information coverage rather than cross-criterion correlation, and a fixed-reference ideal-distance calculation produces an auditable rank. The method is evaluated on 21 historical operating records from an ammonia-oxidation plant, using the published Brownlee stack-loss data, four transparently specified criteria and no fictitious expert panel. With q = 3, the leading historical observation is day 21 (closeness 0.6885). Under 10% randomly masked cells, the mean Kendall rank correlation with the respective complete-data ranking is 0.750 for RAC-qRON, versus 0.806 for median-imputed TOPSIS; the model therefore does not exhibit superior missing-data stability. Rung sensitivity also changes the winning observation. The principal contribution is a mathematically admissible, evidence-traceable decision layer and a reproducible diagnosis of its strengths and limitations, rather than an unsupported claim of universal ranking superiority.
evidence_items.title: Reliability-Calibrated Q-Rung Orthopair Neutrosophic Soft Ranking Under Partial Observability: An Auditable Industrial-Process Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Organic and polymer semiconductors are central to modern electronic and optoelectronic technologies, including organic thin-film transistors (OTFTs), solar cells, and bioelectronic devices. Controlling thin-film morphology is critical for optimizing the performance of organic electronic devices. However, the spin-coating process provides limited morphological control, and conventional characterization tools such as X-ray diffraction (XRD) and atomic force microscopy (AFM) are often insensitive to subtle structural changes that strongly influence charge transport. In this work, we demonstrate that spectroscopic ellipsometry (SE) combined with critical point (CP) analysis enables rapid, non-destructive assessment of microstructural evolution in regioregular poly(3-hexylthiophene) (rr-P3HT) thin films during thermal annealing. OTFTs based on P3HT were selected as a benchmark system due to their simple device architecture and well-defined structure–property relationships. The CP model provides physically meaningful optical parameters (transition energy, amplitude, broadening, and dimensionality) that correlate with electrical performance. Our results reveal a distinct shift in dimensionality of the primary optical transition upon annealing, indicating increased molecular ordering and reduced energetic disorder. These optically derived descriptors complement conventional structural probes and correlate with the observed improvements in charge transport. These findings offer a practical, non-destructive materials-focused approach for early-stage evaluation and process monitoring in organic electronics.
evidence_items.title: From Optical Transitions Through Morphology Changes to Charge Transport: A P3HT Benchmark Study Using the Critical Point Model

evidence_items.summary: Background Artificial intelligence (AI) for oral screening is usually judged by aggregate detection metrics on public benchmarks whose partitions, labels, and relevance to users are rarely checked. Methods We audited a prototype combining a YOLOv8m detector for six conditions (1,500 test images), a DenseNet169 histopathology network, and a ResNet18 router. Under a pre-specified plan, we measured duplication across partitions, tested removal of duplicated test images against 10,000 matched controls, compared duplicated copies' labels and predictions, compared the library versions, and ran every test image through the application pipeline. Results Near-duplicates of training images accounted for 17.3% of test and 17.1% of validation images (lower bounds). Removing duplicated test images changed mean average precision (mAP)@0.5 by +0.001 (95% confidence interval [CI] −0.012 to +0.014). Only 22% of duplicated photographs had identical labels on both copies; exploratory analysis suggested memorization of training labels in orientations seen in training. A library update moved mAP@0.5:0.95 by −0.012 with identical predictions. The router rejected 23% of in-domain photographs and 51% of photographs with ulcers, so ulcer sensitivity per image was 0.36 despite the highest benchmark recall (0.91). A class-mapping defect, still live in a public demonstration in September 2026, gave the wrong name to 73% of findings. The histopathology classifier classified every image as positive; its label was not a diagnosis. Conclusion Duplication compromised the benchmark's independence without detectably changing aggregate mAP; the defects that changed what was reported or displayed lay in the labels, evaluation software, and pipeline. Evaluations should verify partitions and labels, pin the library, and test deployed systems end to end.
evidence_items.title: From benchmark to user: an end-to-end evaluation audit of an AI-based oral health screening prototype

evidence_items.summary: Deep learning solar forecasters depend strongly on their hyperparameters, yet comparisons of hyperparameter optimization methods usually rely on few runs per optimizer, confounding the optimizer with the random seed. A protocol is proposed that tests whether optimizers are practically equivalent and how reliable published comparison designs are. Seven methods (four metaheuristics, two model-based methods, one of them multi-fidelity, and Random Search) tuned three deep networks for one-hour-ahead forecasting of global horizontal irradiance in Querétaro, Mexico, with public reanalysis data, a shared search space, one hundred evaluations, and thirty paired seeds, in nine hundred and thirty runs across all experiments. The tuned models improved on smart persistence by 4–11% in mean absolute error. With the 10-epoch search objective, no pair of optimizers differed after Holm correction, 62 of 63 pairs were equivalent within 1 W/m2, and the optimizer explained 0.8% of the error variance, compared with 7.9% for the seed. In a higher-fidelity check with 50 epochs, two guided methods improved on Random Search by 0.74 W/m2, significantly for one of them, while remaining equivalent to each other, suggesting that, in this setting, objective fidelity mattered more than the choice among guided optimizers. In emulations of published designs, even with 30 runs, 2 studies agreed on the winner in at most 55% of cases. A validated surrogate benchmark, code, data, and predictions are released.
evidence_items.title: Comparative Benchmark of Metaheuristic and Model-Based Hyperparameter Optimization for Deep Learning Models in Global Solar Irradiance Forecasting

evidence_items.summary: Abstract. Available water capacity (AWC) is a fundamental soil hydraulic property controlling plant water supply and drought response, yet existing AWC estimates for Switzerland's forests are an order of magnitude coarser than the scale of an individual tree’s root system. Here we produce 25 m resolution maps of mineral soil AWC for Switzerland's forest soils using ten published pedotransfer functions (PTFs) applied to a common set of gridded 25 m digital soil maps. We introduce a novel method for evaluating these PTF-derived AWC estimates using early leaf discoloration, an indicator of extreme drought stress, in European beech (Fagus sylvatica L.). Performance of single feature logistic regression models, using estimated AWC as a predictive feature and September 2018 early leaf discoloration as a target, varied substantially by PTF (ROC-AUC between 0.42 and 0.63). The strongest relationships between AWC and discoloration showed a negative trend and relatively strong model calibration (R² up to 0.82). Combining AWC with total 2018 summer precipitation and maximum 2018 summer temperature had little impact on model discrimination, but improved model calibration (R² up to 0.90) in late summer 2018 with discoloration proportions of nearly 80% at the most susceptible sites. Averaging the results of the four comparatively best-performing PTFs in these models produced two 25 m soil AWC products for the Swiss forest (mean 1 m and 2 m depth AWC) with uncertainty estimates based on variation among PTFs (± 1σ). While both the mapped AWC values and the relative performance of individual PTFs remain dependent on soil properties of the underlying digital soil maps, these new AWC estimates are immediately applicable to forest drought monitoring and species distribution, ecohydrological, and land-surface modelling.
evidence_items.title: Extreme drought stress provides an ecological benchmark for high-resolution available water capacity maps of Swiss forest soils

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Materials literature contains detailed experimental knowledge, but procedures, chemical entities and measurements remain difficult to aggregate because they are reported in heterogeneous forms and depend on process-specific context. We present SciKGExtract, a schema-guided framework that combines large-language-model extraction with chemical normalization and agent-based evaluation and refinement before knowledge-graph integration. We evaluate the framework on 176 atomic-layer-deposition papers describing zinc oxide (ZnO) and indium--gallium--zinc oxide (IGZO), together with an expert-annotated full-schema subset. PubChem normalization improves exact-match extraction F1 for every tested model. For ZnO, the best F1 increases from 0.591 for direct normalized extraction to 0.805 with agentic refinement, whereas the best IGZO result is 0.344, revealing the greater difficulty of multicomponent supercycle processes. Evaluation against a deeply nested schema containing 65 experimental properties and 155 quantitative measurement nodes further exposes errors in process segmentation and numerical assignment. These results show that chemical canonicalization and targeted agentic verification provide complementary controls for converting complex materials literature into reusable, machine-actionable experimental knowledge.
evidence_items.title: Agentic schema-guided extraction of materials process knowledge from scientific literature

evidence_items.summary: Enterprise agentic AI systems exchange contextual information across functional modules, creating governance challenges when information crosses operational and organizational boundaries. This study distinguishes organizational governance boundaries from information exchange boundaries and proposes an Inter-Module Information Contract (IMIC) architecture for purpose-bounded context exchange. IMIC evaluates provenance, semantic and temporal validity, permitted information scope, and applicable originating constraints before downstream execution, independently of language-model reasoning. We compare IMIC with full-context sharing, reduced-context sharing, and strengthened structured handoff. In a deterministic benchmark of 32 synthetic conditions, joint correctness is achieved in 3, 10, 28, and 32 cases, respectively. The four differences between strengthened structured handoff and IMIC arise from conditions testing onward-transfer permission, recipient, purpose, and field scope. A downstream integration experiment evaluates 14 selected conditions across four local language models and three seeds, yielding 168 case–model–seed blocks and 672 method-level records. IMIC achieves correct exchange actions and information boundaries in all 168 blocks and joint correctness in 165 across four local LLMs and three seeds. Three permitted executions produce incorrect downstream responses despite correctly governed exchanges, demonstrating that information-exchange correctness does not guarantee correct downstream task performance. These results support the functional feasibility of the implemented originating-contract inheritance mechanism under controlled synthetic conditions. Generalizability to independent enterprise workflows, richer policy structures, multiple information providers, and derived information requires further validation.
evidence_items.title: Purpose-Bounded Context Exchange in Enterprise Agentic AI Systems: An Inter-Module Information Contract Architecture

evidence_items.summary:
Bengali, spoken by over 230 million people, remains severely under-resourced in spoken language research. Existing open Bengali ASR corpora are confined to short, read or crowd-sourced speech and lack speaker diarization and long-form audio.
  We present Lipi-Ghor, a large-scale weakly-supervised Bengali speech corpus comprising 885 hours of audio sourced from 998 YouTube videos across 596 unique channels, spanning 17 diverse domains including audiobooks, drama, religious sermons, news, and regional dialects. Each recording is annotated in SSTT format (Speaker, Speech, Transcription, Timestamp), which combines automated diarization with Bengali YouTube caption tracks.
  To our knowledge, Lipi-Ghor is the first Bengali speech corpus to pair large-scale coverage with speaker-diarized, long-form audio annotations, both of which are absent from existing open Bengali resources. We also present the construction methodology as a replicable pipeline for any language with a sufficient captioned YouTube presence. Targeted channel curation across a handful of rich domains yields corpus scales that were previously out of reach for low-resource languages.
  We benchmark four widely-used ASR models under zero-shot and fine-tuned conditions. All four degrade consistently on emotive, dialectal, and long-form content. Because caption targets are noisy, we also release a human-annotated gold evaluation split, verified by 17 volunteer annotators over 30 hours of human-in-the-loop correction and stratified across all 17 domains.
  We release our original contributions (video-ID lists, diarization output, pipeline code, and the gold annotations) under CC-BY-4.0, and distribute caption-derived transcripts for research use only; no raw audio is redistributed.
evidence_items.title: Lipi-Ghor: A Large-Scale, Diarized, Multi-Domain Bengali Speech Corpus and a Scalable Pipeline for Building It

evidence_items.summary: How much of zero-shot benchmark accuracy is captured by word-level alignment between a pre-training corpus and the benchmark target? We study this question through word-level unigram cross-entropy (UCE), a tokenizer-agnostic, model-free measure of lexical alignment between a reference corpus and a target benchmark. Likelihood training shapes the model's predictive distribution from the pre-training corpus, and zero-shot scores under likelihood-based evaluation depend in part on the lexical alignment between that corpus and the benchmark target. Cleanly tracing how the lexical imprint of pre-training data scales with corpus--benchmark alignment requires controlled from-scratch pre-training that varies corpus identity while holding the training recipe fixed. Across this controlled sweep, spanning 10 zero-shot benchmarks, 4 pre-training corpora, and 3 model scales, we find that corpus--benchmark lexical alignment, UCE, consistently tracks zero-shot accuracy on every benchmark, with corpora more aligned with the benchmark (lower UCE) achieving higher accuracy. The same signal extends from measurement to control at finer scopes. At the document level, strengthening the imprint by selecting training documents to maximize lexical alignment with the benchmark produces the accuracy gains predicted by the mechanism. At the prompt level, matching the imprint per prompt by routing each prompt to the drafter whose domain corpus is most lexically aligned with it produces measurable throughput gains over a generalist-drafter baseline. Taken together, pre-training corpora leave a measurable lexical imprint on base-model zero-shot behavior, and UCE provides a model-free probe of lexical alignment between reference and target data.
evidence_items.title: The Lexical Imprint of Pre-training Data

evidence_items.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) is an effective way to strengthen the long-context reasoning of large language models (LLMs), but it needs training data that are long, diverse, challenging, and verifiable. Human annotation of such data is expensive, naturally occurring data are too scarce to sustain RL, and existing synthesis methods depend on external corpora or stronger teacher models, which become harder to obtain as the trained models get stronger. Recently, RL from zero data, in which a model learns from tasks it proposes itself, has achieved excellent performance, but existing methods target short-context tasks. Therefore, we propose LongZero, a method that lets an LLM improve its own long-context reasoning without any external data. Instead of writing questions and answers over existing documents, LongZero first has the model synthesize the question and answer with its supporting evidence in a compact structured form, and only then separately expands the evidence into a long multi-document context. LongZero combines these self-written multi-hop reasoning tasks with self-written multi-round retrieval tasks and trains the model with GRPO. We evaluate LongZero on two LLMs across five long-context reasoning benchmarks and compare it with RL on data synthesized from external corpora. Experimental results show that LongZero can generalize to real tasks, and outperforms both baselines, suggesting a viable and promising path to improving long-context reasoning of LLMs.
evidence_items.title: LongZero: Enhancing Long-Context Reasoning in LLMs from Zero Data

evidence_items.summary: The rapid progress of software engineering agents drives interest in applying them to open-ended problems such as GPU kernel optimization. However, we find that existing coding agents converge to local optima on real-world, expert-written kernels (e.g., FlashInfer). We introduce Evolving Agent Teams, a multi-agent framework that escapes such local optima. It features (1) a central supervisor that diagnoses each local optimum and restructures a team of agents; and (2) a persistent file system that comprises a learning document, an evolution history, and per-team artifacts, grounding restructuring with accumulated experience. Under a matched token budget, Evolving Agent Teams consistently outperforms strong coding-agent baselines. With an extended token budget, Evolving Agent Teams generates a CUDA kernel that reaches 1.2x mean speedup over the production FlashInfer MLA paged decode kernel from scratch and wins on 36 of 47 production workloads from FlashInfer-Bench (0.86-0.99x on the remaining 11). It also demonstrates superior performance on tasks such as KDA prefill on AMD MI350X (3.01x over vLLM) and NVIDIA B200 (3.44x over FlashKDA), MoE expert-offload serving on Apple silicon (30.3 tokens/s decode for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next in MLX 4-bit on a 48 GB M4 Pro), and RoboDojo robot manipulation (62.1 on held-out seeds vs. 55.3 for the best leaderboard entry). Code is available at https://github.com/caoshiyi/EAT.
