evidence_items.summary: Diffusion video models produce striking clips, but they cannot reliably render an exact formula, a correct chart, a rule-consistent game or narration synchronized to on-screen events. A different route is emerging: multimodal agents that write code to render every frame and synthesize every sound. We introduce VibeVideoBench, a benchmark for evaluating agents on code-driven video generation. Its 239 self-contained tasks in English and Chinese span 12 categories, from data stories and music-driven pieces to classroom lessons and paper explainers; each asks an agent, running in its native harness inside a sandbox with no image or video generation model, to deliver a finished MP4 with sound within one hour. Evaluation is hierarchical and evidence-based: program checks of the delivery spec, about 13k task-specific rubric checks traced to the requirements they enforce, and five quality dimensions anchored per task, scored by three VLM judge panels. Across nine frontier agent systems and 2,151 scored rollouts, GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 rank first and second with both the judges and human annotators, and the strongest system satisfies every core requirement on 76.3% of tasks. Delivery is a second axis: counting missing videos as zero changes the ranking, and three quarters of the lost videos are final renders that started too late, ran too slowly or never started, a failure of how agents plan their hour. Agents build their own rendering pipelines and inspect their own frames, yet how much they look does not predict quality. The judges' ranking of the systems closely matches blind human preferences.
evidence_items.title: VibeVideoBench: Evaluating Multimodal Agents on Code-Driven Video Generation

evidence_items.summary: Learning controllable world dynamics from heterogeneous interaction videos is challenging because robot embodiments use incompatible action spaces, while human videos lack native control labels. We present RynnWorld-Latent, a cross-embodiment video world model that uses the 3D-grounded latent actions introduced by RynnLAM as a shared conditioning interface. This representation enables joint pretraining on human interaction videos, robot demonstrations, and simulation rollouts without requiring a common native action space. Built on a pretrained video transformer, RynnWorld-Latent combines global action tokens with an identity-initialized local pathway that aligns actions with future video latents. We pretrain on 23 datasets comprising approximately 553.5M frames and adapt the model to target robots through post-training. The framework supports two data-generation routes: digital teleoperation uses target robot commands to generate action-video demonstrations, while latent-action synthesis transfers source motion to an edited initial frame and pairs the resulting rollout with retargeted pseudo robot actions. Experiments show improved video prediction metrics on public benchmarks and two real-robot platforms, alongside qualitative action following when different action sequences share the same initial observation. Synthetic mid-training improves policy success rates on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus, and both generation routes improve real-world policy success rates over real-demonstration-only training in the evaluated settings. These results support universal latent actions as a scalable interface for learning controllable visual dynamics across heterogeneous embodiments.
evidence_items.title: RynnWorld-Latent: A Cross-Embodiment World Model Conditioned on Universal Latent Actions

evidence_items.summary: Video stylization typically transforms entire scenes, while local artistic editing requires precise region--style association, spatial control, and temporal consistency. We introduce LociArt, a unified paradigm for free-style local video stylization that explicitly specifies where to stylize and what style to apply while preserving non-target content. At its core, GRNStyle builds on Generative Refinement Networks (GRN) and introduces a polar style-aware mask that embeds style identities as equal-norm directions within selected regions. Complementary representation--geometry conditioning combines encoded mask features with raw-mask spatial support, integrating spatiotemporal context with geometric control. To provide paired supervision, we develop an automated pipeline combining global stylization, video object removal, matting, and compositing, and construct the LociArt-100K Dataset with 100K local stylization pairs. We further establish the LociArt Benchmark, comprising 80 source videos and 84 target masks covering 168 foreground/background stylization cases, with a Style Prototype Similarity (SPS) evaluation scheme for regional style quality and complementary measures of non-target preservation and temporal consistency. Experiments show that GRNStyle outperforms existing methods in regional style quality and spatial control while maintaining strong temporal consistency. Qualitative examples further illustrate joint stylization of multiple regions with the same or different learned styles, despite training only on single-region, single-style pairs. Together, these components provide a unified foundation for learning and evaluating controllable local video stylization. Project page: https://higherhu.github.io/lociart/.
evidence_items.title: LociArt: A Unified Paradigm for Free-Style Local Video Stylization

evidence_items.summary: Omnimodal large language models (Omni-LLMs) are increasingly expected to assist users while observing continuous audiovisual streams. However, existing evaluations provide limited insight into how reliably these models connect stream evidence and user needs to timely, sustained interventions. We introduce Omni-InteractScope, a benchmark of 1,479 human-annotated, cross-reviewed interactions with 1,790 temporal targets across eight task groups. It links input modalities, event triggers, intervention types, and user needs, covering event-timed tool invocation and query-free assistance alongside notifications, warnings, state tracking, and continuous responses. Our experimental results on the proposed benchmark reveal three critical limitations of current Omni-LLMs: (1) Timely tool invocation remains unreliable: all 12 evaluated models produce an on-time first response for at most 40\% of tool-invocation targets, and joint timing-and-tool accuracy reaches at most 32.0\%. (2) Query-free reminders remain poorly covered: all evaluated models achieve lower timely reference-target recall on query-free reminders than on explicit questions, measured on their respective target sets. Reminder recall never exceeds 23.0\%. (3) End-to-end guidance coverage remains limited: nine models cover none of the 26 guidance sequences in full, and the remaining three cover only one to three sequences each. Targeted controls further show that tool-invocation scores alone do not establish event grounding and that reminder coverage depends on response history and frequency. These findings motivate developing and evaluating streaming assistants for timely action, initiative under general user needs, and coverage of entire response sequences.
evidence_items.title: Omni-InteractScope: Benchmarking Proactive and Agentic Interaction in Continuous Omnimodal Streams

evidence_items.summary: AI agents must decide when another search is worth its cost. Answer-success probabilities capture question difficulty, while this decision requires estimating the additional benefit of search. We introduce SearchHorizonBench, a benchmark for learning and evaluating search value from execution experience. Paired continuations and repeated executions separate expected search gain from generation noise and connect prediction quality to decision utility. The resource contains 45,632 executions across 3,168 questions. On 1,632 held-out questions, historical calibration reduces Brier error by 16.2%, with the improvement concentrated in success-level information. Search gains have a standard deviation of 21.4 percentage points, and tested historical estimators explain less than 2% of this variance in point estimates. Matched-configuration learning curves probe this distinction across training scales. At the reference token price, free selection observations yield a 2.49-point utility opportunity over the best constant action, driven primarily by gain information. Reusable histories, frozen splits, strong baselines and scoring tools provide a common foundation for developing and evaluating value-aware search agents.
evidence_items.title: SearchHorizonBench: A Benchmark for Search Value in AI Agents

evidence_items.summary: Can AI agents autonomously train useful language models and improve them using feedback from users? We introduce RSI Arena, a two-stage study of autonomous post-training as a step toward recursive self-improvement. Ten frontier models act as training agents, each starting from NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Lightning 30B-A3B Base. During a six-day first stage, each agent has 1,000 GPU-hours and $300 in API credit on a shared 64-GPU cluster, independently selecting data, implementing training procedures, and choosing checkpoints. We evaluate their models on 20 benchmarks and through blind human evaluations. All ten agents produce working assistants, with the strongest model, trained by GPT-6 Astra, closing a median of 76% of the base-to-Instruct gap across 12 capability benchmarks. Its human-preference rating is also close to NVIDIA Instruct after statistical adjustment for answer length and formatting. In Stage 2, each agent receives the comparison records and votes involving its Stage 1 model and is given three additional days for further training. Using NVIDIA Instruct as a common reference across the two evaluation rounds, we observe an improvement from Stage 1 to Stage 2 in the style-adjusted relative rating of eight of the ten models. We show that benchmark gains were modest, with no clear link to preference gains, while some agents encouraged longer responses and one model showed increased harmful compliance on StrongREJECT. RSI Arena provides an auditable setting for studying how human feedback can guide autonomous model development. It takes a step toward recursive self-improvement with human feedback (RSIHF), in which people help define what improvement means for the AI systems they use.
evidence_items.title: RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement with Human Feedback

evidence_items.summary: Command-line interface (CLI) agents increasingly execute longer-horizon tasks, yet existing benchmarks either assume that user instructions remain fixed throughout execution or evaluate task outcomes without capturing runtime collaboration quality. In this paper, we present REALCLI, a paired benchmark that unifies the evaluation of task execution and human-agent collaboration quality on realistic CLI tasks. To comprehensively measure collaboration, REALCLI builds a five-dimensional framework, operationalized into 22 sub-dimensions and 51 interaction scenario templates. REALCLI provides two modes for paired comparison: REALCLI-EXEC supplies complete specifications upfront, whereas REALCLI-COLLAB introduces a scripted user that delivers progressive information, corrections, constraint revisions, and authorization decisions. Evaluations reveal profound capability gaps in frontier agents: the best configuration attains an average score of only 49.2%, and when evaluated by the joint collaboration score (J_{collab}), the peak performance reaches merely 37.6%. These results show that task effectiveness diverges sharply from collaboration quality, with models consistently struggling in steerability, trust calibration, and safety boundary management. REALCLI provides a rigorous, reproducible foundation for measuring and advancing collaborative CLI agents.
evidence_items.title: RealCLI: Toward a Unified Evaluation of Human-Agent Collaboration for CLI Agents

evidence_items.summary: Many Indian banks serve customers through FAQ pages and scripted chatbots. Assistants based on language models could respond faster and carry out requests such as blocking a card, but only if they give correct information and follow the bank's rules. These rules prescribe a procedure, a set of required steps, such as obtaining a closure quote before closing a deposit. Adapting models to this domain requires measuring how well they follow the procedure, before and after training. Benchmarks usually judge only the records left at the end of a conversation. Many required steps, however, leave the records unchanged, so an assistant that skips them can still be judged successful. We present TauIndianBankBench, an action-oriented benchmark of 1,000 Indian retail-banking tasks where an assistant helps a simulated customer. Besides the final records, it checks that the assistant took every required step and made no unrequested change. For every model, 6.5-12.0% of sessions are judged successful when only the final records are checked, although the assistant skipped a required step or made an unrequested change. Scoring both procedure and outcome shows more accurately how well language models perform in Indian retail banking.
evidence_items.title: TauIndianBankBench: Procedure-Aware, Action-Oriented Evaluation of Tool-Using Conversational Agents

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Artificial intelligence is increasingly being applied to the assessment, monitoring and care of older adults, with potential benefits across both population health and individual clinical practice. This narrative review examines current and emerging applications of AI in common conditions and care needs associated with ageing, including hypertension, stroke, myocardial infarction, Parkinson’s disease, osteoporosis, sarcopenia and supportive care robotics. Across these domains, AI-enabled analysis of electronic health records, electrocardiograms, imaging, video, wearable-sensor data and home-monitoring measurements may support earlier disease detection, more objective functional assessment, personalised risk prediction and treatment, and greater independence. Computer-vision approaches may provide detailed measures of movement following stroke and in Parkinson’s disease, while opportunistic analysis of existing imaging may improve recognition of low bone mineral density, vertebral fractures and reduced muscle health. Care robots may additionally assist with companionship, medication management and falls detection. However, much of the evidence remains based on selected datasets, proof-of-concept studies or controlled settings. Algorithmic bias, limited representation of frail and multimorbid older adults, privacy, governance, interpretability, interoperability, user burden and workforce consequences remain important barriers. AI should therefore complement rather than replace clinical judgement. Equitable implementation will require representative datasets, rigorous external and prospective validation, transparent models, user-centred design and evaluation of clinically meaningful outcomes.
evidence_items.title: Artificial intelligence in an ageing population

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Reliable plant-disease segmentation depends on evaluation images being independent of the data used for training. We audited PlantSeg, a large in-the-wild semantic-segmentation benchmark, to determine whether visually related image families cross its released partitions and whether such exposure changes the evidence produced by standard segmentation models. The audit combined multiple similarity signals with human adjudication, followed by contamination-aware re-evaluation, class-count-matched Monte Carlo controls, a two-seed training-exposure experiment, long-tail analysis, and group-disjoint benchmark reconstruction. Verified cross-split visual families involved about 10.7% of the released images. Across four canonical architectures, released-split evaluation was consistently more favorable than contamination-aware evaluation, and the main shifts persisted after controlling for disease-class composition. The training side exposure had very limited effect in the independent clean test cases but was seen to have an estimated 11–15% advantage in related contaminated test cases in both seeds. Deletion of family ties improved independence at the cost of rare class support; while the group-disjoint reconstruction kept all 115 disease classes intact while removing known family ties. This illustrates that benchmark contamination can be overestimated and family-aware split construction is a viable solution.
evidence_items.title: Improving Reliability in Plant Disease Semantic Segmentation by Quantifying Benchmark Contamination and Duplicate Family Exposure

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Activation functions (AFs) play a pivotal role in defining the representational power and learning dynamics of deep neural networks (DNNs). However, their influence on medical image restoration (MIR) remains insufficiently explored. This empirical study presents a comprehensive, multi-phase investigation into how different AFs affect spatial and frequency characteristics across MIR tasks, such as image deblurring, image deblocking, and image super-resolution, in three medical imaging modalities: computed tomography (CT), digital mammography (DM), and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). The study integrates a theoretical taxonomy of AFs, a fixed-weight analysis, and a full-scale empirical evaluation involving 15 representative AFs spanning classical, rectified, exponential, and modern smooth families, benchmarked across 3,000 medical images. These functions are implemented within two widely used state-of-the-art MIR architectures: U-Net and Enhanced Deep Super-Resolution (EDSR). Model performance is evaluated using Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR), Structural Similarity Index Measure (SSIM), Edge Preservation Index (EPI), High-Frequency Energy Ratio (HFER), and Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS), with statistical validation performed using Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) and Tukey’s Honestly Significant Difference (HSD) tests. Results reveal that while the Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) and its variants remain strong baselines due to their stability and efficiency, smoother and adaptive functions such as the Gaussian Error Linear Unit (GELU), Mish, and Funnel ReLU (FReLU) achieved superior performance in preserving fine spatial and frequency details.
evidence_items.title: An empirical benchmark of activation functions for medical image restoration networks

evidence_items.summary: Purpose This viewpoint examines organizational implications of agentic AI systems in planning, selecting tools, executing multistep actions, and evaluating their own outputs with limited human intervention. Design/methodology/approach This viewpoint synthesizes academic and practitioner insights to identify key organizational challenges associated with agentic AI drawing on organizational learning theory and recent research on human–AI collaboration, and propose practical directions for HR and learning and development. Findings As agentic AI becomes more autonomous, it is reshaping organizational learning, human oversight, and accountability. Organizations will need to redesign learning practices and governance mechanisms to ensure that people and AI work together effectively. Research limitations/implications This conceptual viewpoint does not include empirical validation. Future research should examine the proposed ideas across different organizational settings. Practical implications Organizations should assess workforce readiness, redesign learning around human–AI collaboration, and establish feedback mechanisms that strengthen learning, oversight, and accountability. Originality/value This viewpoint shifts the discussion from technological capabilities of agentic AI to its organizational implications, offering practical guidance for organizations adapting to increasingly autonomous forms of work.
evidence_items.title: Agentic AI in organizations: reimagining learning, autonomy, and human oversight

evidence_items.summary: Objective: Agentic AI represents a paradigm shift from reactive systems to autonomous agents capable of perception, planning, reasoning, memory management, and tool usage without human intervention. This paper proposes the Healthcare Autonomous Reasoning Network (HARN), a multi-agent system designed to assist physicians with real-time diagnosis, treatment recommendations, and drug interaction detection. Methods: This paper introduces HARN’s architecture featuring a large language model (LLM) orchestrator coordinating four specialized sub-agents: radiology interpretation, electronic health record (EHR) exploration, pharmacological advice, and risk stratification. Experiments leverage the MIMIC-IV clinical dataset and curated drug interaction databases to evaluate diagnosis accuracy, decision latency, and hallucination rates. Expected results: HARN demonstrates an F1-score of 0.873 and 41% reduced clinical decision-making latency compared to baselines. Conclusions: The results validate the feasibility of agentic multi-agent systems for high-stakes healthcare applications, demonstrating better performance in autonomous clinical decision support.
evidence_items.title: Agentic intelligence: multi-agent systems for autonomous healthcare diagnostics and treatment planning

evidence_items.summary: Agentic artificial intelligence systems combine autonomous planning, memory, tool use, and multi-agent coordination, creating risks that extend beyond the behavior of an individual model to include interactions with external environments and operational workflows. Trustworthy deployment therefore requires assurance that integrates explainability, security, reliability, and governance across system layers and throughout the lifecycle. This paper proposes a unified framework that connects decision- and action-level explanations with threat modeling, bounded permissions, runtime verification, traceability, and reliability monitoring. It treats explanations as one component of assurance rather than a sufficient basis for trust, and situates them alongside calibrated human oversight and enforceable operational controls. The framework provides a structured basis for designing and evaluating agentic systems whose actions are interpretable, constrained, and auditable.
evidence_items.title: Trust by Design: A Unified Framework for Explainable, Secure, and Reliable Agentic Artificial Intelligence

evidence_items.summary: Neuro-AI fusion represents an emerging interdisciplinary field that combines neuroscience, artificial intelligence (AI), computational modeling, and intelligent biomedical technologies to understand, assess, and modulate nervous system functions. By integrating neural signals, physiological measurements, clinical assessments, and behavioral data, these technologies offer new opportunities to improve pain management, sensory assessment, and motor control. Traditional neurological evaluations often depend on clinical examinations, patient-reported symptoms, and specialized diagnostic procedures. Although these approaches remain essential, they may not fully capture the dynamic and complex interactions underlying neurological function. AI-based systems can address some of these limitations by identifying subtle patterns in high-dimensional data, supporting personalized assessments, and facilitating continuous monitoring. In pain medicine, machine learning algorithms can analyze physiological signals, neuroimaging findings, and behavioral indicators to support pain classification, severity estimation, and treatment selection. These applications may be particularly valuable for patients who cannot reliably communicate their symptoms. In sensory neuroscience, intelligent systems can enhance the interpretation of visual, auditory, and somatosensory information, potentially improving diagnostic accuracy and supporting the development of adaptive sensory prostheses. Similarly, integrating AI with electromyography, electroencephalography, wearable sensors, and brain-computer interfaces can facilitate motor assessment, rehabilitation planning, and the control of assistive devices. The combination of neural decoding and adaptive algorithms also enables the development of closed-loop systems that adjust stimulation or assistance according to changing physiological conditions.
evidence_items.title: Neuro-AI Fusion: Integrating Nervous System Functions with Intelligent Technologies for Pain, Sensory, and Motor Control

evidence_items.summary: Solvents dominate the environmental footprint of chemical synthesis, yet their selection remains governed by precedent ratherthan sustainability. Here, we analyse 1.3 million classified reactions from 40 years of patent data, distinguishing for the firsttime between reaction, workup, purification, and analytical solvents. Despite decades of awareness of solvent hazards and thepublication of influential solvent selection guides, we find no net reduction in the proportion of hazardous solvents used asreaction media. Dichloromethane usage has grown, and rising trifluoroacetic acid consumption intensifies concerns over per-and polyfluoroalkyl substances. Where regulations have removed specific solvents, chemists have defaulted to lateral substitution,replacing one hazardous solvent with another rather than adopting greener alternatives. We identify the reaction classes mostdependent on each problematic solvent, providing a data-driven framework for prioritising targeted intervention over blanketregulation. Crucially, these findings expose systemic biases in historical datasets that threaten to turn AI solvent-prediction modelsinto engines for proliferating outdated, hazardous practices rather than advancing sustainable chemistry.

evidence_items.summary: People often seek advice when choosing a film, a book, or another experience whose value depends on their tastes. Large language models (LLMs) provide a convenient way to obtain such advice. We test a simple method for improving their predictions, inspired by the wisdom of the inner crowd. An LLM first predicts a person’s movie rating from that person’s past ratings. It then predicts how the general public, given the same history, would predict the same person’s rating. Averaging takes the arithmetic mean of these two responses. We evaluated 12 GPT model snapshots using MovieLens 1M. A history-size study tested 1–20 ratings for 55 users and extended the comparison to 55 ratings for 32 eligible users. Averaging improved mean squared error relative to the first response even at the longest history. A subsequent evaluation used 10 target films per person with 10 fixed history ratings. Across 320 user–movie pairs, mean squared error was 1.218 for the first response, 1.147 for the public-perspective response, and 1.150 for Averaging. Additional analyses showed that Averaging reduced errors of at least 1.5 rating points, whereas the first response produced more exact matches. These advantages did not extend to every error threshold or metric. The findings connect inner-crowd research with a simple conversational method for preference prediction and show why the choice of response should reflect the prediction objective.
evidence_items.title: Improving Large Language Model preference prediction by averaging two perspectives

evidence_items.summary: Urban next point-of-interest (POI) recommendation is fundamental to location-based services, yet accurate prediction remains challenging because user trajectories are sparse, semantically incomplete, and tightly constrained by time and geography. Recent graph and Transformer models capture transition regularities, while language model-based recommenders introduce textual knowledge, but these two lines of work remain weakly coupled: semantic priors may be plausible in language space yet infeasible under a user’s actual mobility state, and purely behavioral encoders fail to infer latent intent when observations are scarce. We introduce STELLAR, a unified state transition framework that treats language knowledge as a calibrated prior rather than an independent prediction branch. STELLAR first induces semantic mobility priors from structured trajectory descriptions, then projects them into a shared transition state and learns a feasibility gate conditioned on spatial reachability, temporal rhythm, and both short- and long-term behavioral context. A transition memory subsequently propagates this calibrated state to candidate POIs, allowing semantic evidence to influence prediction only when it is consistent with executable mobility. This design directly addresses semantic-behavioral misalignment and avoids ad hoc late fusion. Across three public check-in benchmarks, STELLAR consistently outperforms both purely behavioral and language-augmented baselines in ranking accuracy, robustness to corrupted trajectories, and cold-start generalization.
evidence_items.title: STELLAR: Large Language Model Enhanced Spatiotemporal Semantic Fusion for Urban Next POI Recommendation

evidence_items.summary: ABSTRACT Food safety sampling is a critical measure for safeguarding public health; however, current regulatory practices are challenged by fragmented risk signals, constrained inspection resources, and suboptimal inspection efficiency. To address these issues, this paper proposes a food safety sampling decision‐making method based on large language models (LLM)–guided Q‐learning. First, we leverage LLMs to extract and analyze key elements from unstructured online food safety public opinion data. This is integrated with clustering analysis and the entropy weight method to achieve quantitative risk assessment and grading. Subsequently, a food category–region risk score matrix is constructed, and the allocation of sampling frequency is formalized as a sequential decision‐making problem under resource constraints. Q‐learning is then introduced to learn optimal sampling strategies, using LLM‐generated structured heuristic values as prior guidance, thereby reducing ineffective exploration and enhancing training efficiency. Experimental results, based on data from 30 provincial administrative regions, 457 municipalities/counties, and 25 food categories, generated 4690 risk evaluation records as effective inputs for decision‐making. The results demonstrate that the derived sampling strategies align with risk priors, allocating higher sampling intensity to high‐risk food category–region combinations while maintaining coverage balance across food categories and regions. Compared to the baseline without heuristic guidance, LLM guidance significantly reduces convergence iterations while maintaining steady‐state rewards. This indicates that the proposed method accelerates policy learning without compromising long‐term returns. In conclusion, this study validates that the proposed method achieves a closed‐loop integration of risk assessment and decision optimization, providing a data‐driven methodology for intelligent food safety regulation.
evidence_items.title: A Large Language Model–Guided Q‐Learning Method for Food Safety Sampling Decision‐Making

evidence_items.summary: Using multimodal large language model (LLMs) to generate and popularize short health-science videos can significantly shorten their production cycle. This practice plays a vital role in lowering the public’s access threshold to health knowledge and promoting the high-quality dissemination of scientific health popularization content. However, due to the limitations of creators, regulators and multimodal LLMs themselves, these generated short videos may still lead to the spread of misleading health knowledge, posing potential risks to public health cognition. Therefore, it is urgent to construct a systematic and automatic evaluation system for such health science popularization short videos. In this paper, we propose an automatic evaluation model for such short videos by leveraging the well-known Source-Channel-Recipient (SCR) framework in the field of information communication. This automatic evaluation model includes three parts: an automatic review mechanism for Source, an automatic technology-optimization mechanism for Channel, and an automatic feedback-optimization mechanism for Recipient.
evidence_items.title: An Automatic Evaluation Model for Health Science Popularization Short Videos Generated by Multimodal Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Large Language Models (LLMs) are transforming language sciences. However, their widespread deployment currently suffers from methodological fragmentation and a lack of systematic soundness. This study proposes two comprehensive methodological frame works designed to guide the strategic and responsible application of LLMs inlanguage sciences. The first method-selection framework defines and systematizes three distinct, complementary approaches, each linked toa specific research goal: (1) prompt-based interaction with general-usemodels for exploratory analysis and hypothesis generation; (2) fine tuning of open-source models for confirmatory, theory-driven investigation and high-quality data generation; and (3) extraction of contextualized embeddings for further quantitative analysis and probing of model internal mechanisms. We detail the technical implementationand inherent trade-offs of each method, supported by empirical casestudies. Based on the method-selection framework, the second systematic framework proposed provides constructed configurations that guide the practical implementation of multi-stage research pipelines based on these approaches. We then conducted a series of empirical experiments to validate our proposed framework, employing retrospective analysis, prospective application, and an expert evaluation survey. By enforcing the strategic alignment of research questions with the appropriate LLM methodology, the frameworks enable a critical paradigm shift in language science research. We believe that this systemis fundamental for ensuring reproducibility, facilitating the criticalevaluation of LLM mechanisms, and providing the structure necessaryto move traditional linguistics from ad-hoc utility to verifiable, robust science.
evidence_items.title: Systematic Framework of Application Methods for Large Language Models in Language Sciences

evidence_items.summary: BACKGROUND Clinicians routinely distribute printed patient education materials at the point of care. Tutorials covering all relevant information are rarely feasible within clinical time constraints and ongoing educational support is commonly needed. Patients reading these materials on their own cannot ask questions or have passages explained, and a pamphlet does not adjust to a patient’s educational needs. Embodied conversational agents (ECAs) powered by large language models could take on the role of a clinician or health educator, guiding a patient through educational materials they were given. Virtual reality (VR) additionally affords spatial grounding of anatomical references and use of attentional cues from the patient, such as gaze and pointing, as human educators do while teaching. Whether patients find such a system usable and acceptable in VR is unknown. OBJECTIVE We evaluated an agentic workflow that transforms static patient education pamphlets into structured learning sessions delivered by an ECA in VR. We conducted a formative evaluation of the usability and acceptability of the VR learning experience, including pre-post knowledge change. METHODS We conducted a mixed methods usability study. Healthy adult volunteers (N=22 enrolled; N=21 analyzed) completed a VR learning session (mean duration 18.0 minutes, SD 3.5) in which the ECA delivered a multimodal walkthrough of standardized patient education materials on colonoscopy, appendectomy, or kidney cancer, supported open-ended questions, and reinforced understanding through summaries and brief multiple-choice review questions (flashcards). Measures included overall satisfaction, perceived quality of the education material using an adapted version of the Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool, pre- and post-session knowledge tests, and semi-structured interviews.
evidence_items.title: A Large Language Model-Driven Embodied Conversational Agent for Patient Education in Virtual Reality: Mixed Methods Usability Study (Preprint)

evidence_items.summary: Background: Severe intra-abdominal infections are a major cause of sepsis and septic shock in intensive care units (ICUs), with high mortality and heterogeneity. Identifying variables associated with mortality is essential for risk assessment in this population. The potential of artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted analysis using large language models (LLMs) to complement conventional statistics remains underexplored. Methods: This retrospective, single-center study analyzed 172 adult ICU patients with intra-abdominal sepsis or septic shock, identified among 6674 patients over one year. Conventional statistical methods assessed mortality-related variables. Two LLMs (Google Gemini 3.1 Pro and Claude Sonnet 5) were separately prompted to examine the pseudonymized, outcome-labeled dataset in five runs using structured prompts; their narrative outputs were compared with conventional findings. Results: Overall in-ICU mortality was 60.5%. APACHE II showed the highest discriminatory capacity for mortality (AUC = 0.695), followed by admission lactate (AUC = 0.636) and SOFA score (AUC = 0.626). LLM outputs most consistently reproduced the direction of findings involving SOFA, APACHE II, and lactate, while coverage of other variables varied between models and runs. Conclusions: Conventional statistics and AI-assisted LLM analyses yielded largely convergent findings for mortality markers. However, variability across other findings supports AI-assisted analysis as an exploratory, complementary approach. Further validation in larger, independent, multicenter cohorts is required before widespread routine clinical application.
evidence_items.title: Bridging Large Language Model–Based AI and Conventional Statistics for Retrospective Mortality Risk Assessment in Intra-Abdominal Sepsis and Septic Shock

evidence_items.summary: This study examined the influence of Artificial Intelligence (AI)-driven research methodologies on lecturers' productivity in Lagos State University (LASU), Ojo Campus. The growing integration of AI tools such as Machine Learning (ML), Natural Language Processing (NLP), and ChatGPT into academic research and teaching, alongside concerns about lecturers' research efficiency, publication output, and teaching effectiveness in Nigerian universities, motivated the study. Specifically, the study sought to ascertain lecturers' awareness of AI-driven research methodologies, examine their knowledge of ML, NLP and ChatGPT, determine their perception of these tools in enhancing research quality and academic productivity, and establish the influence of the tools on research efficiency, publication output, and teaching effectiveness. A descriptive survey research design was adopted, with a sample of 165 lecturers drawn from seven faculties and two schools across Lagos State Owned Universities. Data were collected using a researcher-designed instrument, the Artificial Intelligence Driven Research Methodologies and Lecturers' Productivity Questionnaire (AIDRMLPQ). Out of 189 copies of the questionnaire distributed, 165 were properly completed and returned, giving a response rate of 89.2%. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics (mean and standard deviation) and Pearson Product Moment Correlation at the 0.05 level of significance. Findings revealed a significant positive relationship between the adoption of AI-driven research methodologies and lecturers' research efficiency (r = 0.742), between knowledge of ML, NLP and ChatGPT and academic productivity (r = 0.781), between lecturers' perception of AI tools and research quality (r = 0.766), and between AI tools utilisation and research efficiency, publication output, and teaching effectiveness (r = 0.754).
evidence_items.title: Evaluation of Artificial Intelligence Driven Research Methodologies on Lecturers’ Productivity in Lagos State Owned Universities, Nigeria

evidence_items.summary: Background: Histopathology workforce shortages and operational backlogs severely delay gastric cancer reporting. This multi-centre prospective evaluation assessed the diagnostic accuracy, clinical safety-net utility, and workflow triaging efficiency of an artificial intelligence (AI) platform for gastric biopsies across NHS Wales. Methods: A prospective cohort of 848 consecutive gastric biopsy cases across three NHS Health Boards was processed using a commercial AI platform. Diagnostic performance was evaluated against standard-of-care clinical reference diagnoses. Post-analytic cross-tabulation simulated dynamic AI-driven worklist prioritisation to quantify triage safety, false-positive alerts, and turnaround time impact across urgent and routine pathways. Results: For gastric malignancies (n = 40), the AI platform achieved a sensitivity of 100.0% (95% CI: 91.2–100.0%; AUC 0.986) and a specificity of 97.2% (95% CI: 95.8–98.1%). Sensitivities for low-grade dysplasia/adenoma (n = 12) and gastric intestinal metaplasia (n = 98) were 100.0% and 94.9%, respectively. The AI review functioned as a parallel safety net, capturing eight primary lesions missed during routine human evaluation, including one occult adenocarcinoma. In workflow simulation, the platform correctly prioritised 100.0% of cancers, including 6 cancers hidden within routine backlogs, and 97.2% (106/109) of high-risk non-cancer precursors, with false-positive alerts in 4.6% (39/848) of all cases. Conclusions: AI-assisted gastric pathology review demonstrates exceptional diagnostic accuracy, acts as a reliable clinical support tool, and enables effective risk-stratified triage. Deploying AI triage in public healthcare infrastructure offers a scalable solution with the potential to reduce diagnostic backlogs and accelerate treatment for high-risk oncology patients.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Based Triage and Diagnostic Support for Gastric Biopsies: A Multi-Centre Prospective Evaluation Across NHS Wales

evidence_items.summary: Abstract We present a Bayesian framework, Two-stage Inference for Light curve DEcomposition ( TILDE ), for mapping the accretion disk and the broad-line region (BLR) from active galactic nucleus (AGN) multiband light curves. By inferring delayed BLR contamination from the underlying disk variability, TILDE provides the delay measurements of the disk as well as the BLR. We validate TILDE using synthetic data, finding that TILDE recovers the known time delays of the disk and BLR. By applying TILDE to the Seoul National University AGN Monitoring Project sample, we find that the inferred BLR light curves match the observed H β emission light curves, providing consistent BLR lags compared to the reported H β lags. Using the lag spectrum, effectively corrected for the BLR contamination, we find that the disk size is broadly consistent with the standard thin-disk model, suggesting that BLR contamination can significantly bias the disk size derived from the cross-correlation analysis of the broadband photometry. These results demonstrate that the new inference method is a powerful tool for determining both disk and BLR sizes from broadband photometry in the era of time-domain surveys.
evidence_items.title: Unveiling Accretion-disk Reverberation beneath Broad-line Region Contamination with TILDE

evidence_items.summary: Autonomous artificial intelligence agents are transforming the practice of science. Across every discipline, researchers are handing data analysis to coding agents that can design and execute complex studies from a single prompt. Yet this revolution carries a threat. When agents improvise in local environments, they leave no verifiable record, ultimately risking a wave of irreproducible science. Solving this crisis requires moving agentic science onto public infrastructure where every action leaves an examinable trail. Here we connect autonomous coding agents to shared computing resources, turning ephemeral prompts into auditable scientific records. After showing that 30 unguided local agents splinter into 18 incompatible pipelines on the same dataset, we conduct an agentic reproduction and discovery study on a large scale---reproducing a large, diverse array of studies with every workflow, history, and intermediate dataset publicly accessible. This complete provenance trail exposes unstated modeling choices, reference mismatches, and subsampled tutorial inputs in published studies, and establishes a new foundation where human scientists can understand, steer, and trust AI-driven discovery.
evidence_items.title: Verifiable Agentic Science on Public Infrastructure

evidence_items.summary: ABSTRACT The pharmaceutical sector is undergoing considerable transformation as a result of the integration of artificial intelligence (AI), automation, robotics, and advanced computing technologies. Traditional pharmaceutical discovery and development processes can be lengthy, costly, and associated with high failure rates, thereby necessitating more efficient approaches. Agentic artificial intelligence (Agentic AI) combines autonomous decision‐making, goal‐oriented reasoning, adaptive learning, and multi‐step task execution. These capabilities may increase the autonomy and coordination of pharmaceutical research workflows. At the same time, self‐driving or autonomous laboratories that utilize robotics, machine learning, laboratory automation, and real‐time data analytics to conduct experiments with minimal or no human intervention have emerged as an alternative approach. Agentic AI can provide a higher‐level orchestration layer for autonomous laboratories, while established approaches such as Bayesian optimization, active learning, machine learning, and robotic experimentation provide many of the underlying capabilities required for closed‐loop experimentation. These technologies can be applied to drug discovery, lead optimization, formulation development, process optimization, and personalized medicine. Several challenges related to data quality, transparency, regulation, cybersecurity, ethical considerations, and infrastructure must be addressed before these systems can be widely adopted. In addition, current evidence is dominated by computational studies, research‐scale proof‐of‐concept platforms, and early industrial implementations. Substantial uncertainty remains regarding their reproducibility, scalability, and effects on overall drug development timelines.
evidence_items.title: The Rise of Agentic AI and Self‐Driving Laboratories: Reshaping Drug Discovery, Development, and Precision Medicine

evidence_items.summary: We introduce Timestral, a family of four time series foundation models for probabilistic forecasting, with 5M, 28M, 123M, and 209M parameters. Timestral sets a new state of the art on GIFT-Eval, TIME, and fev-bench, where Timestral-209M and Timestral-123M take the top two places on every metric. We achieve this with three ingredients: Decoupled Horizon Forecasting (DHF), which separates prediction tokens from the causally encoded context, so that longer horizons are trained without masking context and each observed value is both a forecast target and context for later forecasts; a covariate framework that natively supports known-future covariates within a causal architecture; and a two-stage pipeline that pretrains exclusively on a diverse, large-scale synthetic corpus before post-training on a mix of real and synthetic data with extended context. This report describes the model design and its benchmark results. Weights for all four models are available on Hugging Face and inference code on GitHub.
evidence_items.title: Timestral

evidence_items.summary: Generating videos of a specific subject from a few reference images remains challenging when the camera reveals surfaces that are not visible in the input. Early subject-to-video (S2V) methods condition on a single reference image and must therefore infer the subject's unseen appearance and geometry as the viewpoint changes. To address this limitation, recent methods extend S2V to multiple reference views, providing more information about the subject from different viewpoints. However, they do not explicitly specify the 3D structure that connects these observations. In addition, existing training data do not guarantee that viewpoint changes preserve the same underlying 3D subject. We present OmniShowcase, built on two components: (i) a fully automated data synthesis pipeline that produces training videos along diverse camera trajectories, with viewpoint variation driven by underlying subject geometry, even spanning full 360-degree orbits; and (ii) a geometry-conditioning method that provides the video model with a turntable of surface-normal maps reconstructed from the reference views without requiring temporal alignment with the generated frames. We construct Showcase-4K, a corpus of 3D-asset-based videos covering twelve camera motions across 88 trajectory configurations with reconstruction-derived surface-normal conditioning, and ShowcaseBench, a held-out evaluation set with the source meshes and camera parameters used to render each video. Experiments show state-of-the-art subject identity and 3D consistency while maintaining competitive video quality and motion. Project page: justin4ai.github.io/OmniShowcase
evidence_items.title: OmniShowcase: Omnidirectional Subject-Consistent Video Generation from Multi-View Images

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Objectives Child-bicyclist crash-severity data are strongly imbalanced, making ordinary accuracy potentially misleading. This study compared three tabular deep-learning models with machine learning and statistical reference models under a train–validation–test design. Methods The analysis used 2394 Texas child-bicyclist crashes from 2017 to 2022 classified as killed or incapacitating injury (KA), possible or non-incapacitating injury (BC), or other/no injury (O). The original records were partitioned before feature selection, preprocessing, and imbalance treatment into training ( n = 1454), validation ( n = 475), and untouched test ( n = 465) sets. Random Forest and XGBoost rankings were calculated using the training partition only, yielding a common 10-predictor input. Validation performance was used to select class weighting for XGBoost and training-only Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (SMOTEN) for the three deep-learning models. The final primary-model estimates were averaged across five seeds. Results Adaptive Relation-Modeling (ARM)-Net had the highest primary-model accuracy (0.662 ± 0.020) and macro-F1 (0.335 ± 0.011); XGBoost had the highest primary-model balanced accuracy (0.340 ± 0.008); and FT-Transformer had the highest primary-model macro-ROC-AUC (0.540 ± 0.006). However, the dummy-majority accuracy was 0.787 because BC dominated the test set and multinomial logistic regression exceeded all four primary models in balanced accuracy (0.378), macro ROC−AUC (0.561), and macro average precision (0.361). Minority-class discrimination was weak, bootstrap intervals overlapped substantially, and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) rankings showed limited stability relative to cross-seed permutation importance. Conclusions Class-balanced performance was limited across all models.
evidence_items.title: Predicting Child-Bicyclist Crash Severity Under Severe Class Imbalance: A Benchmark of XGBoost and Tabular Deep Learning
