evidence_items.summary: We present EmbeddingGemma 2, an open multimodal embedding model which natively represents text, images, audio, video, and combinations thereof in a unified space. Our approach introduces improvements such as simplified per-layer embeddings and a multi-stage curriculum with modality and objective progression which ensure strong quality across unimodal, cross-modal, and mixed-modal evaluations. Notably, in comprehensive embedding benchmarks across all modalities, EmbeddingGemma 2 establishes a new Pareto frontier, outperforming both specialist models and models two to twelve times larger. Furthermore, our design offers flexibility for resource-constrained environments, supporting selective modality encoder loading, adjustable vision token budgets, truncatable embedding dimensions, and quantized weights. We present ablations analyzing key decisions and release EmbeddingGemma 2 to promote further research.
evidence_items.title: EmbeddingGemma 2: Unified and Efficient Multimodal Representations

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal perception forms the foundation of multimodal intelligence. In particular, spatial perception and multimodal long-context understanding are two pivotal tasks that underpin embodied AI and multimodal agents. However, synthesizing targeted, high-quality training data for these tasks remains difficult and costly. Our key insight is that these tasks share an underlying capability, which we call connecting evidence: identifying relevant visual facts, binding them to the correct entities, recovering their relations, and composing them into an answer. Crucially, targeted training data are far easier to synthesize for this capability than for these tasks themselves. To strengthen this capability, we propose EvidenceConnect, an easy-to-implement data synthesis framework that uses zoomed views of related regions within a single image to generate questions requiring comparison, aggregation, or chaining of visual evidence. To ensure quality, a reference answer is retained only when independent VLMs agree on it, and region-ablation tests discard questions whose answer survives the removal of selected regions. We then train base VLMs on the resulting data with RLVR, obtaining Zooming without Zooming v2 (ZwZ2). Although the synthesized data are not tailored to any downstream benchmark, ZwZ2 improves fine-grained and spatial perception, with further gains on embodied spatial reasoning, multimodal long-context understanding, multimodal agent tasks, and general visual reasoning. These results establish EvidenceConnect as an effective framework for supervising evidence connection and suggest that strengthening this shared capability leads to more generalizable multimodal perception.
evidence_items.title: Zooming without Zooming v2: From Seeing Details to Connecting Evidence for Generalizable Multimodal Perception

evidence_items.summary: Vision--Language--Action (VLA) models generate robot actions from visual observations and language instructions, but their understanding of physical dynamics remains limited. Video world models can capture scene dynamics, yet generating future videos introduces high latency into the control loop. We introduce PDRVLA, whose lightweight Physical Dynamics Module extracts physical tokens from vision--language features to condition action generation without online video generation. The module learns through direct prediction of future RGB, depth, and optical-flow features, with auxiliary supervision through a frozen pretrained video world model. Training relies entirely on publicly available data, expanded through human-to-robot synthesis, subtask annotation, and embodied chain-of-thought (ECoT) annotation. Across four simulation benchmarks, PDRVLA achieves success rates of 99.3% on LIBERO, 89.9% on LIBERO-Plus, 93.6% on RoboTwin~2.0, and 81.5% on SimplerEnv. Ablations show improved future prediction with world-model supervision and evaluate how subtask conditioning, future object-pose supervision, and ECoT training affect action success.
evidence_items.title: PDRVLA: A Vision-Language-Action Model with Physical Dynamics Representations

evidence_items.summary: AI research agents can propose, execute, and improve programs that solve machine learning tasks. However, executing each candidate program requires training and evaluating ML models, limiting how many candidates an agent can explore at each step. We introduce MLE-World, a world model finetuned from Qwen3.5-4B that predicts a program's terminal output (error traces, training logs, and validation scores) from its code and data description without executing it, together with a confidence score estimating the prediction's correctness. Because a prediction costs one inference call rather than a training run, MLE-World makes test time scaling (TTS) affordable for these agents. We build five TTS policies, guided by MLE-World, that compare several candidates per step by their predicted outputs: Sequential revision, Best-of-N, Pairwise judging, Fusion, and a UCB style rule that also adds an exploration bonus from this confidence score. Since predictions can be wrong, we run a candidate for real only when its confidence score is low. On 17 MLE-bench Lite tasks, MLE-World matches the real terminal output on 77.9% of held out programs, versus 41.1% for much larger prompted models. MLE-World guided TTS achieves up to 22.1% higher observed mean performance than the agent without a world model, with less real execution. Project webpage: https://mle-world.github.io/.
evidence_items.title: MLE-World: Predicting Machine Learning Experiment Outcomes with a Learned World Model

evidence_items.summary: Interactive world generation requires models to follow successive commands while preserving relevant history and action consequences. We present Hy-Nomas, a video world model with an 8B diffusion backbone that supports free-form text instructions and continuous camera control across multiple interaction turns. It generates variable-length segments conditioned on current inputs and cached history. Our central design aligns structured video captions with action-aware causal attention: descriptive context remains accessible across segments, while action instructions are restricted to their intended temporal windows. A vision-language Prompt Enhancer (PE) translates user requests and multimodal interaction histories into structured conditions for the next segment. A multi-stage curriculum progressively introduces causal generation, text interaction, camera control, and training on model-generated histories, followed by diffusion distillation. In human evaluation, Hy-Nomas shows superior performance over existing world models. We release model weights, code and benchmarks, together with a lightweight adaptation workflow, to support reproducible research on interactive world generation.
evidence_items.title: Hy-Nomas: Towards Free-form Interactive World Generation

evidence_items.summary: Scientific discovery often begins with an unexpected observation that prompts a new research question. In a world with altered physical laws, can large language models (LLMs) notice unexpected behavior, such as heavier objects falling more slowly, and discover the law through experiments without being told what to investigate? To evaluate this ability, we introduce LongChang, an automated framework that creates simulated worlds with altered physics, where one or more laws differ from ordinary physics. The evaluated LLMs act as explorers, manipulating objects and building tools to investigate their own questions without research tasks or hints about these laws. Separate LLM agents generate and review scenes, review tool designs, and evaluate reports for correctness and experimental support using the altered physical laws and exploration records. These records guide scene evolution for further exploration, allowing the full cycle to run without human intervention. Among 12 LLMs, GPT-6-Astra achieves a discovery rate of 16.7%, while the other 11 score 0%. The exploration records reveal uninvestigated anomalies and only partial identification of the altered physical laws.
evidence_items.title: Can LLMs Uncover Hidden Physical Laws through Free Exploration?

evidence_items.summary: Safe household navigation requires robots to regulate clearance and speed according to what an obstacle is and how close it is, without unnecessary conservatism. Yet existing evaluations do not test whether semantic safety distinctions are reflected in continuous motion. To that end, we introduce OSMA-Bench, an Obstacle-Conditioned Safe Motion Adaptation Benchmark built on spatially matched scenario sets that differ only in obstacle type. We also propose the Semantic Sensitivity Index (SSI), which measures whether clearance and distance-dependent speed and smoothness follow the caution ordering of obstacles. Evaluating VLM-based and vision-language-action (VLA) policies on the benchmark, we find that neither consistently adapts its motion to obstacle safety, even with explicit safety prompts. Our analysis shows that the policies can correctly distinguish obstacles by safety relevance but fail to reflect this distinction in the motion parameters or actions they produce. For VLM-based policies, which recognize the obstacle and then generate a navigation program, adding an explicit parameter-inference step between these two stages improves adaptation. These findings expose a gap in semantic-to-motion grounding, highlighting the need to translate semantic caution into appropriately safe motion.
evidence_items.title: Benchmarking Obstacle-Conditioned Safety in Household Robot Navigation

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal intelligence can be viewed as human-guided co-evolution between worlds and agents through interaction. However, scaling this process faces two bottlenecks: constructing heterogeneous, verifiable environments is costly, and manual Harness iteration cannot keep pace with growing task diversity and complexity. A key insight is that tasks with different modalities and surface forms can share the same underlying capability requirements. We therefore introduce The Trinity, a recursive self-improvement framework coupling world generation with Harness evolution through three roles: Creator, Explorer, and Evolver. Drawing on verified execution trajectories, Evolver shifts the basis of task organization from surface categories to shared requirements, reorganizing the original task tree into a hierarchical capability tree. We introduce Capability-Driven Real2Sim2Real: for heterogeneous tasks at the same node, Creator abstracts their common requirements into simplified, verifiable simulated worlds for capability learning, while evaluation on original tasks measures transfer. Along this capability tree, Explorer progressively evolves reusable capability modules through selective inheritance, forming a Harness tree whose validated updates accumulate across iterations within a fixed topology. The resulting Harnesses specialize in different capabilities, motivating a Capability-Aware Harness Router that uses public task information to select compatible module configurations from the tree. Our evolved Harnesses improve mean performance by 34 points across 28 training benchmarks and 26 points across 18 unseen benchmarks, including two real-world embodied tasks.
evidence_items.title: The Trinity:Capability-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Multimodal Agents

evidence_items.summary: Despite rapid advances in large language models (LLMs), their deployment in the sports and health domain remains high-risk due to the absence of domain-specific evaluation benchmarks. Existing general-purpose benchmarks (e.g., MMLU and HELM) primarily assess broad knowledge and reasoning capabilities, but fail to capture critical domain requirements such as exercise safety, physiological appropriateness, personalization, and actionable coaching quality. This gap is particularly concerning in fitness and health applications, where incorrect or unsafe recommendations can lead to physical harm. To address this limitation, we introduce MoveBench, the first comprehensive benchmarking framework specifically designed for evaluating LLMs in sports and health coaching. The proposed benchmark integrates heterogeneous task formats, including multiple-choice questions (MCQs) and open-ended question answering (OpenQA), grounded in real-world user scenarios and paired with structured rubrics emphasizing safety compliance, scientific validity, and training logic. Through large-scale evaluation of 15 diverse LLMs on 809 questions with 5,012 rubric-level criteria, our results reveal substantial performance variability, particularly in safety awareness, structured program design, and personalization capability, highlighting a critical gap between knowing and doing. Our work establishes a foundational evaluation standard for sports and health LLM applications and provides a reproducible framework for advancing safe, reliable, and context-aware AI-driven coaching systems. Open resources are available at https://github.com/SatoSakula/MoveBench.
evidence_items.title: MoveBench: A Rubric-Based Benchmark for Evaluating Large Language Models in Sports and Health Coaching

evidence_items.summary: Memory is increasingly used in long-horizon agents, yet the net value of building memory over direct retrieval from raw history remains largely unclear. Through a large-scale evaluation across multiple benchmarks and model backbones, we find many dedicated memory systems underperform naive RAG in many cases, indicating a negative net value. Taking RAG as a reference, we dissect the net value of memory into the gains and losses over direct retrieval, termed memory benefit and memory tax. These gains and losses arise because memory process changes how the raw information is organized and accessed. We view such changes as the double-edged deviations from the raw history. They are originally designed and introduced to benefit the task, for example by reorganizing facts or distilling preferences, but some may also remove or obscure evidence, giving rise to memory tax. Since memory benefit reflects the expected gains of its design, we then focus more on the overlooked memory tax, study how it arises from the system and evaluation side, and generalize the concept to more application scenarios of memory. We hope the notion of memory tax can provide a new lens and shift more attention from standalone performance to the net value of memory, informing more reliable memory designs and evaluations. We will open-source the code and results to the community. Project Page: https://hexuan21.github.io/MemoryTax/
evidence_items.title: Memory Tax: Dissecting the Net Value of Agent Memory

evidence_items.summary: Generative models increasingly expose a reasoning effort setting that lets users scale inference-time compute, trading higher cost for potentially improved performance. Users must choose an effort level before knowing whether extra reasoning will help, and even a successful run does not reveal whether the effort purchased was necessary. Reasoning effort is therefore a credence good: buyers observe the outcome but cannot assess the marginal value of the computation they paid for. In this work, we measure the counterfactual effect of effort levels on both proprietary and open-weight models on four benchmarks, spanning single-call reasoning and long-horizon agentic tasks. Effort, it turns out, does not consistently preserve tasks that lower effort solves, can overspend, and can change trajectory behavior. First, we find that although higher effort can raise accuracy in aggregate, it frequently fails on tasks that lower effort solved. Second, on the subset of easy tasks that every effort level solves, higher effort is generally more costly, with the highest effort level costing up to 42x as much as the lowest. Lastly, effort changes not only how many tokens are used, but also how agents solve tasks: at higher effort, agents verify their own work more heavily and more often search for solutions than work through problems directly, both of which lengthen trajectories without necessarily altering the outcome. These findings show that naively choosing the highest level is not only cost-inefficient but also offers no guarantee of the best instance-level performance. A simple alternative, starting at the lowest effort and escalating only after a verified failure, matches or improves on fixed top effort across all models and benchmarks at lower cost for most proprietary models.
evidence_items.title: What Effort Level Should I Choose? On the Economics of Reasoning Effort in LLM Agents

evidence_items.summary: Streaming audio-visual target speaker extraction (AVTSE) is essential for latency-sensitive applications. However, current causal systems face two coupled gaps. First, standard benchmarks fix the number of speakers at two and ignore the near-/far-field interference, reverberation, and sudden noise of real scenes. Second, high-performance causal architectures are too heavy for edge deployment. Lightweight alternatives try to reclaim capacity by repeatedly invoking a small separator, which offsets the savings. To address the first gap, we release RealSSA, a realistic AVTSE benchmark consisting of RealSSA-Sim and RealSSA-Real. RealSSA-Sim provides controllable simulated scenes with 1--5 dynamic near-field interfering speakers; scenes with far-field interference additionally include 10--15 far-field interfering speakers. RealSSA-Real provides a held-out real-recorded evaluation set. To address the second gap, we propose Falcon, a causal AVTSE method. Its Separator performs multi-scale time-frequency separation in a single encoder--decoder pass. We train Falcon with an encoder-space speaker contrastive loss. This loss suppresses near-field leakage at zero inference cost and transfers across backbones. Falcon achieves state-of-the-art extraction quality on RealSSA-Sim, LRS2-2Mix, LRS3-2Mix, and VoxCeleb2-2Mix. Compared with the causal AV-TFGridNet baseline, it cuts parameters by 91.9%, computation by 20.2 times, and GPU inference latency by 11.1 times. Code and demo are available at https://cslikai.cn/Falcon/.
evidence_items.title: Efficient Streaming Audio-Visual Target Speaker Extraction for Real-World Acoustic Scenes

evidence_items.summary: Data science agents can automate end-to-end machine learning workflows, yet they remain far from competitive on human leaderboards. Agents make process errors such as insufficient exploration, unsound validation, coding bugs, and poor use of a fixed budget (re-running the same exploratory data analysis and baseline models in every attempt). We propose AdaPRA to address these issues: a persistent coding agent harness that accumulates knowledge across attempts on the same task, with rubric-guided process supervision that identifies and corrects errors. Our process reward agent audits the agent's trajectory and workspace by executing checks, and adapts its rubrics to each task. We find that rubrics seeded from easier tasks generalize to harder tasks, with rubric adaptation further improving performance. With five attempts per task, AdaPRA improves an 80B Qwen model's leaderboard percentile by 24.5 points on DSPredict-Easy and 14.8 points on DSPredict-Hard while reducing process errors. We also show that supervision with rubrics mined from one base model's runs improves another (DeepSeek-V3.2), and that AdaPRA beats DataPRM, a competitive PRM for data science. We also share our code for reproducibility.
evidence_items.title: AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) show promising reasoning capabilities, but reliable physical interaction requires planning that accounts for when actions are executable and how they change the world. These preconditions and effects are environment-dependent and often not captured by MLLMs, making adaptation challenging. Yet existing approaches either require costly environment-specific training or rely on unstructured interaction experience that is difficult to reuse. Therefore, we introduce CausGround, a non-parametric causal interaction grounding framework that distills interaction experience into reusable action-centered causal knowledge. CausGround identifies action preconditions and effects and organizes them in a factorized world-state representation capturing object attributes and inter-object relations. At planning time, task-relevant causal dependencies are grounded in current observations to support backward reasoning over preconditions and forward reasoning over effects for action selection and multi-step planning. We evaluate CausGround on simulated high-level planning, interaction reasoning, and real-world robot manipulation. On adapted VirtualHome and RoboCasa benchmarks, CausGround improves vision-based high-level planning across MLLM backbones, increasing average task success from 24.9% to 53.3% on VirtualHome and closed-loop planning success from 43.0% to 57.0% on RoboCasa. On SWITCH, average interaction reasoning accuracy increases from 25.8% to 31.9%, indicating improved action selection, recovery, and verification. Moreover, real-world experiments show that CausGround reasons backward from MLLM-interpreted goals to derive executable high-level action sequences for sequential manipulation. These results demonstrate that reusable action preconditions and effects support long-horizon embodied planning across diverse environments without parameter updates.
evidence_items.title: CausGround: Causal Interaction Grounding for Adaptive Embodied Planning

evidence_items.summary: Recent advances in search agents have enabled large language models to tackle complex tasks by retrieving and synthesizing external information. However, existing search agents often lack search-state awareness, i.e., the ability to recognize what information has been obtained and what remains missing, leading to hallucinated reasoning and prematurely terminated search. To address this limitation, we propose Self-Assessment Reinforcement Learning (SARL), a reinforcement learning framework in which models learn to recognize their own search state during training and improve their search behavior accordingly, without requiring additional assessment at test time. SARL achieves this through a dual reward design that captures the corrective effect of each assessment while penalizing excessive reliance on it, jointly encouraging effective and efficient search trajectories. Under this setup, SARL achieves a 24.3% relative improvement over the strongest baseline, with average gains of 35.9% on multi-hop reasoning and 27.9% on deep research benchmarks against the strongest per-benchmark baselines. SARL further surpasses methods built on auxiliary supervision or multi-agent coordination, despite operating as a standalone RL framework with no inference-time scaffolding. Beyond final performance, SARL maintains training stability under extended search horizons, a regime where existing methods consistently degrade, enabling sustained gains as task complexity grows.
evidence_items.title: Self-Assessment Reinforcement Learning for Search-State Awareness in Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Text-to-image (T2I) platforms typically return several images per prompt so users can explore different visual interpretations and choose one that matches their intent. However, T2I models are usually optimized for single-image quality which comes at a cost of multi-image diversity, limiting this exploration. Diversity is also contextual: one user wants variations in background, while another wants them in artistic style, and the same user may later want variations in clothing. The generated images should differ along whatever axis the user cares about. In this paper, we introduce T-DIG, a text-conditioned diversity framework for image generation and editing. T-DIG is an iterative framework comprising multiple modules that lets users type prompts, inspect default generations, request variations using natural language, and continue refining outputs until they're satisfied. At its core, T-DIG uses an LLM policy that produces K axis-conditioned prompts or edit instructions for a frozen generator or editor. We train this policy with GRPO using a text-conditioned diversity reward and alignment penalties. Because the image generator remains frozen, T-DIG applies to open-weight, distilled, and proprietary models. We also release the first dataset for text-conditioned prompt diversity in image generation, with the training and validation splits built from human-written axes and a test set drawn from real user interactions with T-DIG. T-DIG far exceeds baselines in improving text-conditioned diversity, while preserving base-prompt alignment across a variety of metrics and human judgements. We show that user-directed diversity exploration can be added to a wide range of image generation models, open and closed, without the need to access their weights. Website: https://image-study.org/t-dig/
evidence_items.title: T-DIG: Text-Conditioned Diversity for Image Generation

evidence_items.summary: We introduce OvisOCR3, a 0.8B model for a broad range of OCR-related tasks. OvisOCR3 unifies document parsing, general OCR, key information extraction (KIE), document figure captioning, and cross-page table reconstruction in a single model. We train the model on real and synthetic data through continued pretraining and use domain-balanced mid-training to balance supervision across tasks with different data volumes and response lengths. Multi-teacher on-policy distillation transfers expertise from five domain-specific 4B teachers into the shared model, followed by mixed-task reinforcement learning with domain-specific rewards. We compare OvisOCR3 with general-purpose vision-language models and specialized OCR models on public and in-house benchmarks covering all five task families. In these comparisons, it achieves an overall score of 96.74 on OmniDocBench v1.6 and the highest overall scores on PureDocBench, Real5-OmniDocBench, and MDPBench. On OCRBench v2, it ranks first, scoring 65.9 and 61.3 on the English and Chinese splits, respectively. It also outperforms the baselines on OCRBench and all four KIE benchmarks. On DocFigCapBench, it achieves the highest localization F1 and a caption score close to that of Qwen3.8-Max. For cross-page tables, it leads in Relation F1 on CrossTabBench and truncated-table TEDS on MPDocBench-Parse. These results demonstrate that a compact 0.8B model can achieve strong performance across diverse OCR-related tasks. OvisOCR3 is available at https://huggingface.co/ATH-MaaS/OvisOCR3.
evidence_items.title: OvisOCR3 Technical Report

evidence_items.summary: In long-term interactions with large language model (LLM) agents, users reveal habits through their choices and actions. These habits capture implicit user information that agents must infer across conversations. However, individual observations may provide only partial evidence about a habit or when it applies. Retaining past interactions alone does not ensure that agents can infer habits and apply them appropriately. We introduce HABIT-Bench to evaluate how well agent memory systems infer habits from weak evidence and apply them to later requests. We construct synthetic user histories from task-oriented dialogue data and controlled habit graphs. The histories span hundreds of sessions across food, finance, software, and travel. Four-choice tasks assess agents' ability to infer user habits and apply them appropriately. They include temporary exceptions, changes in habits, and suggestions that users have not accepted. Sampled tasks undergo independent human review. We evaluate eight memory methods with Qwen3-235B-A22B and GLM-5.3-Flash. The best-performing memory method achieves 33.61\% macro accuracy across the four domains. Performance remains limited even when annotated evidence is supplied directly. These results expose a persistent gap between access to past interactions and the ability to infer and appropriately use user habits.
evidence_items.title: HABIT-Bench: Evaluating Habit Induction from Longitudinal Weak Evidence in Agent Memory

evidence_items.summary: Objective: To evaluate the triage accuracy, response quality, safety, and repeatability of widely used large language models (LLMs) in urologic emergencies and to examine their potential clinical utility and risks. Methods: We developed 50 standardized clinical vignettes covering 10 categories of urologic emergencies, including testicular torsion, acute urinary retention, and Fournier gangrene. The set comprised high-risk vignettes requiring immediate emergency care, borderline vignettes, and atypical vignettes containing misleading cues. Six commercially available LLMs—Kimi 3.0, DeepSeek V4, Qwen 3.8-MAX, GPT-5.6 Sol (ChatGPT), Claude Opus 4.8, and Ant Afu (AQ)—were evaluated in Chinese-language interactions. Each vignette was submitted three times in independent conversations. Two urologists with more than 10 years of clinical experience assessed triage accuracy using a three-level reference standard (immediate emergency department [ED] evaluation, routine outpatient evaluation, or home observation). They also rated response quality across eight dimensions using a 5-point Likert scale and evaluated medical-error severity (0–3), response stability, and Chinese readability. Overall differences were assessed using the Friedman test, followed by pairwise Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Holm adjustment. Results: A total of 900 responses were generated. Overall three-class accuracy was 89.11%, and the macro-averaged F1 score was 85.73%. Qwen achieved the highest accuracy (94.00%), whereas Claude achieved the lowest (80.67%). However, none of the pairwise comparisons between models reached statistical significance after Holm adjustment. All models generally recognized scenarios requiring immediate ED evaluation, but their ability to distinguish routine outpatient evaluation from home observation varied substantially.
evidence_items.title: Evaluation of Large Language Models for Emergency Triage in Urology: A Multi-Model Study
Domain Adaptation of a Large Language Model for Radiology Impression Generation – Multi-Reader Evaluation

organizations: Rush University Medical Center, Chicago, IL, USA
evidence_items.summary: Background: Large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, and Mistral are increasingly used to obtain medical information, but their accuracy in carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS) management is uncertain. This study evaluated whether LLM-generated recommendations align with American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS) clinical practice guidelines (CPGs). Methods: Four LLMs (ChatGPT-4, Gemini, Claude-3, Mistral-7B) were queried with standardized prompts derived from AAOS CTS CPGs. Each prompt was asked 3 times per model, and responses were synthesized. Two blinded reviewers graded outputs as concordant, discordant, or indeterminate, with disagreements resolved by consensus. Concordance distributions were compared using χ 2 testing with Bonferroni correction. Inter-rater reliability was measured with Cohen’s κ. Results: Across 252 recommendations, 72.6% were concordant, 11.5% discordant, and 15.9% indeterminate. ChatGPT achieved the highest concordance (92.1%) and lowest discordance (1.6%), while Mistral performed poorest (52.4% concordance, 17.5% discordance). Reviewer agreement was excellent (κ = 0.91). Conclusions: Over 1 in 4 LLM-generated CTS recommendations were not concordant with AAOS CPGs. ChatGPT outperformed other models, though variable performance underscores the need for clinician oversight and careful validation before clinical use.
evidence_items.title: Evaluation of Large Language Model Concordance With AAOS Clinical Practice Guidelines for Carpal Tunnel Syndrome

evidence_items.summary: Background The Functional Independence Measure (FIM) is a standard functional assessment tool in rehabilitation medicine; however, formal assessments are often conducted only at limited intervals. Free-text clinical notes contain more frequent observations of patients’ functional status and may complement these assessments. Objective This study aimed to estimate item-level FIM scores from Japanese free-text rehabilitation notes using a locally deployed large language model (LLM) and to evaluate estimation performance; item-level estimability; and differences across diseases, therapy types, and admission FIM severity groups. Methods We retrospectively analyzed free-text notes from physical therapy (PT), occupational therapy (OT), and speech-language pathology (SLP) for patients hospitalized with cerebral infarction (CeI), hip fracture (HF), or vertebral fracture (VBF) at Saiseikai Moriyama Municipal Hospital between October 2019 and September 2024. Using zero-shot prompting, an LLM estimated all FIM items from each note. Estimated scores were matched to reference FIM scores recorded for the same patient on the same calendar date. Performance was evaluated using the mean absolute error (MAE), root mean squared error, and quadratic weighted kappa. Estimation rates and comparisons with modal-score and last-observation-carried-forward (LOCF) baselines were also examined. Results Among 2,952,702 eligible note-item pairs from 164,039 retained rehabilitation-note-level outputs, the model produced 980,000 valid estimates, corresponding to an overall estimation rate of 33.2%. Among 170,744 note-item opportunities with an available same-day reference score, 57,246 (33.5%) were estimable, of which 77.7% (44,481/57,246) were within 1 point of the reference score. Estimates derived from OT notes had a lower MAE than those derived from PT notes in CeI and HF, whereas the difference was not significant in VBF.
evidence_items.title: Estimating Functional Independence Measure Scores From Japanese Rehabilitation Notes Using a Large Language Model: Retrospective Study

evidence_items.summary: Masked diffusion language models repeatedly compute representations for unresolved tokens, but conventional denoisers do not explicitly retain these representations for reuse across steps. We introduce Temporal Self-Conditioning Diffusion Language Model (TDLM), which lets each unresolved position attend to its own history of hidden representations within a frozen denoiser. This gives later predictions access to computation already performed. Training uses self-generated trajectories and a simple cross-entropy objective for tokens revealed between consecutively sampled decoding steps, while causal temporal attention permits parallel evaluation during training. On LLaDA, the temporal modules add only approximately 0.84% trainable parameters. Across LLaDA and Dream, the main comparison shows up to 7.15× faster generation than the corresponding original diffusion language model, with competitive answer quality on the evaluated tasks. These results motivate temporal memory as a practical way to make more effective use of repeated denoising computation.
evidence_items.title: TDLM: Temporal Self-Conditioning Diffusion Language Model

organizations: Liaquat National Hospital and Medical College, Karachi, Pakistan

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Objective To evaluate the extent to which large language models (LLMs) reproduce human assessments of the quality of stroke-related information on social media. Background Social media is a major source of health information, yet content quality varies. The reliability of LLMs in evaluating stroke-related social media content against human assessments remains uncertain. Methods This cross-sectional study evaluated 50 TikTok and Instagram videos using human reference scores and three AI models: ChatGPT, Microsoft 365 Copilot, and Claude. Publicly unavailable videos and those featuring songs or lacking transcribable speech were excluded. Spoken audio was transcribed using a free tool, and transcripts were submitted to all three models with an identical standardized prompt. Scores were compared using Mann–Whitney U tests; Spearman’s correlation assessed associations with human ratings, and linear regression quantified explained variance. Results The median human reference score was 37.00 (IQR, 35.00–45.00). All AI models scored significantly lower: ChatGPT, 34.50 (p = 0.001); Microsoft Copilot, 33.50 (p < 0.001); and Claude, 26.00 (p < 0.001). All models correlated significantly with human ratings, with the strongest association for Claude (ρ = 0.593; p < 0.001), followed by ChatGPT (ρ = 0.550; p < 0.001) and Copilot (ρ = 0.396; p = 0.004). Claude explained 32.1% of the variance in human scores (R² = 0.321), compared with 31.4% for ChatGPT and 14.8% for Copilot. Inter-model correlation was strongest between ChatGPT and Copilot (ρ = 0.862; p < 0.001). Conclusions All three LLMs showed significant positive correlations with human ratings but systematically assigned lower scores. Claude showed the strongest correlation, whereas Microsoft Copilot showed the weakest. These findings highlight the limitations of LLMs in reproducing human judgments and the need for further validation before their use as standalone evaluators of social media content.
evidence_items.title: Can Large Language Models Judge Stroke Information on Social Media? A Cross-Sectional Comparison of Large Language Models Against Human Ratings of Health-Related Videos

evidence_items.summary: Background Shared decision-making (SDM) is a core competency in patient-centered care, yet it is challenging for physicians. Simulation-based education with standardized patients (SPs) offers valuable practice opportunities for undergraduate medical education (UME), but is limited by cost, scalability, and variable feedback quality. Advances in large language model (LLM) technology and virtual patient (VP) design present a promising pathway toward accessible, realistic, and high-quality SDM skill training. Objective This study aimed to develop LLM-powered, real-time interactive 3D avatars for SDM training in UME and to evaluate their acceptance among undergraduate medical students. Methods We conducted a descriptive, cross-sectional mixed methods study at KU Leuven, Belgium (November-December 2025). The avatar system was developed through an iterative, interdisciplinary collaboration between medical educators, SDM experts, software developers, user experience designers, and AI engineers, grounded in prior work on physicians’ educational needs and SDM learning mechanisms. Development comprised prototype case authoring, usability testing with medical students, and iterative refinement. The final system is a web-based platform featuring real-time, LLM-powered spoken dialogue with diverse, photorealistic 3D patient avatars; layered prompts configuring avatar personality, clinical scenario, and difficulty; an educator panel for case authoring; and automated AI-generated formative feedback structured around 6 phases of SDM. After using the system for 1 month, a convenience sample of UME students completed a 9-item, 5-point Likert scale questionnaire grounded in the technology acceptance model (TAM), assessing perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, and intention to use. Optional open-text responses were narratively analyzed to triangulate these findings. Results Of 25 recruited participants, 24 were included in the analysis.
evidence_items.title: Large Language Model–Powered 3D Avatars to Train Shared Decision-Making in Undergraduate Medical Students: Design and Mixed Methods Acceptance Study

evidence_items.summary: Formal mathematics has a data problem, and large language models have become one of the tools applied to it. LeanConjecturer mined 40 seed files from Mathlib and produced 12,289 candidate statements, of which 3,776 resisted the automated tactic used as a filter. AlphaGeometry solved 25 of 30 olympiad geometry problems by letting a language model propose auxiliary constructions whenever symbolic deduction stalled. FunSearch improved on earlier results for the cap set problem by having an evaluator score programs written by a model. Evidence of this kind still supports a narrower claim than mathematical discovery. Five studies are compared in this review: LeanConjecturer, the Conjecturing-Proving Loop, AlphaGeometry, FunSearch, and Unlearning as Ablation. Using literature analysis and comparative case analysis, task objectives, generation mechanisms, verification procedures, and evidential limits are examined side by side. Two findings stand out. External verification is what makes candidate selection and iterative repair function in each system, and each system demonstrates a different slice of the work: conjecture supply, proof repair, geometric construction, program optimization, and, in the case of Unlearning as Ablation, a proposal for auditing knowledge provenance. Correctness, novelty, and independence from previously acquired target knowledge remain three separate questions that require three separate kinds of evidence. A more reliable evaluation framework would combine auditable knowledge boundaries, dependency checking, and expert assessment of mathematical significance.
evidence_items.title: Large Language Models for Mathematical Discovery: Generation, Verification, and Knowledge Provenance

organizations: Mayo Clinic Alix School of Medicine, Scottsdale, AZ, USA
George Washington University, Washington, DC, USA
evidence_items.summary: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) has been utilized as a supplemental tool by patients and providers in the evaluation of common hand pathology. This study evaluated the ability of 3 large language model (LLM)-based AI systems (ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude) to characterize Dupuytren’s contracture involvement and recommend treatment based solely on patient images. Methods: A heterogeneous set of publicly available images was obtained from open-access databases and literature sources. Images were evaluated by LLMs in independent stateless sessions using a standardized prompt to identify contracture characteristics and recommend treatment. Artificial intelligence outputs were compared with consensus assessments from 3 board-certified hand surgeons. Results: Large language models demonstrated limited accuracy in characterizing Dupuytren’s contracture involvement from patient images. Treatment recommendations were often within 1 ordinal tier of surgeon consensus; however, agreement with surgeons was no greater than chance. No consistent differences in performance were observed among the models. Conclusions: Large language model-based AI systems demonstrated limited capability in the image-based assessment and treatment recommendation of Dupuytren’s contracture. These findings highlight a gap between current LLM performance and surgeon consensus when evaluating Dupuytren’s contracture from single-patient-submitted images. Further research is needed to determine whether the incorporation of standardized clinical information can improve the reliability of AI-assisted treatment recommendations.
evidence_items.title: Performance of Large Language Models in Image-Based Evaluation of Dupuytren Contracture

organizations: Facultad de Salud Pública, Escuela Superior Politécnica de Chimborazo (ESPOCH)
evidence_items.summary: Introduction Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being explored in dental education as a tool to support teaching, learning, assessment, and clinical decision-making. This systematic review synthesized current evidence on the implementation and educational impact of AI technologies in undergraduate, postgraduate, and continuing dental education. Methodology A PRISMA-guided systematic review was conducted using Scopus, PubMed, and IEEE Xplore. Studies published between 2020 and 2025 evaluating AI applications in dental education were identified using predefined PICO criteria. Educational outcomes included knowledge acquisition, diagnostic accuracy, clinical reasoning, procedural skills, learner engagement, and perceptions of AI-assisted learning. Results The included literature reflects an expansion from machine learning, deep learning, and computer vision systems primarily evaluated for diagnostic support toward generative AI platforms, including large language models and retrieval-augmented generation systems. Across the included studies, AI applications were frequently associated with favorable diagnostic and examination performance and, in selected educational contexts, with supportive findings related to clinical reasoning, technical competency, feedback, and self-directed learning. However, the evidence was predominantly based on technical performance assessments and observational or cross-sectional designs. Discussion AI is increasingly being explored as a potential complementary educational resource, with applications including interactive tutoring, adaptive learning, and support for clinical reasoning. Nevertheless, heterogeneous methodologies and limited longitudinal evidence indicate the need for standardized educational evaluation and responsible curricular integration. Conclusion AI shows potential as a complementary resource in dental education.
evidence_items.title: Artificial intelligence in odontology education

organizations: Department of Organization and Management, Faculty of Economics and Business, University of Zagreb, Trg J. F. Kennedyja 6, 10000 Zagreb, Croatia
evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence in corporate boards refers to the use of data-driven computational systems, including machine learning, predictive analytics, natural language processing and generative models, to support the work of boards of directors in one-tier systems and supervisory boards in two-tier systems. Executive management, including management boards in two-tier systems, is considered insofar as it supplies information to or is overseen by these bodies. Such systems are applied to the established functions of the board: monitoring and control, strategic direction, advice and counsel to executive management, and the provision of information, expertise and external linkages. Applications range from anomaly and compliance monitoring to environmental scanning, scenario modeling and the synthesis of board materials. A distinction is essential between decision support, in which systems supply information and analysis; decision augmentation, in which board members and systems jointly shape an evaluation; and autonomous decision-making, in which a system determines an outcome without human deliberation; board-level use is discussed in the literature almost entirely in the first two modes. The central governance tension is that capabilities which expand the information-processing capacity of a body constrained by limited meeting time and by dependence on management-supplied reporting also introduce opacity, vendor dependence and new difficulty in attributing responsibility. Under prevailing corporate governance arrangements, formal responsibility for board decisions remains with the human members of the relevant governing body. Responsible use therefore rests on explicit governance arrangements: defined human oversight, documentation, verification, data governance and board-level competence.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Corporate Boards

evidence_items.summary: Objective Traditional ultrasonic detection for kidney stones is prone to variability due to the experience and skill of the operating physician, leading to inconsistent diagnostic outcomes. Factors such as stone size, location, and surrounding tissues can further compromise accuracy. Artificial intelligence (AI), with its advanced data processing and deep learning capabilities, offers a solution by automating the analysis of medical images to improve diagnostic accuracy and efficiency. Methods This cross-sectional study was conducted at our hospital between 01/06/2022 and 03/07/2024. After excluding 50 poor-quality ultrasound images, the final dataset included 1,130 images: 918 stone images and 212 non-stone images. At the patient level, 791 stone images were used for training/validation, and 127 stone images plus 212 non-stone images ( n = 339) were held out as an independent test cohort. The High-Resolution Network (HRNet) was employed for model training to detect kidney stones in ultrasound images. Detailed image annotations were created using the labelme tool and converted to COCO format for compatibility with AI algorithms. Results In the independent test cohort ( n = 339), the confusion matrix was: TN = 200, FP = 12, FN = 34, and TP = 93, corresponding to 212 actual negatives and 127 actual positives. The HRNet model achieved an accuracy of 86.4% (95% CI 82.4–89.7%), sensitivity of 73.2% (95% CI 64.9–82.2%), specificity of 94.3% (95% CI 90.4–96.7%), positive predictive value (PPV) of 88.6% (95% CI 81.1–93.3%), and negative predictive value (NPV) of 85.5% (95% CI 80.4–89.4%). The model showed high specificity but moderate sensitivity, missing approximately 26.8% of renal stones in the test cohort. Conclusions HRNet-based AI may improve specificity and reduce false-positive findings in ultrasound-based renal stone detection.
evidence_items.title: Enhancing renal stone detection through artificial intelligence models

organizations: Old Dominion University (ODU) Virginia Modeling, Analysis, and Simulation Center (VMASC)

evidence_items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly support time-consuming conceptual modeling tasks such as building or combining models from text. In this context, causal maps are labeled, directed graphs that represent causal relationships (edges) between selected factors (nodes) in a problem domain. Modelers control the output through the LLM’s prompt and decoding parameters such as temperature, and recent studies either use a default temperature or minimize it by expecting that it supports replicability. However, evidence about this expectation remains limited, as does our understanding of how different LLMs and decoding or prompting strategies shape results. We assess the extent to which findings are an artifact of the LLM or its variability rather than a reflection of the modeler’s controls. We focus on the common conceptual modeling task of combining models, exemplified through three algorithms that reflect a variety of prompting techniques. We use five LLMs (DeepSeek, Gemini, GPT, Qwen, Ministral) and different versions to account for the potential impact of the architectures. Using the Design of Experiments approach of factorial analyses (supplemented by paired tests and confidence interval checks), our results show that outcomes differ significantly across LLMs and versions. Depending on the algorithm, randomness from the LLM can be the dominating factor, responsible for up to 96% of the variation in results. This happens even if we directly control the decoding, as evidenced by our comparison of greedy, beam-search, and contrastive decoding. We find that prompt effects are systematic but metric-dependent, while decoding affects performance but there is no universally best strategy. Since our findings suggest that replicability of conceptual modeling studies using LLMs may be limited, future studies may report the distribution of performance measures alongside exact model, decoding, replication, and baseline-normalization settings.
evidence_items.title: On the variability of generative artificial intelligence methods in conceptual modeling: an experimental evaluation on combining causal maps

organizations: University of Birmingham, School of Computer Science, University of Birmingham, Birmingham, United Kingdom
evidence_items.summary: Learning paths personalized by behavior have become common among personalized learning systems. However, the traditional methods are usually inefficient at building coherent paths as the learner's knowledge state changes dynamically, and the prerequisite structure exists. In light of this problem, we present a generative learning-path optimization framework based on EdNet-KT1 interaction dataset, Transformer knowledge tracing model, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct candidate generator, and constraint-aware reranking. Mastery profiles of learners are extracted, and then five ten-resource candidate paths are generated and sorted according to learning gain, prerequisites, difficulty deviation, and repetition. We compare our method to collaborative filtering, GRU4Rec, and knowledge-tracing greedy recommendation on offline experiments. The generative optimizer gets NDCG@10 of 0.589, future-concept coverage of 0.721, and prerequisite violation rate of 0.031, and thus outperforms the best baseline on all three metrics. Ablation analysis shows that the prerequisite violation rate rises to 0.091 without constraints, and the learning gain drops to 0.104 without the learning gain term, respectively. Moreover, the full model still achieves better NDCG@10 performance on all learner history categories than other baselines, costing 0.84 s per learner with the memory peak of 13.6 GB. This research demonstrates the effectiveness of combining the generation of learning paths with pedagogical constraints.
evidence_items.title: Personalized Learning Path Optimization Based on Generative Artificial Intelligence

evidence_items.summary: Objective Clarify the effects of large-language-model types and health-education content categories on generated-text quality (patient-education suitability, overall quality) and readability, so as to provide empirical evidence for standardized AI-assisted health-communication applications. Methods This cross-sectional study was conducted between July 10 and July 15, 2026. Twenty herpes zoster-related questions were developed by a dermatologist and a pharmacist and categorized into five themes. The questions were then entered into five mainstream large language models (GPT-5, Doubao, DeepSeek, Qianwen, and Gemini), generating 100 textual responses. Response quality was assessed using the Chinese version of the Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool for Printable Materials (C-PEMAT-P) and Global Quality Score (GQS). Readability was evaluated via seven indices including the Automated Readability Index (ARI) and Flesch Reading Ease Score (FRES). Readability outcomes were compared using one-way repeated-measures analysis of variance with Greenhouse–Geisser correction. C-PEMAT-P raw totals and ordinal GQS scores were compared using Friedman tests. Post-hoc comparisons were adjusted using the Holm method. Category-level comparisons were performed using linear mixed-effects models with likelihood-ratio χ 2 tests for continuous outcomes and an ordinal generalized estimating equation with a Wald χ 2 test for GQS. Results Significant overall differences among models were observed for all seven readability indices and both assessment scores (all p &lt; 0.001). Median C-PEMAT-P raw total scores were 12.50, 11.00, 10.00, 9.00 and 9.00 for GPT-5, Doubao, DeepSeek, Qianwen and Gemini, respectively; corresponding median GQS scores were 5.00, 4.00, 4.00, 3.00, and 3.00. After Holm correction, GPT-5 achieved higher scores than each of the other models on both assessment measures.
evidence_items.title: Artificial intelligence chatbots as information sources for herpes zoster: an evaluation of patient-education suitability, overall quality, and readability
Structural Entanglement in Historical Benchmark Cases

evidence_items.summary: Background. Knowledge-graph models can rank existing drugs for a disease, but their benchmarks mostly reward rediscovering known treatments, and their scores rarely come with evidence a researcher can check. We built OREVID, an open tool that shows a ranked candidate only when an evidence line supports it and reports how often each line was right on held-out data, and compared it with TxGNN on identical data. Methods. The graph combines PrimeKG, Open Targets, STRING and PubTator3 (157,822 nodes, 9.46 million edges). For each disease, 22 degree-weighted metapath features and two gene-level columns (whether the drug moves its targets in the direction human genetics asks, from protein and expression QTLs that colocalise with the disease's genome-wide association studies, and whether it acts on a gene Orphanet lists for the disease) feed a LightGBM LambdaRank model trained with masked neighbourhoods. A candidate is shown only if it is indicated for an ontology-neighbour disease or for a disease sharing at least 3 associated genes (hypergeometric p < 10⁻⁵ over the genes with at least one associated disease). The acceptance criteria for these rules were set in advance; the rules were revised on the hidden-treatment benchmarks and then measured on an external set of approvals not used to choose them. TxGNN was retrained with its official code on the same PrimeKG splits, and all tasks and predictions are released as OREVID-bench. Results. Zero-shot Recall@100 (mean ± SD over five splits) was 0.812 ± 0.038 for OREVID, 0.412 ± 0.042 for TxGNN and 0.358 ± 0.040 for a popularity baseline, with OREVID ahead on every split (paired difference with TxGNN 0.400, 95% CI 0.354–0.444, resampling diseases). On nine disease areas held out it was 0.627 against 0.237, ahead in all nine, although TxGNN had the higher AUPRC in four. Training OREVID without validation labels and excluding diseases where TxGNN outputs constant scores gave 0.815 against 0.421.
evidence_items.title: OREVID: Open, Evidence-Based Drug Repurposing with a Benchmark Against TxGNN

organizations: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, Hong Kong. Part of this work was done while the author was at Huawei Taylor Lab.

evidence_items.summary: Abstract. We study revenue maximization in the unit-demand single-buyer setting. Our main result is that Uniform-Ironed-Virtual-Value Item Pricing guarantees a tight 3-approximation to Duality Relaxation Benchmark (Chawla, Malec, and Sivan, EC’10 and GEB’15; Cai, Devanur, and Weinberg, STOC’16 and [ SIAM J. Comput., 50 (2021), pp. STOC16-160–STOC16-200]), breaking the barrier of 4 since Chawla et al. [ Proceedings of STOC’10, 2010, pp. 311–320] and Chawla, Malec, and Sivan (EC’10 and GEB’15). To our knowledge, this is the first benchmark-tight revenue guarantee of any simple multi-item mechanism. Technically, all previous work employs Myerson Auction as an intermediary. The barrier of 4 follows as Uniform-Ironed-Virtual-Value Item Pricing achieves a tight 2-approximation to Myerson Auction , which then achieves a tight 2-approximation to Duality Relaxation Benchmark . Instead, our new approach avoids Myerson Auction , thus enabling the improvement. Central to our work are a benchmark-based 3-competitive prophet inequality and its fully constructive proof. Such prophet inequality variants will likely find applications in, e.g., multi-item mechanism design, when the optimal revenue objective is relaxed to various more accessible benchmarks. We complement our benchmark-tight ratio with an impossibility result. All previous works, including ours, follow the single-dimensional representative approach introduced by Chawla, Hartline, and Kleinberg [ Proceedings of EC’07, 2007, pp. 243–251]. Against Duality Relaxation Benchmark , it turns out that this approach cannot beat our bound of 3 for a large class of Item Pricing .
evidence_items.title: Benchmark-Tight Approximation Ratio of Simple Mechanism for a Unit-Demand Buyer

evidence_items.summary: Introduction Assessing residual contamination in coastal wetland soils after oil-well retirement requires comparisons with both active oil-well sites and natural reference wetlands. Methods We analyzed a September 2022 soil survey from the Liao River estuary wetlands in northeastern China, comprising five active oil-well plots, five retired oil-well plots, and three reference wetland plots. Three separately collected surface soil samples were averaged per plot, giving 13 independent analytical units. Soil properties, total petroleum hydrocarbons (TPHs), and five trace metals were compared among well-status groups. Results Mean TPH concentrations were 35.71 g/kg in active plots, 12.95 g/kg in retired plots, and 1.20 g/kg in reference plots (exact Kruskal–Wallis P &lt; 0.001; false-discovery-rate-adjusted q = 0.0015). Total organic carbon (TOC) followed the same ordering (43.15, 29.76, and 18.99 g/kg, respectively; P &lt; 0.001; q &lt; 0.001) and was positively associated with TPHs (Spearman rho = 0.76, P = 0.003). No overall group differences were detected for As, Cd, Cr, Cu, or Pb after multiple-testing correction, although one active plot showed locally elevated As, Cd, and Cr benchmark ratios. Discussion Retired plots had lower mean TPH concentrations than active plots, but all retired-plot values exceeded the reference range. These findings support monitoring residual petroleum contamination after oil-well retirement and targeted assessment of local metal enrichment.
evidence_items.title: Contrasting petroleum hydrocarbon contamination across active, retired and reference wetlands in the Liao River estuary

evidence_items.summary: Embodied foundation models now allow robots to act on open-ended instructions, yet success on long-horizon physical tasks also depends on the runtime around the model, which organizes the task, invokes skills, guards execution, and retains experience. Digital agent research treats this runtime, known as the harness, as a first-class design object that can be engineered and even improved from experience, since the same model can perform very differently under different harnesses. Such harness designs do not carry over directly, because physical execution is embodiment-specific, partially observed, time-constrained, and often irreversible, which also makes experience costly to learn from. Embodied AI systems increasingly build similar runtimes, yet the field still lacks a unified view of them. This survey treats the physical agentic harness as a research object in its own right. We define it as the runtime system that maintains task and execution state for an embodied foundation model and mediates the model’s interaction with the physical world through one or more physical bodies. We then review over 200 works and organize them by six functional responsibilities: task orchestration, digital resources, embodied capabilities, execution governance, digital-physical interaction, and persistent evolution. This organization offers a common lens for comparing methods across communities, making explicit how model decisions reach physical execution and how grounded evidence flows back. The reviewed benchmarks and applications provide limited evidence of individual runtime contributions, particularly the effects of execution governance and sustained gains from persistent evolution. We close with open problems in model-harness co-design, capability composition, real-time decision making, distributed execution, and continual improvement from physical experience.
evidence_items.title: Where the Harness Meets the Physical World: A Survey of the Physical Agentic Harness

evidence_items.summary: The convergence of large language models (LLMs), federated learning (FL), and edge computing offers a pathway to autonomous decision systems that can reason near data sources while limiting reliance on centralized infrastructure. Edge-deployed LLMs can support latency-sensitive and privacy-conscious applications, although their computational demands challenge resource-constrained devices. FL enables collaborative adaptation without directly pooling private data, but heterogeneous devices, non-identically distributed data, and communication constraints complicate training. This paper proposes an agentic edge-intelligence framework that combines local LLM inference, federated model adaptation, and multi-agent coordination for sensing, planning, and decision execution. The framework identifies interfaces among reasoning, learning, and edge-resource management, and articulates design considerations for privacy, communication efficiency, and device heterogeneity. It provides a systems-oriented basis for developing and evaluating autonomous edge applications under practical network and resource constraints.
evidence_items.title: Agentic Edge Intelligence: Integrating Large Language Models, Federated Learning, and Edge Computing for Autonomous Decision Systems

evidence_items.summary: Physical reasoning underpins how embodied systems understand and act in the physical world, yet vision-language models (VLMs) remain unreliable on questions about dynamics and physical causality. Progress is critically constrained by the scarcity of grounded counterfactual training data, as observational videos capture only the factual trajectory that occurred. The self-evolving paradigm offers a route beyond fixed datasets by enabling models to construct their own training problems. Extending this paradigm to physics, however, requires an external source of truth that can both validate model-proposed environments and verify alternative physical outcomes under intervention. We introduce , a verifier-grounded self-evolving framework that trains VLMs for causal physical reasoning from model-proposed executable worlds and simulation-authored tasks. At each round, a shared VLM proposes executable world programs and evidence schemas; a deterministic physics engine freezes each valid world, simulates matched baseline and body-elided counterfactual branches, and synthesizes discrete, answer-bound visual tasks. Exact verifier feedback from task solving updates both the shared policy via GRPO and an adaptive curriculum over physical intents. Starting from Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct,  achieves targeted gains across PhysBench, CausalPhys, and ContPhy without human intervention data, improving PhysBench Throwing by 8.8 points and ContPhy Counterfactual Removal and Goal-Pit by 7.4 and 24.4 points. These gains concentrate on interaction-sensitive and altered-world questions, demonstrating zero-shot transfer of causal principles to unseen complex dynamics (cloth, fluid, soft bodies) and real-world video.
evidence_items.title: PhysEvolve: Verifier-grounded Self-evolution for Physical Reasoning with Executable Worlds
